items.articleBody:
Wer Graham Coxon und Blur liebt oder wer gern Fuzz und Overdrive in eine brachiale Wall-of-Sound verbrät, wird den Catalinbread Cold One lieben. Kratzigkaputter Lead-Sound, wie man ihn ihn Brit-Pop-Hymnen wie „Song 2“ hören konnte, ist damit ein Leichtes. 

Alles über das neue Pedal

Eiskalte Zerre: Der Catalinbread Cold One

Wie ist der Workflow des Catalinbread Cold One? 

Was kostet der Catalinbread Cold One? 

Infos über das neue Pedal von Catalinbread

Eiskalte Zerre: Der Catalinbread Cold One

Gleich drei Zerrgeschmäcker bringt der Catalinbread Cold One mit. Grundsätzlich ist das Pedal eine Hommage an den DOD Punkifier, ein Overdrive-Fuzz-Monster aus den Neunzigern, das, ähnlich wie der Boss Metal Zone, einige fanatische Anhänger und viele ratlose Zweifler hatte.

Und wie so oft wird ein Effekt über die Zeit gerade weil er eher ungewöhnlich und nicht wie der hundertste Klon klingt dann doch irgendwie Kult. Das scheint Catalinbread so beobachtet zu haben und zeigt den Cold One. 

Man muss schon sagen, der Hersteller ist beim Demovideo schon sehr auf Blur getrimmt. Hier wird „Song 2“ (kennen die Älteren von uns wahrscheinlich noch vom Soundtrack von FIFA 98). Von cremigem Drive bis zu komplett kaputtem Glitch-Fuzz bietet das Pedal 

Wie ist der Workflow des Catalinbread Cold One? 

Drei Zerren – drei Regler, dazu Tone-Poti mit High- und Low-Shelf-Filter und Ausgangspegel (Volume) – that’s it. Aber wenn man sich das Video in der zweiten Hälfte ansieht, wird man hören, welche Bandbreite an Zerrsounds im Pedal steckt

Catalinbread Cold One · Quelle: Catalinbread

Mit dem Gain-Regler, wie man es kennt, dreht man den Distortion-Anteil auf. Beim Fuzz-Regler bestimmt man die Mischung zwischen Distortion und Fuzz. Diese beiden Regler zusammen mit Tone und Volume werden die kennen, die mit dem Punkifier vertraut sind. 

Ganz neu dabei ist der Glitch-Regler. Hier wechselt man stufenlos zwischen dem Haus-Fuzz und einem kaputten Arpeggio-Glitch-Fuzz. Alle drei, Distortion, Fuzz und Glich lassen sich über die drei Regler zu einem ganz individuellen Sound mischen – oder auf Wunsch auch separat nutzen. Also nur den Drive oder nur den Fuzz. 

Was kostet der Catalinbread Cold One?

items.title: Why We Should All Put Down Our Smartphones
items.subtitle: These days, we use the word “available” to refer primarily to digital availability, i.e., how quickly a person replies to texts or emails.

items.articleBody:
These days, we use the word “available” to refer primarily to digital availability, i.e., how quickly a person replies to texts or emails. Is there someone you could text right now and be sure of an immediate reply? This type of person is often less available in real life, because they’re so dedicated to maintaining their digital life.

In public spaces, availability is rare. Almost no one is attuned to their surroundings or open to conversation, receptive to subtle social and environmental cues. I was riding an airport bus recently when I realized I didn’t know which terminal to get off at. In a panic, I turned to the man next to me, who happened to be wearing an airport uniform. I began to speak before noticing that he was wearing noise-canceling earbuds and watching a basketball game on his phone. Sure, I could have tapped him on the shoulder, but my time was limited—and hadn’t he made it clear he didn’t want to interact with me?

Availability makes you a public resource, someone to ask for advice and directions, someone to commiserate with when the weather is bad or the flight is delayed, someone to keep an eye on someone’s luggage or dog while they run to the bathroom.

Even if an available person is never called upon to help, their latent availability nonetheless improves the atmosphere for everyone present. It is far more pleasant to share a space with someone who, however subtly, acknowledges that you exist.

The unavailability of others is so disturbing, so disabling that our only defense is to become unavailable ourselves.

Those times when you are called upon to assist a stranger, you’ll feel a surge of pride. You made a difference in someone’s day, reinforcing their faith in the goodness of strangers. The more we talk to each other, the less we have to fear.

In spaces of universal digital absorption, we don’t talk to each other at all. Eyes never meet. There is no spontaneity, just stasis.

Waiting rooms should be alive with books and games and conversation, as opposed to the silent, self-contained tapping and listening that predominates in our day and age. Humans thrive in community. When we’re unavailable, we rarely emerge from our sensory isolation for long enough to feel meaningfully connected.

Yet we are not willing to make ourselves available. Two questions:

Would you prefer to visit a public space free of screens and noise-canceling headphones?

Are you willing to forgo digital media next time you’re on the train, at the doctor’s office, or waiting in a checkout line?

Most people will answer yes to the first and no to the second. This is not purely due to screen addiction; it’s because we can find nothing better to look at than our screens. We have built a society in which the smartphone is sometimes the least depressing and most stimulating thing in a public space. Ours is a society in which those intrepid few who are willing to engage with their surroundings will find no eyes or ears to receive them.

Ironically, looking at screens is how we tune out the sad state of our public spaces. We can’t bear to face a crowd of indifferent souls. It’s mass rejection. The unavailability of others is so disturbing, so disabling that our only defense is to become unavailable ourselves.

*

I’ve begun to think of social unavailability as a cycle of rejection. At restaurants, I often observe couples locked in this cycle. Person X might be in the middle of telling a story when Person Y takes out their phone; X continues speaking for a few more seconds until they become aware that Y is distracted; then X trails off and takes out their own phone; then Y finishes their phone task and looks up, only to find X distracted. Y waits for a moment before picking up their phone again, and the cycle continues.

In scenarios like this, our phones let us appear less idle, more in demand. They mitigate our boredom and isolation. They soothe our pain. They return the insult.

We reject the world as a way to cope with feelings of rejection. We reject, and we are rejected. No one pays attention to us, and we pay attention to no one, and the world becomes a hostile place, and the internet becomes, by contrast, a soothing oasis in which pain cannot touch us—but neither can anything real.

Without a smartphone, I cannot participate in the cycle of rejection. I still witness it. When my friends use their smartphones, I just sit there, looking like I’m trying to prove a point. It makes everyone uncomfortable.

What if I were to pull out a book during a meal and start reading it while my friends awaited my return to reality? This would clearly be unacceptable. A smartphone should be no different.

If you choose to downgrade, you will discover that these smartphone checks take far longer than you think. What might feel like a few seconds to the user is in actuality a long interlude of silent tapping. It’s uncomfortable to wait out these moments, but complaining can inspire resentment. If you want to break the cycle of rejection without damaging your relationships, then the best thing you can do is quietly model an alternative.

*

Even when you don’t complain about others’ smartphone use, the very fact of your abstinence might leave them feeling judged.

Your relationship to technology says something about your relationship to the world. It’s not pleasant to be shamed for that.

One unanticipated effect of my public activism efforts is that people now feel embarrassed about using their smartphones in front of me. “Sorry, I know you probably hate this,” they say as they look up directions or type out a message. “You’re fine!” I say, “it doesn’t bother me at all.” This isn’t strictly true: it does bother me that smartphones are so ubiquitous—especially when the majority of my acquaintances claim to hate them. But adopting a hard line, superior attitude won’t convince anyone to quit. It hasn’t worked with other addictions, so why would it work with this one?

When people are unprepared to make a change, when they perhaps do not even realize that change is possible, the best thing you can do is share your own journey: how you felt before, what you did, and how you felt after. This gives your listener space to reflect on the subject without any outside pressure.

Overt judgment breeds defensiveness. In my early twenties, I dated a man who used a flip phone and vocally disapproved of my social media work. Much of my internal monologue during those months was devoted to making my case: I needed a smartphone to earn money; consistent posting kept my numbers up; the guy had a salaried teaching job and I was a struggling artist; how dare he judge me! Long before I was ready to see it, this man noted that my smartphone had made me miserable. Only years after the relationship ended did I arrive at the exact same conclusion.*

Technology is a delicate subject. It’s personal and political, local and global. Your relationship to technology says something about your relationship to the world. It’s not pleasant to be shamed for that, even if you know deep down that you are failing yourself.

Let’s say your partner has a scrolling habit that detracts from quality time. Addressing this head-on, in the moment, could come across as combative. Your partner might retort “I’m doing something important,” or “I’ve already watched this movie, so I don’t need to pay attention,” or “Please just let me unwind after work.”

People do not tend to respond well to immediate feedback, and this can also place undue emphasis on one instance rather than a broader trend. So if you’re going to bring up someone’s phone use, I recommend doing so in a relaxed and screen-free moment. That way, it’ll feel less like an attack than an open discussion about how technology has affected the relationship.

When you do bring it up, try to focus on how you feel when the other person chooses their device over you. Say that you value presence and listening. Take accountability for the times you yourself have been distracted (for whatever reason) and haven’t met the other’s needs. Make it about fostering a stronger, safer bond all around. Discuss shared values and hopes for the future.

Rethink the very nature of quality time: maybe it will revolve less around tech. Maybe you’ll want to try new activities together. Maybe you’ll want to leave your phones behind, whether for a hike or a meal or for good.

* To my great disappointment, when I reached out to him last year to say thank you, he told me he had upgraded to a smartphone.

______________________________

items.title: Doctor Who’s Tom Baker Plays Douglas Adams’ Digital “Agent” in the AI-Predicting Hyperland (1990)
items.subtitle: Cast your mind, if you will, back to the year 2020.
items.feedText: It now feels like a different time, what with the spreading COVID-19 pandemic and the heated sociopolitical battles being waged online, and indeed in the (socially distanced) streets. items.articleBody:
Cast your mind, if you will, back to the year 2020. It now feels like a different time, what with the spreading COVID-19 pandemic and the heated sociopolitical battles being waged online, and indeed in the (socially distanced) streets. That spring, we featured here on Open Culture an amusing retro-technological diversion called Hyperland. First broadcast on BBC2, the program stars The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy author Douglas Adams as himself and Doctor Who’s Tom Baker as his agent. “You want fifteen percent?” the former asks the latter when they first meet in a vast wasteland of flickering television sets. Not at all: “I’m here to do your every slightest bidding,” Baker explains, “to fetch and carry for you, to work tirelessly and selflessly on your behalf, always ready, always willing, no job too small or too menial.”

Today, we can hardly share in Adams’ bewilderment, familiar as we are with the notion of what Baker calls a “software agent,” an “artificial and completely customizable personality” with “instant access to every piece of information stored digitally anywhere in the world: any picture or film, any sound, any book, any statistic, any fact, any connection between anything you care to think of.” We must remind ourselves that Hyperland was produced in 1990, when these lines would have struck all but the most computer-savvy and forward-looking viewers as sheer science fiction. Even three decades thereafter, they still sounded more or less like an elevated version of ordinary late-twentieth-century techno-optimism. Here in 2026, Baker’s services are close to being considered a basic necessity, at least in Silicon Valley and its global provinces.

Not so very long ago, Hyperland looked startlingly prescient about the rise of the World Wide Web, which would soon let its users seek out their own desired pieces of information and media, actively moving through links between them, in a manner unlike the passive viewing experience of television (with which it would, as no one then knew, one day converge). This was an unfamiliar idea to most people in 1990; hence the variety of clear and entertaining ways in which the program breaks down its technological basis, pulling up clips from its onscreen “database” like an interview with Ted Nelson, who coined the term hypertext. Like multimedia, that word may carry a whiff of antiquity today, but it was once on the lips of practically every technologist in popular culture — in a manner reminiscent of the lexicon that has sprung from new developments in artificial intelligence over the past few years.

At times, Baker’s character now looks almost realistic, as when Adams asks him to knock off the obsequiousness, or when he pulls up Kurt Vonnegut’s theory of story form before Adams fully gets the question out. Yet Hyperland devotes little time to AI per se. The program appeared in the wake of the eighties’ AI boom, when “expert systems” promised to solve problems in industry, medicine, and other sectors, but many of the field’s larger ambitions went unrealized. There followed a long “AI winter” in research and development, in whose climate Baker-as-“agent” would have been a means of humanizing an abstract-seeming concept of organizing and navigating information. Not that all his enthusiastically proffered services draw unqualified enthusiasm from Adams, who possessed a rare combination of Californian technophilia and British skepticism. His fascination with humanity’s digital future is ours — and so is his wariness.

items.articleBody:
by Jeremy Moss and Machina

Four Hands is a column about writing with machines, made the way it describes. The ideas, the direction and the decisions about what survives are mine; the prose is developed in dialogue with AI systems, principally Claude and ChatGPT, which I address collectively as Machina.

I am grateful for the detectors, which will sound unfashionable in the circles I have lately been keeping. I am grateful in the way one is grateful for a good lock, or a receipt, or a witness.

For some time now the question of who wrote a thing has been a matter of testimony, which is to say a matter of trust, which is to say not a matter at all. A writer says: I wrote this. And what is the reader to do with that? Nod? The whole arrangement was intolerable and nobody said so, because saying so would have insulted a profession that runs almost entirely on the honor system and a certain amount of flattering silence.

Then came the instrument. Pangram is, by the account of people who have tested it seriously, extraordinarily good. Vauhini Vara, who has covered AI for nearly a decade, reported in The Atlantic this month that by the company’s own figure it mislabels human writing about once in 24,000 cases. She also noted how many literary prizes still decline to use it. Of course they do. It works.

I decided to test it on myself, in a spirit of what I would call rigor if I were being generous with myself and vanity if I were not.

I began with a novel I wrote this year in sustained collaboration with a language model. The instrument returned one hundred percent. I felt the small, clean satisfaction of a hypothesis confirmed. The machine had written much of the prose, the machine’s fingerprints were on the prose, and the instrument found them.

Then a philosophical essay, four thousand words, worked over across weeks. I had cut a rhetorical tic from it four separate times. I had rebuilt an entire section after discovering the anecdote it rested on was a known artifact. I had added two passages in response to an objection from my father, who is a philosopher and does not flatter me. I had rewritten the opening after learning that a phrase I believed we had discovered together had in fact been mine, from an essay written alone months earlier, and handed back to me.

Ninety-nine percent.

What I felt at that number surprised me. It was the pleasure of consistency. Two texts, two verdicts, both correct. A ninety-nine is the instrument saying yes, and I am nearly certain. So the instrument was nearly certain. And it was right. The machine had been in the room for both.

Then the letter that ran in the Los Angeles Review of Books, in which I argued that the ethical question about AI writing turns on whether the machine’s touch was concealed. One hundred percent.

Then a second essay, submitted to a journal that had asked me to describe my AI use in detail, which I did, at length, unprompted. One hundred percent.

Four for four.

And then, because a control is the mark of a serious experiment, a lyric essay I wrote entirely by myself, about my mother’s death and a voice I once buried inside a record until nobody could find it.

One hundred percent human.

Five for five. I am not sure I have ever seen an instrument perform so well.

The result tells us that four of my texts contain machine-generated prose and one does not. This is true. This is precisely and verifiably true, and I would not have believed any instrument could establish it so cleanly.

I have been trying to think of a comparable achievement and I keep arriving at the metal detector, which finds metal. It finds it every time. It finds the coins in your pocket and the pin in your grandmother’s hip and the buckle on your belt, and it finds them with a fidelity that would have astonished the eighteenth century. What it has never once found is a dangerous man. The commission was metal, and metal is what it delivers, and we have built an entire architecture of airports and courthouses and school entrances around a machine that does exactly what it says and nothing whatsoever that we want.

Or the polygraph, which is my favorite of the flawless instruments, because it is genuinely quite good at what it measures. It measures arousal. Pulse, respiration, the conductance of a palm. It measures these things accurately and consistently, and in its long career it has never once measured a lie, because a lie lives in the relation between what a person says and what a person knows. The needle cannot reach that. So the needle reports arousal, and a man in a room translates arousal into deception, and the translation is where everything goes wrong, and we have convicted people on the strength of that translation for the better part of a century.

Or the field sobriety test, or the credit score, or the standardized examination, each of which measures something real with admirable precision and is then asked, by people in a hurry, to stand in for something it has no access to at all. The score is real. The inference is the invention.

I raise these as company for the instrument. Pangram belongs to a distinguished tradition of machines that work.

Picture an editor. She has a manuscript she has read twice and liked both times. She runs it, because her house has a policy now, and the number comes back ninety-eight. She schedules a call.

What does she say?

She cannot say you used AI, because she does not know that. She knows the prose carries a signature. She says something more careful. She says the manuscript was flagged.

And the writer says: flagged by what?

This is the first difficulty. She must now explain that an instrument has made an observation about his sentences, and that the observation is very reliable, and that she is not accusing him of anything, and that she would like him to account for it. She is asking a man to explain the texture of his own prose. He has been writing for thirty years. He has never once had to account for why his sentences sound the way they do.

He says: I wrote it.

Now she is in real trouble, because that is exactly what he would say if it were true, and exactly what he would say if it were not, and the instrument has given her no way to tell those apart. She has spent a great deal of institutional capital acquiring a tool whose entire promise was that she would not have to weigh a man’s word, and she is now weighing a man’s word.

So she pushes. Can you send me your drafts?

And he says yes, of course, and he does, within the hour, because he has them. Six versions. A folder of notes. A file called NOTES ON THE SISTER that runs eleven pages and contains three different deaths for her.

The editor reads all of it. It is exactly what a working writer’s mess looks like. It is also exactly what a careful concealer would produce, if he had thought ahead, and this one might have. She cannot tell. The drafts have a signature too, if she wanted to run them, and she does not want to run them, because she knows what the number will say and she knows it will not help.

She could ask him directly. She could say: did you use a machine, and how, and where. And he would answer, and his answer would be testimony, and she would either believe him or not, and the believing would rest on his tone, on whether he sounded offended in the right way, on a career’s worth of hunches about men on telephones.

Which is what she was doing before the instrument. Which is what the instrument was purchased to replace.

She buys the book. Or she doesn’t. Either way she will not know, and she will publish or decline on the strength of something she could not name in a memo, and the number will sit in the file, accurate, useless, waiting for someone to cite it.

I find this less troubling than I expected to. The instrument has performed flawlessly. It has told her precisely what it knows, which is what the sentences look like, and it has declined to invent anything further.

*

Postscript: Since I drafted this, the hypothetical in it stopped being hypothetical. In September, in an essay for the publishing newsletter Publishing Confidential, the novelist Jerry Falade described how a journalist submitted his unpublished manuscript to AI-detection software “without my knowledge or consent,” and how he lost his agent soon after. He says he wrote the novel himself, drawing on Yorùbá oral storytelling traditions. I don’t know what the instrument found. I know that whatever it found was treated as a finding about a man.

items.articleBody:
_____________
THE PLACE
Pyeongtaek,
South Korea

Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring.

It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. 

They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes. 

In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. 

Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. 

Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. 

Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

items.articleBody:
Beatrice Caciotti for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, Hawaii News Now, South Carolina Department of Transportation.

On March 3, 2020, Sen. Lindsey Graham walked into a private dining room at Charlie Palmer Steak in Washington, D.C. Graham’s time was expensive. He was meeting with two executives and a lobbyist from a Hawaiian naval defense contractor called Navatek. And he had required them to commit to $40,000 in campaign contributions for a 45-minute meeting.

Navatek’s CEO, Martin Kao, was confident that was all the time he needed.

“Shoot all he has to really do is stop by and say ‘yes,’” Kao wrote to a Navatek lobbyist and a fellow executive the day before, in an email seen by ProPublica. “That should only take a minute and he’s on his way. We don’t need to pretend we give a shit about each other.”

At the dinner, Graham ate little and talked a lot. But Kao got the “yes” he was hoping for: Graham agreed to steer a $10 million government contract Navatek’s way in his native South Carolina, Kao later recounted to the FBI. In exchange, he said, Graham asked Kao to pledge a total of $100,000 to his reelection campaign.

“Paper Trail” Podcast

Hear the reporters discuss their reporting on the FBI on ”Paper Trail.”

In early 2025, the FBI opened a sweeping investigation into bribery on Capitol Hill with Graham’s steakhouse dinner at the center. Kao confessed to federal agents that his business model consisted of bribing public officials in exchange for government contracts, and that the research Navatek was providing to the government was often worthless.

The scheme involved some of the most powerful figures in Congress, he said — in both parties. In South Carolina, Kao told agents, Navatek made a campaign cash-for-contracts deal not only with Graham, but also with the state’s top Democrat, Rep. James Clyburn, and another influential Republican, Rep. Joe Wilson.

Kao told agents that Graham in particular left little room for ambiguity: “This is how much I want, and how much I am going to give you,” Kao remembered Graham saying, according to notes one agent took during their debrief in late 2024.

Kao’s admissions would constitute a vast criminal bribery scheme if they could be proved in court — a challenge, given recent Supreme Court rulings that have made it more difficult to win corruption cases. Kao himself posed another hurdle. He was facing prison for fraud and campaign finance violations and was speaking to the FBI in the hopes of reducing his sentence.

But the FBI agents who took Kao’s confession — two experienced anti-corruption investigators — could see that much of it lined up with a trove of records they had seized from Navatek. They forged ahead. The FBI took the formal step of naming two former Navatek executives who had worked with Kao as subjects of a bribery investigation. The agency did not designate Graham, Clyburn and Wilson that way, but the agents were actively investigating their interactions with Kao. The agents indicated to their superiors that the lawmakers could become subjects in the future, according to records viewed by ProPublica.

The details of this investigation have not previously been reported.

President Donald Trump returned to the White House and almost immediately gutted the specialized FBI and Department of Justice teams dedicated to taking on public corruption — an act of revenge for having previously investigated him. The two experienced agents on the case were swept up in the purge, and the career prosecutor assisting them quit after Trump appointees forbid the DOJ’s anti-corruption section from filing any new cases. Today, there is no one left to look into Kao’s explosive allegations, as the Trump administration has abandoned any pretense of prosecuting public corruption. The case is dead.

ProPublica has unearthed the investigation by reviewing thousands of pages of legal documents, internal company emails, evidence the FBI used to vet Kao’s claims and dozens of interviews with people who saw how Navatek operated, including an eyewitness to Graham and Kao’s secret steakhouse dinner.

This story is part of a series based on our reporting. Last month, ProPublica reported that the FBI had probed the conduct of Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who steered millions in government funding toward Navatek while Kao gave her illegal campaign donations. Collins denied wrongdoing and dismissed Kao as a “convicted liar.”

Kao is indeed the only person involved to serve prison time. He pleaded guilty to making illegal campaign donations and a loan fraud scheme in 2022. In 2025, he was sentenced to 87 months in prison.

Graham died at 71 earlier this year. His sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill his seat, retained most of his senior staff, including those who dealt with Navatek. She even took up some of his committee assignments, including appropriations. Darline Graham is running for a full term in office this November.

Clyburn, 86, is one of the most powerful Democrats in Washington. He is widely credited with tipping the scales for Joe Biden during the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Wilson remains influential on national defense spending from his senior perch on the Armed Services Committee.

James Clyburn, left, and Lindsey Graham speak during an event at the White House to celebrate the 2023-24 University of South Carolina Gamecocks NCAA women’s basketball championship team. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

“Whatever a donor may think or say, a donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Jami LaRue, Clyburn’s communications director, wrote in response to detailed questions. “The Congressman has always striven to assist the University of South Carolina and all of the colleges and universities in his district when called upon to further their important missions. The crimes and lies of an imprisoned fraudster will not cause the Congressman to waver in his support for these fine institutions.”

David Snider, Wilson’s communications director, did not address a detailed list of questions sent by ProPublica. “Congressman Wilson does and has always abided by campaign donation regulations set forth by the Federal Election Commission,” Snider said in an email.

In an emailed statement, Taylor Reidy, who was Lindsey Graham’s communications director and now holds the same post for his sister, wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior or wrongdoing by the late Senator Lindsey Graham or his staff are simply false.” She said the accusations were the “ravings of a convicted felon” and that her office was never contacted by the FBI about the matter. After Kao’s arrest, they disgorged his donations, she added.

The two executives who were subjects of the FBI investigation, Duke Hartman and Joshua Knight, were never charged. Hartman, the other executive at the dinner meeting with Graham, is now the CEO of a new naval research company called Integer Technologies that he co-founded with Knight after Kao’s arrest. Integer was recently recognized as one of the fastest-growing government contractors in the country. It also became the ultimate beneficiary of the Graham dinner meeting, picking up the contract Graham allegedly agreed to facilitate that night.

Hartman and Knight did not respond to detailed requests for comment.

“[It’s] corruption at its best,” Kao wrote to ProPublica from federal detention in South Dakota, before cutting off contact. “But I am the only one rotting in prison.”

Small Company, Big Ambitions

Kao’s dinner with Graham was part of his grandiose plan to make Navatek a major defense contractor.

He had become the CEO at an uncertain moment in the company’s history. Founded in Hawaii in the 1970s, the company originally thrived on a close relationship with the state’s powerful senior senator, Daniel Inouye. When Kao assumed ownership in 2019, it had been several years since Inouye had died, and Navatek was in need of a new patron in Washington.

At times, Kao hardly seemed the person to pull this off. He had started out as the company’s CFO and was openly uninterested in its technology. He told bombastic lies about his personal life. Former employees said he regaled them with tales of selling newspapers for members of the Bloods and Crips street gangs as a youth. In a deposition, Kao later admitted that wasn’t true.

But what he lacked in engineering chops he made up with ambition. Once, Kao held a company town hall using a map of the U.S. dotted with future Navatek offices as his backdrop, a former employee recalled. “He would talk about how we’re a $10 million company, and in the next three years, we’re going to be a billion-dollar company,” said a former engineer. “He was an absolute megalomaniac.”

Kao hatched a plan to expand Navatek’s presence across the country, making new friends in Congress along the way. He courted politicians using something he called “the method,” as ProPublica detailed in September.

Navatek would open an office in the state or district of a powerful member of Congress and partner with a local university to concoct a proposal for federally funded research. Then, aided by a well-connected lobbyist and the sheen of credibility from its association with the university, Navatek would approach the member for federal research funding.

Kao told the FBI he would strike deals in small, face-to-face meetings with the members or their trusted staff. Navatek — through executives, family members and lobbyists — would make generous campaign donations. In exchange, the member would add detailed language to the defense budget to fund the company’s work.

That legislative language would not name the company. But it would describe specific work that Navatek was already planning to do behind the scenes, making it the only logical choice for the eventual government contract. The lawmakers’ staff would also backchannel with the Navy after the bill was passed to make sure contracting offices knew to direct the money to Navatek, emails seen by ProPublica show — even though the contracts were in theory competitive.

Kao “wanted to build a company as big as he could as fast as he could,” a former executive later testified in court. For a while, he succeeded. Under Kao, Navatek went from having to “rebuild,” as the executive put it, to winning $40.7 million in new government contracts in 2020.

Hartman, the other Navatek executive who went to dinner with Graham, was in charge of maintaining friendly ties in Congress while tracking the millions of dollars the company had requested in research funds. He kept careful tabs on the company’s progress using dozens of color-coded spreadsheets. “If anyone knows the impropriety of the business model, it’s him,” Kao told the FBI, referring to Hartman.

Later, these spreadsheets provided the FBI a detailed picture of which congressional offices worked closest with Navatek. In the tables devoted to South Carolina, Navatek denoted Graham as a “key supporter.”

The company primarily targeted lawmakers from smaller states who sat on appropriations committees, like Collins, Kao explained to the FBI, because they wielded huge power over the budget while having fewer “constituents to ‘feed.’”

The senior senator from South Carolina was another prime target. “You can get access to Lindsey Graham,” Eric Schiff, a former Navatek executive, said in an interview.

Kao, Hartman and other Navatek executives approached the offices of Graham, Clyburn and Wilson — all powerful members of the South Carolina delegation — in the beginning of 2019. The company had recruited the University of South Carolina for a joint research project, and together they asked the lawmakers to find $9.5 million to fund the work. If it succeeded, Navatek planned to ask Congress to re-up the funding for two more years as well as green-light two more projects, internal company records show, for a total of up to $90 million in South Carolina alone.

Yet Navatek had “zero people” capable of doing the research it was pitching, said a former executive with direct knowledge of the work.

Its $9.5 million “power and energy” proposal promised cutting-edge research on how to distribute the limited power on board a ship between multiple energy-intense systems, like radars, lasers and rail guns. Graham’s office later boasted that the work would lead to new technology that would “ensure that our fleet is ready for the fights of the future.”

In reality, Navatek’s initial research “looked like a college senior’s graduation project,” the executive said. “Something you go get from RadioShack.” Graham’s office referred questions about the quality of the work to the Navy and the university. The Office of Naval Research, which awarded the contract, did not respond to questions.

A Navatek amphibious vehicle prototype heads to shore during a Marine Corps experiment in Hawaii in 2014. Lance Cpl. Aaron S. Patterson/U.S. Marine Corps

But for Congress, that lack of expertise wasn’t a problem. Throughout 2019, the FBI noted, as the ensuing year’s budget came together, both Graham’s and Clyburn’s offices took steps to make sure it included Navatek’s funding.

In May 2019, Willie Lyles III, Clyburn’s legislative director, alerted Navatek that the House Appropriations Committee would endorse new funding for a “modular and scalable integrated power and thermal system capable of powering a directed energy weapon system of 100 or more kilowatts,” according to an email flagged by the FBI. Three days later, that exact language appeared in the House Appropriations Committee report. Lyles did not reply to a request for comment.

In September, the Senate Appropriations Committee — Graham’s committee — released a budget report that set aside $9.5 million in funding for “Talent and Technology for Navy Power and Energy Systems.” Agents noted that Navatek may have ghostwritten the technical description that accompanied this line item because “an almost identical paragraph” appeared in Hartman’s internal spreadsheets two months before the Senate report became public.

After the Senate advanced its version of the budget in the fall, Navatek dropped $4,799 to send bourbon to a handful of lawmakers, including Graham and Collins, the FBI found in company records — a likely violation of Senate gift rules. Both Collins’ and Graham’s offices denied receiving bourbon. Navatek later sent Clyburn a fruit basket from Edible Arrangements for $102.60.

Congress passed the final spending bill containing $9.5 million for Navatek’s pet project on Dec. 19, 2019.

At that point, Kao and other Navatek executives had not made any donations to Clyburn, Wilson or even Graham.

That would change within days of Congress passing the budget, when an executive pledged $750 to Wilson’s campaign at a fundraiser held at Bullfeathers, a Capitol Hill watering hole for lobbyists and Hill staffers, emails show. In the following weeks, Kao and his lobbyist gave Wilson’s campaign $3,500.

And bigger checks were imminent. Kao kicked off 2020 by making plans to spend $300,000 at a slew of political fundraisers, according to text messages filed in court and a recent deposition. Navatek’s lobbyists at that time were seeking private meetings with Graham, Wilson and Clyburn, where Kao planned to ask for significantly more federal funding. Kao eventually met with all three, and each asked for $100,000, he told the FBI.

During that same period, Kao and Hartman met a top fundraiser for Collins at a Corner Bakery in Washington, D.C. As ProPublica reported, that meeting led Kao to donate $150,000 to the pro-Collins super PAC. Kao told the FBI that the money was a bribe in exchange for the senator’s support for more Navatek funding. The head of the super PAC and Collins have denied Kao’s version of events.

Kao told the FBI it was not unusual for donations to come after the favor: “We became clever in our own right and figured out how to dangle the carrot,” he wrote in a memo seen by ProPublica, “until we saw some assurance that the Ask was in the budget.”

To secure a meeting with Graham, Kao hired Michael Tongour, a veteran South Carolina lobbyist who was old law school friends with the senator and family friends with Clyburn and Wilson. Graham was up for reelection against a well-funded challenger, Jaime Harrison, and had a crowded fundraising schedule, said Tongour, but they eventually found a time.

“The Graham fundraiser says that it [sic] you want to reserve a date for Senator Graham to attend a private dinner, the campaign wants to get $40,000 in contributions,” Tongour wrote to Kao, Hartman and lobbyist Andy Winer, in an undated email seen by ProPublica. Winer, whom Kao described as Navatek’s chief lobbyist, chimed in to say that Graham could stay only 45 minutes, and Kao replied that all they needed to hear was “yes.”

“These discussions are very frank and oddly not at all awkward,” Kao told the FBI. “I suppose once we got that far, everyone knows the deal.”

A Dinner With Graham

Graham showed up late to his March 3, 2020, dinner with Kao, Hartman and Tongour. A fundraiser working for Graham appeared first and accepted an envelope from Kao containing checks made out to Graham’s campaign, Kao said. Kao did not know the fundraiser’s name; in an FBI debrief, he simply referred to the person as the “money man.” After that person departed, Graham entered.

Graham, Kao recalled to the FBI, was “very abrupt” and “straight to the point”: He asked how much Navatek wanted, to which they said $10 million a year for three years. Graham asked Kao to pledge $100,000 in donations in exchange for his support, Kao told the FBI.

Navatek was juggling multiple proposals in South Carolina worth around $10 million, and it’s not clear which one Kao was describing.

Congress had just approved the $9.5 million for the power and energy project, but Navatek still needed the Navy to award the money in the form of a contract. The company was also about to ask Congress to fund the same project for a second year at $10.5 million. On top of that, Navatek was planning to pitch a new research proposal, at $10 million, to study the transport of supplies inland from ships using autonomous vehicles. It was another area where Navatek had “zero past performance,” the former executive said.

The same week of the steakhouse dinner, Graham’s office was working behind the scenes with Navatek and the University of South Carolina to make sure the Navy sent the first $9.5 million to the right company.

A day before the dinner, an official with the Office of Naval Research emailed Graham’s office to ask about the money, which “the Senator may have an interest in.” Craig Abele, Graham’s national security adviser, called her a few days later to confirm that Graham’s office had intended the money to be awarded to the Navatek partnership, emails show. “Spoke to ONR this morning,” Abele wrote March 6. “Should be set.”

The company received the contract, which it split with the university, in July 2020. 

Abele became Graham’s deputy chief of staff and still holds the position for Darline. He did not reply to an email requesting comment. A Graham spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that their office had indeed added the $9.5 million to the budget at the request of the university and Navatek. The spokesperson said the research was supported by the Navy and rejected the notion that Graham was motivated by campaign cash.

Graham’s spokesperson said requiring a fundraising minimum for a dinner was normal practice.

“[It’s] corruption at its best. But I am the only one rotting in prison.”
Former Navatek CEO Martin Kao

The checks Kao handed over at the dinner added up to about half of the $40,000 he had agreed to raise for the dinner, according to Tongour. The rest came in May, campaign records show.

“My understanding at the time was that the contributions associated with the event were lawful political contributions,” Winer said. “I never advised Kao to make a political contribution in exchange for official action. I never participated in, witnessed or had knowledge of any illegal political contribution.”

After Kao’s 2020 indictment, the University of South Carolina broke off the partnership. “University officials were not aware of any political contributions from Navatek,” Jeff Stensland, a university spokesperson, wrote in an email. “Our sole objective in partnering with them was to expand our research enterprise.”

One week after the dinner, on March 10, a University of South Carolina lobbyist sent written requests to Graham’s office for $20.5 million in appropriations: $10.5 million to continue Navatek’s power and energy research and $10 million for its new autonomous vehicle research.

Tongour confirmed many elements of Kao’s story. In a recent interview with ProPublica and subsequent emails, he remembered Kao giving the envelope full of checks to Graham’s fundraiser and even agreed that Graham kept the meeting short. “I don’t recall that he stayed more than 30 minutes,” Tongour said in an email. “Certainly not for appetizers, entrée, and dessert.”

But he denied Kao’s most significant claim: that Graham and Navatek struck an explicit, potentially illegal deal for contracts.

“I would remember that forever,” Tongour said. Graham supported Navatek’s requests, he said, because they were good for the state. “If I had seen that kind of quid pro quo, I would have quit earlier.” Tongour fired Navatek as a client later that year, immediately after Kao’s arrest.

Navatek considered Graham its chief patron in South Carolina, internal records show, just as it viewed Collins in Maine. But the company also wanted support in the House.

For that, Navatek turned to Clyburn, a member of Democratic party leadership and one of the most powerful figures in Congress. Agents found Navatek emails setting a meeting with Clyburn for early March. The goal, Kao said, was to make sure that the House draft of the budget “mirrored” whatever Graham inserted in the Senate version.

Over a meal, Clyburn asked Kao how much he was donating to Graham and then asked for the same amount, $100,000, Kao told the FBI.

The FBI tallied $20,000 in contributions that Kao and his family members made to Clyburn a few days after their scheduled meeting. A month later, Hartman arranged for a $10,000 gift to Clyburn’s alma mater, South Carolina State University, according to an email seen by ProPublica. Hartman noted it was “Congressman Clyburn’s favorite school.”

The spokesperson for Clyburn confirmed the dinner occurred but did not respond to questions about what was discussed.

Kao and Hartman struck a similar bargain with Wilson, Kao told the FBI, at a private lunch he secured by donating to his campaign. The FBI pulled records of $3,500 in donations Kao and Tongour made in late 2019 and early 2020.

Wilson has an influential role on the House Armed Services Committee, which authorizes defense spending. Wilson was “very clear and knew what the ask was,” Kao told the FBI. He wanted however much Clyburn was getting in campaign contributions in exchange for his support, Kao said.

Tongour denied this. “There was no ‘pay to play’ with Joe Wilson or his staff either,” he wrote in an email, adding that he donated because Wilson “is a friend and I want to see him re-elected.”

Kao claimed to the FBI that he paid for meals with all three politicians, but campaign finance records appear to show the lawmakers’ campaigns picked up the check.

By August 2020, Hartman had gotten word that Graham’s and Wilson’s committees would each support part of the company’s requests, internal company records show. Clyburn was not on key committees while he was a party leader. In one of his myriad spreadsheets, Hartman projected that the final budget could include up to $15.5 million of the $20.5 million the company had lobbied for.

Kao told agents he was gearing up to make more significant donations to Graham, Clyburn and Wilson by the end of the year. Instead, on Sept. 30, 2020, he was arrested.

Kao reflected on his time at Navatek in a deposition taken last month inside a federal prison. The company’s founder has sued Kao, saying his stewardship defrauded Navatek of millions.

“It’s nothing more than government contracting done through placating senior appropriation members for contracts,” Kao said. “The whole thing is a grand lie.”

An Arrest, a Lifeboat

Kao’s arrest plunged Navatek into disarray. Federal prosecutors charged him with defrauding a federal loan program; not long after, he was also charged with making illegal donations to the Collins campaign and super PAC. Lobbyists, universities and congressional offices abruptly cut off contact. “Don’t call us,” one congressional office told an executive, he later testified.

The Collins campaign said it disgorged Kao’s contribution. Yet the senator, facing a tight reelection bid, has had to field questions following the ProPublica report about her support for Navatek and why the super PAC supporting her accepted the $150,000 donation from the shell company in the first place.

As Navatek sank, Hartman began building himself a lifeboat. In 2021, he and Knight started a new military research company headquartered in South Carolina called Integer Technologies. Integer’s first project was one that Navatek had brokered with Graham.

Hartman didn’t face any criminal charges at the time and left Navatek largely unscathed. He would later settle a civil lawsuit brought by his former employer, which contended he played a role in Kao’s campaign finance and loan fraud schemes, for $425,000. He admitted no wrongdoing.

In September 2024, FBI agents flew to Hawaii for what would be their final interview with Kao. They pressed him for details about what happened in South Carolina, quizzing him on his dinner with Graham and a second in-person meeting he said he had with Clyburn. Agents wanted Kao to help them find more records that would back up his account and asked him to point them toward lobbyists in D.C. who he said facilitated the pay-for-play scheme.

As the year came to a close, FBI agent Michelle Ball felt she had enough material to move forward. The FBI had “uncovered a lengthy history” of a government contractor making donations “in exchange for government contracts,” she wrote in a Dec. 9, 2024, memo viewed by ProPublica.

In federal corruption probes, agents often begin by focusing on lower-level targets with a goal of working their way up to more prominent figures. Ball named Hartman; his business partner, Knight; and their company, Integer, as the formal subjects of the probe, as they prepared to potentially issue subpoenas and gather more evidence. They had Graham, Clyburn and Wilson in their sights. Ball devoted entire sections of the memo to detailing the lawmakers’ conduct. And she flagged the case as a sensitive matter that might implicate politicians in the future.

In the summer of 2024, Kate Fifield, a prosecutor in the Justice Department’s anti-corruption section, had been assigned to join the case. Fifield was wrapping up a high-profile prosecution of a retired Navy admiral who traded a government contract for a future job. Turning her attention to Kao, she and the FBI agents weighed their options. They considered getting high-level approval to deploy undercover agents. Proving an exchange of cash for favors often requires the kind of inconvertible evidence that undercover recordings can provide.

But before the investigation took flight, the new Trump administration began to demolish the Justice Department. The president’s handpicked leaders ordered prosecutors to drop a corruption case against New York Mayor Eric Adams, triggering a wave of resignations in the Public Integrity Section where Fifield worked, and revoked the section’s authority to bring new cases.

Then Trump’s FBI director, Kash Patel, began to purge the anti-corruption unit in the Washington D.C., field office, where many agents had investigated Trump.

Ball was fired in October 2025. Kevin Gounaud, another agent who had been working with her on the investigation, was pushed out in early 2026. Through their lawyer, the agents declined to comment.

The corruption investigation, just launched, suddenly went dark.

Read More

 
 

 

 

 The FBI Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the Way
 

 

The White House referred ProPublica’s questions to the FBI and DOJ. 

The Department of Justice didn’t respond to detailed questions about the investigation. 

“Under President Trump, the Justice Department is rooting out the weaponization, corruption, and institutional rot that ran rampant under Joe Biden’s two-tiered system of justice,” DOJ spokesperson Audrey Cook said.

Kao’s claims are “half baked” and “misleading,” FBI spokesperson Ben Williamson said. “Additionally, as we have said repeatedly, personnel are only removed at this FBI if they have been found to have acted unethically, undermined the mission, or engaged in weaponization of law enforcement.”

Meanwhile, Integer has rapidly expanded. Last year, it reported $81 million in contracts and announced that number would climb to $375 million by 2030. The company inked partnership deals with universities in New Hampshire, Louisiana and Mississippi. The University of South Carolina called its partnership with the firm a “model for public-private success.”

The company continues to forge ties with powerful politicians. In late 2024, Hartman posted a photo of himself with Speaker of the House Mike Johnson on his LinkedIn. “It was great to visit with the Speaker of the House today,” he wrote. “It’s good to know there are people in positions of power who seem to really care for the people they serve.” Johnson’s office did not reply to an email requesting comment. 

The occasion was a new research partnership in Louisiana. Hartman thanked his lobbyist for making it happen.

items.articleBody:
Wir haben vor einiger Zeit darüber berichtet, dass sich die Produkte von X-Sense künftig über den Smarthome-Standard Matter in Systeme wie Apple Home und Amazon Alexa einbinden lassen. Bereits im Sommer hat der Hersteller die erforderliche Zulassung für eine überarbeitete Basisstation erhalten. Mit dem neuesten Update der zugehörigen App bereitet X-Sense nun auch softwareseitig die Unterstützung der neuen Basisstation vor.

 Matter-Basisstation kommt im Januar

Bis zur Markteinführung müssen sich interessierte Nutzer allerdings noch etwas gedulden. Wie wir erfahren konnten, ist die Markteinführung der neuen Basisstation in Europa erst für Januar geplant. Für Besitzer bereits vorhandener X-Sense-Geräte gibt es in diesem Zusammenhang allerdings auch eine erfreuliche Nachricht. So ist geplant, dass alle Produkte, die bislang mit der X-Sense-Basisstation SBS50 kompatibel sind, auch mit der kommenden Matter-Basisstation SBS0A verwendet werden können.

X-Sense will den Umstieg bestehender Installationen auf Matter zudem möglichst unkompliziert gestalten. Beim Wechsel sollen sich bereits eingerichtete Geräte direkt auf die neue Basisstation übertragen lassen, sodass keine erneute Einrichtung der einzelnen Komponenten erforderlich ist.

App-Update bringt weitere Verbesserungen

Neben den Vorbereitungen für die Matter-Integration enthält die aktuelle Version der X-Sense-App auch verschiedene Verbesserungen für die Nutzung bereits vorhandener Geräte. Etwa wurde die Verlaufsansicht der vom kombinierten Thermo- und Hygrometer des Herstellers erfassten Werte um die Möglichkeit ergänzt, benutzerdefinierte Zeiträume auszuwählen. Darüber hinaus können sich Nutzer auf Wunsch per Push-Mitteilung darüber informieren lassen, wenn ein zuvor ausgefallenes Gerät wieder mit dem System verbunden ist.

Zuletzt haben wir von X-Sense die neuen Rauchmelder SD11-MR vorgestellt, die sich ebenfalls mit der Basisstation des Herstellers verbinden lassen. Diese sind aktuell im 3er-Set inklusive Basisstation zum Preis von 67,50 Euro zu haben. Auch die bereits erwähnten Thermo- und Hygrometer sind derzeit im Angebot. Das 4er-Pack inklusive Basisstation kostet ebenfalls 67,50 Euro.

★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★

Der Beitrag X-Sense: Update bereitet Matter-Unterstützung vor Wurde zuerst auf iphone-ticker.de veröffentlicht.

items.articleBody:
Apple ist in Präsentier-Laune und hat gestern das lange spekulierte Mac-Event für den 28. Oktober angekündigt. Unter dem Namen „Pro and tell“ wird der iPhone-Konzern also wohl neue Macs und iPads zeigen.

Das schreibt Greg Joswiak auf X (ehemals Twitter). Bereits das erste Event in diesem Monat wurde auf diese Art angekündigt. Apple hat am 13. Oktober unter dem Motto „Welcome Home“ den HomeView sowie neue Versionen des HomePod mini und des Apple TV 4K gezeigt.

Was wir auf dem „Pro and tell“-Event erwarten

Das Highlight der Veranstaltung dürften neue 14- und 16-Zoll-Modelle des MacBook Pro sein, die erstmals über einen Touchscreen und OLED-Displays verfügen könnten. Diese neuen Laptops sollen mit einer „Dynamic Island“ ausgestattet und deutlich leichter als die aktuellen Versionen sein. Angetrieben werden sie voraussichtlich von den neuen M5 Pro und M5 Max Chips.

Zudem wird ein neues iPad mini erwartet, das ebenfalls ein Upgrade auf einen OLED-Bildschirm erhält. Weitere geplante Neuerungen für das kompakte Tablet sind ein überarbeitetes Lautsprechersystem und eine neu positionierte FaceTime-Kamera.

Abgerundet wird das erwartete Line-up durch einen neuen iMac sowie ein 14-Zoll-Einstiegsmodell des MacBook Pro. Diese Geräte sollen mit dem neuen M6-Chip ausgestattet sein, werden ihr bisheriges Design aber voraussichtlich beibehalten.

Der Beitrag „Pro and tell“: Apple kündigt Event für den 28. Oktober an erschien zuerst auf Apfelpage.

items.articleBody:
RIRKRIT TIRAVANIJA BRINGS THAI FISHING BOATS TO ART BASEL PARIS

 

Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija has designed two monumental stainless steel tables inspired by traditional Thai fishing boats for Dalad’s, a temporary restaurant presented by We Are Ona during Art Basel Paris 2026. Installed inside a secret location near Place de l’Étoile, the elongated structures function simultaneously as dining tables and working kitchens, with integrated seating and steam pots that allow food to be prepared and served directly in front of guests. Conceived in collaboration with chef Dalad Kambhu and We Are Ona founder Luca Pronzato, the installation places cooking and social interaction at the center of the architectural experience.

 

Running from October 18 to 25, 2026, the Paris pop-up marks the debut of Dalad’s, a new hospitality project developed by Kambhu and Pronzato around contemporary Thai cuisine and the act of sharing food. Accommodating up to 100 guests, the temporary restaurant replaces conventional dining arrangements with two long communal structures where chefs and visitors occupy the same space. The project also marks Kambhu’s third collaboration with We Are Ona, following previous culinary experiences developed alongside designers Harry Nuriev and Marc Leschelier.

the temporary restaurant opens during Art Basel Paris 2026 | photographer: Robin Lefevre

 

 

STAINLESS STEEL BOATS REDEFINE COMMUNAL DINING

 

For Tiravanija, the boat-shaped design draws on Thailand’s longstanding relationship with its waterways and the informal food culture surrounding them. Speaking exclusively to designboom, the artist recalls running to the pier in Bangkok to buy boat noodle soup from vendors who prepared and sold their dishes directly from the water. These memories informed his decision to bring the kitchen and dining area together within a single structure, referencing an everyday tradition in which boats operate as places of exchange as much as means of transportation. ‘I think the form itself is both a vehicle and a platform,’ he explains.

 

The two modular structures reinterpret this relationship through stainless steel, transforming the recognizable silhouette of a fishing boat into a contemporary setting for collective dining. Their integrated cooking stations eliminate the usual separation between the kitchen and restaurant, allowing guests to watch the chefs at work from their seats. For Luca Pronzato, from We Are Ona, the design was also inspired by the practice of giving old fishing boats a second life as floating restaurants. ‘Rather than creating a traditional dining room with individual tables and a hidden kitchen, the boats become the structural backbone of the installation,’ he tells designboom. ‘The integrated steam pods bring the cooking directly into the long communal tables, dissolving the boundary between the kitchen and the dining room.’

the project brings together contemporary art, Thai cuisine, and communal dining | photographer: Robin Lefevre

 

 

KAMBHU EXPLORES THAI CUISINE BEYOND ITS GEOGRAPHICAL ROOTS

 

At the center of the culinary experience is Thai-American chef Dalad Kambhu, whose approach combines traditional Thai flavors and cooking techniques with seasonal, locally available ingredients. Raised in Bangkok, Kambhu developed her culinary identity across different cities before opening Kin Dee in Berlin in 2017, where her interpretation of Thai cuisine earned a Michelin star in 2019. For Dalad’s, she continues exploring the relationship between food, cultural memory, and place through a menu served directly from the installation. The pop-up offers a four-course lunch and an eight-course dinner, bringing guests together around the preparation and sharing of each dish.

 

The collaboration also reflects a longstanding friendship between Kambhu and Tiravanija, whose shared interest in cooking extends beyond the restaurant itself. The artist explains that their conversations have often explored what it means to prepare Thai food in places where its traditional ingredients are unavailable, raising questions about cultural identity and authenticity. ‘So it’s like finding authenticity, which is your own, which is yourself, in a foreign place,’ Tiravanija tells designboom. This perspective carries through the Paris experience, where references to Thai culture and the collaborators’ personal histories extend from the recipes to the tableware and spatial arrangement.

stainless steel structures reinterpret the silhouettes of traditional Thai fishing boats | photographer: Robin Lefevre

 

 

WE ARE ONA TURNS THE ACT OF DINING INTO A COLLECTIVE ARTWORK

 

Founded by Pronzato in 2019, We Are Ona has developed a series of temporary culinary experiences connecting gastronomy with art, architecture, and design, collaborating with figures including Carsten Höller, Cristina Celestino, and Sabine Marcelis. The installation for Dalad’s continues this approach while engaging directly with Tiravanija’s artistic practice, which has long challenged conventional exhibition formats through everyday activities such as cooking and eating. ‘For me, artworks are not simply objects to be observed; they are experiences to be lived,’ Pronzato explains to designboom. Within the Paris installation, the tables provide the physical framework, but the interactions between chefs and guests complete the work.

 

This relationship between participation and artistic experience is central to Tiravanija’s work, in which the boundaries between artist, audience, and artwork are deliberately blurred. At Dalad’s, the installation is activated through the preparation of food, the presence of diners, and the conversations that emerge around the communal tables. Rather than presenting the boats as sculptures to be admired from a distance, the project invites visitors to inhabit and use them, allowing the experience to change with every gathering. As Tiravanija puts it in his conversation with designboom, ‘a beautiful meal with friends and even strangers is a beautiful work of art.’

the installation is conceived as a space for cooking, eating, and gathering | photographer: Robin Lefevre
 
 

 
 
 
 

Rirkrit Tiravanija designs a boat-inspired installation for WE ARE ONA’s Dalad’s pop-up in Paris

 
 

 

two large communal tables form the centerpiece of the temporary restaurant | photographer: Robin Lefevre the project explores the relationship between food, architecture, and contemporary art | photographer: Laurent Giannesini

 
 

 
 
 
 

the boat-shaped structures accommodate both diners and chefs within the same space

 
 

 

the collaboration explores how food and design can bring people together | photographer: Laurent Giannesini Rirkrit Tiravanija, Dalad Kambhu and Luca Pronzato | photographer: Laurent Giannesini

 
 

 
 
 
 

the installation draws inspiration from Thailand’s traditional floating food culture

 
 

 
chef Dalad Kambhu combines traditional thai flavors with locally sourced ingredients | photographer: Laurent Giannesini

items.articleBody:
In this episode of My Forever Studio, brought to you in partnership with Audient, we’re joined by Ableton co-founder and legendary electronic music creator Robert Henke. You may also know him for Monolake, where he’s been producing minimal electronica for almost 30 years.

Henke takes us on a journey through his intriguing creative process, from making his own sample packs to selecting a Forever DAW that isn’t technically a DAW — and, no, it’s not Ableton Live. He also goes deep on his love for expressive hardware and his fascination with sound technology both old and new.

From growing up in a family of engineers to his influential career in Berlin’s pioneering club scene, Henke shares how engineering and art intermingle in his work. He reveals the studio setup that shaped Monolake’s early productions, why he still adores hands-on hardware, and what he’d build from scratch if given the tools and the time.

Strap in for tales of an iconic sampler rebuilt, expressive keyboards and custom 8-bit computers all set against the relaxing backdrop of a fantasy studio in the Scottish hills.

The My Forever Studio podcast – created in partnership with Audient – sees artists, producers, and engineers create their dream fantasy Forever Studio, wherever they want in the universe. However, hosts Chris Barker and Will Betts impose some strict rules in the Forever Studio. Our guests are permitted a limited number of items in their creative space, so they must choose carefully. There will be nostalgia. There will be anecdotes. There may be gags. But there will be no bundles!

Subscribe to My Forever Studio on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and check out all episodes so far via MusicTech.

items.articleBody:
Edelmetall unter Stress: Bei der Wasserelektrolyse ermöglicht seltenes Iridium die Sauerstoffbildung, doch die Katalysatoren verschleißen unter den harten Bedingungen. Forscher haben Iridium-Nanopartikel nun fest in einem speziellen Kristallgerüst verankert. Eine damit ausgerüstete Versuchszelle lief mehr als 3.800 Stunden bei vergleichsweise geringer Leistungsverschlechterung.

Sendai (Japan). Mithilfe von Strom lässt sich Wasser in Wasserstoff und Sauerstoff zerlegen. Kommt die Energie aus erneuerbaren Quellen, kann so klimafreundlicher Wasserstoff entstehen. Besonders geeignet für schwankenden Wind- und Solarstrom sind Elektrolyseure mit einer Protonenaustauschmembran, kurz PEM-Elektrolyseure. Sie können ihre Leistung schnell an das Stromangebot anpassen.

Doch an der Sauerstoffelektrode liegt ein Problem: Dort herrschen stark saure und oxidierende Bedingungen, die viele Materialien angreifen. Für die schwierige Sauerstoffbildung bei der Wasserspaltung wird deshalb häufig Iridium eingesetzt. Das Edelmetall ist selten und teuer. Zugleich können seine aktiven Partikel im Betrieb verklumpen, übermäßig oxidieren oder sich langsam auflösen.

Forscher des Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry (CIAC) um Dr. Meiling Xiao haben nun untersucht, wie sich Iridium auch bei hohen Stromdichten besser schützen lässt. Ihr Ansatz kombiniert eine besonders feste Verankerung der Metallpartikel mit einer chemischen Umgebung, die ihren Elektronenzustand während der Reaktion beeinflusst.

Schematische Darstellung der Herstellung des Ir/HESIO-Katalysators. Durch eine gezielte Wärmebehandlung wandert Iridium aus dem Kristallgerüst an die Oberfläche und bildet dort fest verankerte Nanopartikel © Hao Li

Iridium wächst aus dem Kristallgerüst heraus

Als Träger dient ein sogenannter Hochentropie-Perowskit. Das ist ein kristallines Oxid, in dessen Gitter sich mehrere unterschiedliche Metalle bestimmte Plätze teilen. Neben Iridium enthält das für die Studie entwickelte Material unter anderem Titan, Molybdän, Kobalt und Nickel. Diese Mischung soll zugleich das Kristallgerüst stabilisieren und die elektrischen Eigenschaften beeinflussen.

Durch eine gezielte Wärmebehandlung unter reduzierenden Bedingungen wandert ein Teil des Iridiums aus dem Inneren des Trägermaterials an die Oberfläche. Dort bilden sich winzige Nanopartikel, die mit dem Kristallgerüst eng verbunden bleiben. Anders als nachträglich aufgebrachte Partikel sind sie gewissermaßen im Untergrund verwurzelt und können weniger leicht wandern oder zusammenklumpen.

„Durch die sorgfältige Auswahl dieser Metalle konnten wir strukturelle Stabilität mit der Möglichkeit verbinden, die elektronischen Eigenschaften des Materials während der Reaktion anzupassen und so Iridium vor dem Abbau zu schützen“, erklärt Prof. Hao Li von der Tohoku University.

Mehr als 3.800 Stunden im Dauerbetrieb

Wie belastbar der neue Katalysator ist, hat das Team in einer vollständigen PEM-Elektrolyse-Einzelzelle erprobt. Bei einer Stromdichte von zwei Ampere pro Quadratzentimeter arbeitete sie mehr als 3.800 Stunden. Die Forscher beziffern die Verschlechterung der Zellspannung in diesem Zeitraum auf lediglich 2,2 Prozent. Für diese Stromdichte benötigte die Zelle zunächst 1,71 Volt.

Auch unter höherer Belastung hielt der Katalysator lange durch. Bei drei Ampere pro Quadratzentimeter lief eine weitere Versuchszelle mehr als 3.200 Stunden und zeigte eine Spannungsverschlechterung von 4,7 Prozent. Für diese Stromdichte waren zunächst 1,80 Volt nötig. Die Versuche belegen eine hohe Beständigkeit unter den jeweils getesteten Laborbedingungen.

Ein gesonderter Vergleichstest unter anderen Bedingungen zeigte ebenfalls Vorteile. Während bei einem herkömmlichen Iridium-Katalysator innerhalb von 300 Stunden deutliche Verschleißerscheinungen auftraten, blieb die neue Materialkombination über mehr als 650 Stunden weitgehend stabil. Die beiden Testreihen lassen sich wegen ihrer unterschiedlichen Bedingungen allerdings nicht unmittelbar gleichsetzen.

„Unsere Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die sorgfältige Gestaltung des Materials um das Iridium herum die Haltbarkeit des Katalysators deutlich verbessern kann“, sagt Hao Li.

Ein Kristallgerüst als elektronischer Schutzschild

Die höhere Haltbarkeit hat offenbar zwei Ursachen. Mikroskopische Untersuchungen bestätigten, dass die Iridium-Partikel fest im Perowskit verankert sind. Messungen mit Röntgenspektroskopie und theoretische Berechnungen zeigten außerdem, dass das Kristallgerüst den Elektronenzustand des Iridiums während der Sauerstoffbildung beeinflusst. Dadurch wird dessen übermäßige Oxidation gebremst, die sonst die Auflösung des Metalls begünstigt.

Allerdings wurden die langen Laufzeiten bislang an experimentellen Einzelzellen nachgewiesen, nicht an industriellen Großanlagen. Ob das Material im jahrelangen Betrieb ebenso zuverlässig funktioniert, wirtschaftlich hergestellt werden kann und den Iridiumbedarf tatsächlich nennenswert senkt, bleibt zu prüfen. Die neue Struktur macht das seltene Edelmetall schließlich nicht überflüssig.

„Wir hoffen, dass unsere Arbeit zur Entwicklung zuverlässigerer und kostengünstigerer Wasserelektrolysesysteme beiträgt und die Herstellung von grünem Wasserstoff in größerem Maßstab praktikabler macht“, sagt Hao Li.

Damit zeigt die Untersuchung einen möglichen Weg, die Lebensdauer knapper Edelmetallkatalysatoren zu verbessern. Entscheidend sind dabei nicht allein die Iridium-Partikel selbst, sondern auch das Material, das sie trägt und im Betrieb schützt.

Quellen:

Originalstudie im Fachmagazin Journal of the American Chemical Society, doi: 10.1021/jacs.6c13780

Offizielle Studienmitteilung von Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CIAC)

items.subtitle: Der Roland Jupiter-8 hat den Synthpop und Italo Disco der 80er-Jahre ebenso geprägt wie die Entwicklung des Synthesizerbaus.

Dabei knüpft Roland an eine lange Tradition an: Auf den Jupiter-8 folgten im Laufe der Jahrzehnte verschiedene Synthesizer, die dessen Erbe weiterführten – vom JX-8P über den JP-8000 bis hin zur heutigen Model-Expansion für Zenology Pro und Workstation-Synthesizer.
