items.articleBody:
Where the hard edge of physics meets the vulnerable metaphysics of the human heart. 

Few people have enchanted the popular imagination with science more powerfully and lastingly than physicist Richard Feynman (May 11, 1918–February 15, 1988) — the “Great Explainer” with the uncommon gift for bridging the essence of science with the most human and humane dimensions of life.

Several months after Feynman’s death, while working on what would become Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman (public library) — the masterly biography plumbing the wellspring of Feynman’s genius — James Gleick discovered something of arresting strangeness and splendor. 

“My heart stopped,” Gleick tells me. “I have never had an experience like that as a biographer, before or since.”

In a mass of unread papers sent to him by Feynman’s widow, Gweneth, Gleick found a letter that discomposed his most central understanding of Feynman’s character. A generation after computing pioneer Alan Turing tussled with the binary code of body and spirit in the wake of loss, Feynman — a scientist perhaps uncommonly romantic yet resolutely rational and unsentimental in his reverence for the indomitable laws of physics that tend toward decay — penned a remarkable letter to a physical nonentity that was, for the future Nobel-winning physicist, the locus of an irrepressible metaphysical reality. 

Richard Feynman as a youth

In high school, the teenage Richard spent summers at the beach in his native Far Rockaway. There, he grew besotted with a striking girl named Arline — a girl he knew he would marry. Both complement and counterpoint to his own nature, Arline met Richard’s inclination for science with ardor for philosophy and art. (The art class he took just to be near her would lay the foundation for his little-known, lifelong passion for drawing.) By his junior year, Richard proposed. Arline accepted. With the eyes of young love, they peered into a shared future of infinite possibility for bliss. 

Richard and Arline, 1940s

But they were abruptly grounded when a mysterious malady began afflicting Arline with inexplicable symptoms — a lump would appear and disappear on her neck, fevers would roil over her with no apparent cause. Eventually, she was hospitalized for what was believed to be typhoid. 

Gleick writes:

Feynman began to glimpse the special powerlessness that medical uncertainty can inflict on a scientific person. He had come to believe that the scientific way of thinking brought a measure of calmness and control in difficult situations — but not now.

Just as Feynman began bombarding the doctors with questions that steered them toward a closer approximation of the scientific method, Arline began to recover just as mysteriously and unpredictably as she had fallen ill. But the respite was only temporary. The symptoms returned, still shorn of a concrete explanation but now unambiguously pointing toward the terminal — a prognosis Arline’s doctors kept from her. Richard refused to go along with the deception — he and Arline had promised each other to face life with unremitting truthfulness — but he was forced to calibrate his commitment to circumstance. 

Gleick writes:

His parents, Arline’s parents, and the doctors all urged him not to be so cruel as to tell a young woman she was dying. His sister, Joan, sobbing, told him he was stubborn and heartless. He broke down and bowed to tradition. In her room at Farmingdale Hospital, with her parents at her side, he confirmed that she had glandular fever. Meanwhile, he started carrying around a letter — a “goodbye love letter,” as he called it — that he planned to give her when she discovered the truth. He was sure she would never forgive the unforgivable lie. 

He did not have long to wait. Soon after Arline returned home from the hospital she crept to the top of the stairs and overheard her mother weeping with a neighbor down in the kitchen. When she confronted Richard — his letter snug in his pocket — he told her the truth, handed her the letter, and asked her to marry him.

Arline and Richard, 1940s

Marriage, however, proved to be a towering practical problem — Princeton, where Feynman was now pursuing a Ph.D., threatened to withdraw the fellowships funding his graduate studies if he were to wed, for the university considered the emotional and pragmatic responsibilities of marriage a grave threat to academic discipline. 

Just as Feynman began considering leaving Princeton, a diagnosis detonated the situation — Arline had contracted a rare form of tuberculosis, most likely from unpasteurized milk. 

At first, Feynman was relieved that the grim alternative options of Hodgkin’s disease and incurable cancers like lymphoma had been ruled out. But he was underestimating, or perhaps misunderstanding, the gravity of tuberculosis — the very disease which had taken the love of Alan Turing’s life and which, during its two-century heyday, had claimed more lives around the globe than any other malady and all wars combined. At the time of Arline’s diagnosis in 1941, immunology was in its infancy, the antibiotic treatment of bacterial infections practically nonexistent, and the first successful medical application of penicillin a year away. Tuberculosis was a death sentence, even if it was a slow death with intervals of remission — a fact Richard and Arline faced with an ambivalent mix of brave lucidity and hope against hope. 

Meanwhile, Richard’s parents met the prospect of his marriage with bristling dread. His mother, who believed he was marrying Arline out of pity rather than love, admonished him that he would be putting his health and his very life in danger, and coldly worried about how the stigma attached to tuberculosis would impact her brilliant young son’s reputation. “I was surprised to learn such a marriage is not unlawful,” she scoffed unfeelingly. “It ought to be.”

But Richard was buoyed by love — a love so large and luminous that he found himself singing aloud one day as he was arranging Arline’s transfer to a sanatorium. Determined to go through with the wedding, he wrote to his beloved:

I guess maybe it is like rolling off of a log — my heart is filled again & I’m choked with emotions — and love is so good & powerful — it’s worth preserving — I know nothing can separate us — we’ve stood the tests of time and our love is as glorious now as the day it was born — dearest riches have never made people great but love does it every day — we’re not little people — we’re giants … I know we both have a future ahead of us — with a world of happiness — now & forever.

On June 29, 1942, they promised each other eternity. 

Richard and Arline on their wedding day

Gleick writes:

He borrowed a station wagon from a Princeton friend, outfitted it with mattresses for the journey, and picked up Arline in Cedarhurst. She walked down her father’s hand-poured concrete driveway wearing a white dress. They crossed New York Harbor on the Staten Island ferry — their honeymoon ship. They married in a city office on Staten Island, in the presence of neither family nor friends, their only witnesses two strangers called in from the next room. Fearful of contagion, Richard did not kiss her on the lips. After the ceremony he helped her slowly down the stairs, and onward they drove to Arline’s new home, a charity hospital in Browns Mills, New Jersey.

Meanwhile, WWII was reaching its crescendo of destruction, dragging America into the belly of death with the attack on Pearl Harbor. Now one of the nation’s most promising physicists, Feynman was recruited to work on what would become the Manhattan Project and soon joined the secret laboratory in Los Alamos. 

Feynman’s Los Alamos badge

Arline entered the nearby Albuquerque sanatorium, from where she wrote him letters in code — for the sheer fun of it, because she knew how he cherished puzzles, but the correspondence alarmed the military censors at the laboratory’s Intelligence Office. Tasked with abating any breaches to the secrecy of the operation, they cautioned Feynman that coded messages were against the rules and demanded that his wife include a key in each letter to help them decipher it. This only amplified Arline’s sense of fun — she began cutting holes into her letters, covering passages with ink, and even mail-ordered a jigsaw puzzle kit with which to cut up the pages and completely confound the agents. 

But the levity masked the underlying darkness which Richard and Arline tried so desperately to evade — Arline was dying. As her body failed, he steadied himself to her spirit:

You are a strong and beautiful woman. You are not always as strong as other times but it rises & falls like the flow of a mountain stream. I feel I am a reservoir for your strength — without you I would be empty and weak… I find it much harder these days to write these things to you.

In every single letter, he told her that he loved her. “I have a serious affliction: loving you forever,” he wrote. 

Richard and Arline at the Albuquerque sanatorium

In early 1945, two and a half years into their marriage, Richard and Arline made love for the first time. He had been too afraid of harming her frail health somehow, she too afraid of infecting him with the deadly bacterium consuming her. But Arline insisted that this pent up desire could no longer be contained and assured Richard that this would only bring them closer — to each other, and to the life they had so lovingly dreamt up for themselves:

I’ll always be your sweetheart & first love — besides a devoted wife — we’ll be proud parents too… I am proud of you always Richard –[you are] a good husband, and lover, & well, coach, I’ll show you what I mean Sunday.

But heightened as their hopes were by this new dimension of shared experience, Arline’s health continued to plummet. Her weight dropped to eighty-four pounds. Exasperated by the helplessness of medicine, which Feynman had come to see not as a manifestation but as a mutilation of the scientific method, he invested all hope in an experimental drug made of mold growths. “Keep hanging on,” he exhorted Arline. “Nothing is certain. We lead a charmed life.” She began spitting blood. 

At twenty-seven, on the precipice of a brilliant scientific career, he was terminally in love. 

On June 16, 1945, while working at the computing room at Los Alamos, Feynman received a call from the sanatorium that Arline was dying. He borrowed a colleague’s car and sped to the hospital, where he found her immobile, her eyes barely tracing his movement. Early in his scientific career, he had been animated by the nature of time. Now, hours stretched and contracted as he sat at her deathbed, until one last small breath tolled the end at 9:21PM.

The wake of loss has a way of tranquilizing grief with the pressing demands of practical arrangements — a tranquilizer we take willingly, almost gratefully. The following morning, Feynman arranged for his beloved’s cremation, methodically collected her personal belongings, and on the final page of the small spiral notebook in which she recorded her symptoms he wrote with scientific remove: “June 16 — Death.”

And so we arrive at Gleick’s improbable discovery in that box of letters — improbable because of the extreme rationality with which Feynman hedged against even the slightest intimation of metaphysical conjectures untestable by science and unprovable by reason. During his courtship of Arline, he had been vexed by her enthusiasm for Descartes, whose “proof” of God’s perfection he found intellectually lazy and unbefitting of Descartes’s reputation as a champion of reason. He had impishly countered Arline’s insistence that there are two sides to everything by cutting a piece of paper and half-twisting it into a Möbius strip, the ends pasted together to render a surface with just one side. 

Everything that appeared mystical, Feynman believed, was simply an insufficiently explained mystery with a physical answer not yet found. Even Arline’s dying hour had offered testing ground for conviction. Puzzlingly, the clock in the room had stopped at exactly 9:21PM — the time of death. Aware of how this bizarre occurrence could foment the mystical imagination in unscientific minds, Feynman reasoned for an explanation. Remembering that he had repaired the clock multiple times over the course of Arline’s stay at the sanatorium, he realized that the instrument’s unwieldy mechanism must have choked when the nurse picked it up in the low evening light to see and record the time. 

How astonishing and how touchingly human, then, that Feynman penned the letter Gleick found in the box forty-two years later — a letter he wrote to Arline in October of 1946, 488 days after her death:

D’Arline,

I adore you, sweetheart.

I know how much you like to hear that — but I don’t only write it because you like it — I write it because it makes me warm all over inside to write it to you.

It is such a terribly long time since I last wrote to you — almost two years but I know you’ll excuse me because you understand how I am, stubborn and realistic; and I thought there was no sense to writing.

But now I know my darling wife that it is right to do what I have delayed in doing, and that I have done so much in the past. I want to tell you I love you. I want to love you. I always will love you.

I find it hard to understand in my mind what it means to love you after you are dead — but I still want to comfort and take care of you — and I want you to love me and care for me. I want to have problems to discuss with you — I want to do little projects with you. I never thought until just now that we can do that. What should we do. We started to learn to make clothes together — or learn Chinese — or getting a movie projector. Can’t I do something now? No. I am alone without you and you were the “idea-woman” and general instigator of all our wild adventures.

When you were sick you worried because you could not give me something that you wanted to and thought I needed. You needn’t have worried. Just as I told you then there was no real need because I loved you in so many ways so much. And now it is clearly even more true — you can give me nothing now yet I love you so that you stand in my way of loving anyone else — but I want you to stand there. You, dead, are so much better than anyone else alive.

I know you will assure me that I am foolish and that you want me to have full happiness and don’t want to be in my way. I’ll bet you are surprised that I don’t even have a girlfriend (except you, sweetheart) after two years. But you can’t help it, darling, nor can I — I don’t understand it, for I have met many girls and very nice ones and I don’t want to remain alone — but in two or three meetings they all seem ashes. You only are left to me. You are real.

My darling wife, I do adore you.

I love my wife. My wife is dead.

Rich.

And then, with the sole defibrillator for heartache we have — humor — Feynman adds:

PS Please excuse my not mailing this — but I don’t know your new address.

Complement this particular portion of the altogether magnificent Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman with Rachel Carson’s stunning deathbed farewell to her beloved and Seneca on resilience in the face of loss, then revisit Feynman on science and religion and the meaning of life.

items.articleBody:
As the song goes, we all need a little help from our friends. And that applies to apps for our Macs and iPhones as well.

Fortunately, the apps in the spotlight this week all aim to lend a helping hand, whether it’s tracking down files to free up space on your devices, expanding text or storing clippings to save time or even doing things with the photos and screenshots you’ve accrued over the years.

Do you know of any helpful macOS and iOS offerings? Drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description. We won’t be able to respond to every email we receive, but we will give any and all suggestions a helpful once-over.

Crumb

I’m not as diligent about keeping my Mac free of detritus and cruft as I should be, to the point where gigabytes are often in short supply on my laptop’s drive. Crumb promises to do the hard work of freeing up space on your Mac, with some more sophisticated tools to help you track down the files that have outlived their usefulness.

At its most basic, Crumb clears out your caches, which can remove a surprising amount of filler if you’ve not used a cleaner app in a while. Running the app for the first time, I wound up with 2.4GB of cache and logs that could be safely jettisoned — I imagine that number won’t be as garish with more frequent cleanings, but anything that helps me keep my drive free of cruft is welcome.

Crumb has some other modes, like a Visualize tool that shows you what’s in different folders and how much space that folder takes up. An analysis tool can spot whether the content in the folder contains things you’ve created and, therefore, should be reviewed manually before deleting. You can also tap a shortcut button to head straight to a folder to review its contents.

I find Crumb’s Duplicate tool particularly useful, since I’m in the habit of downloading images, tweaking their sizes for stories and then keeping copies in multiple places. Duplicate tracks down the extras for purging, while an Uninstall feature helps you remove apps and any files they leave behind.

The free tier of Crumb entitles you to one full cleanup — a trial of the app, in essence. A one-time $9 payment unlocks unlimited cleanups as well as the Uninstall, Duplicates and Organize tools. (The latter feature sorts things into folders such as Images, Videos, Documents and more.) A Crumb license works on up to two Macs.

Klackey

Klackey is a multipurpose text expander that works on both Windows machines and Macs, though it’s only the macOS version we’re concerned with here. And while some may find the extensive toolset to be overkill — Klackey brings a lot to the table — the text expansion features certainly impress.

I get a lot of email submissions, as you might imagine, and I’ve been struggling with a way to send out a reply that doesn’t make responding to emails my full-time job. In Klackey, I can write a general reply and give it a simple code preceded by a semicolon — say ;reply — so that when I type that code into a Mac app that accepts text input like a mail client, my form letter shows up automatically. I can do that for any other frequently used text snippets I want to store in Klackey as well.

Klackey offers other features like a clipboard history for keeping everything you copy close at hand, a notes tool for organizing your thoughts and even an encrypted secure folder for storing items like passwords. I found the text expansion to be the real selling point, but you can decide for yourself with a free 14-day trial when you download Klackey. After that, a payment unlocks all the current features with a year of updates, with a cross-platform license covering up to two computers.

As I write this, Klackey is available for $35, a discount from the regular price of $49.

MemoryString

You’re not hurting for options when it comes to assembling your photos and videos into a movie that you can view or share with others. MemoryString is betting you’ll give this macOS offering a try for a couple of reasons, not the least of which is that it’s free.

That’s not “free” as in you get to assemble a video or two before you’re required to unlock the full app. MemoryString won’t cost you a dime to download — neither initially nor through any in-app purchases. Just grab the app, import some photos or videos and fiddle around with the transitions, titles and audio. (There’s a royalty-free library included with the app, or you can add your own music.) A MemoryString watermark does appear at the end of the finished video.

MemoryString looks to be an alternative to iMovie by getting you to the finished product faster, while also offering more control over your project than the Memory Movie feature included in Photos.

I found that the app works best when you import an image or folder, as MemoryString crashed when I tried dragging things directly from the Photos app on my Mac. However, MemoryString’s developer responded promptly to my bug report.

In other words, it’s a promising alternative if you’re looking for a tool that helps you turn the photos on your Mac and iPhone into moving pictures, and the free status means there’s no barrier to giving MemoryString a try.

Pixph

Just as there are lots of ways to assemble your photos into a video or slideshow, you also have many options for managing all the things you save to your clipboard. So why turn to the $10 Pixph as a place to stash text, URLs or anything else you care to copy? Besides the convenience of having a storage space on the side of your display — or wherever you choose to position the Pixph window — there’s also the matter of organizing all those clips.

It’s easy to copy something over to Pixph: just highlight and tap your shift button twice to capture it in the app. But Pixph also lets you organize clippings into projects, so that if you’re researching something, all the related text strings, links and images you’ve saved are all in one place, ready to move back into the window that you’re working in. Pixph lives in the menu bar of your Mac, and it’s easy to pivot between projects when you find a relevant clip to save.

I found Pixph’s commitment to the Liquid Glass interface a little bit distracting, though it was easy enough to open up settings and switch to dark mode so that the app behind the Pixph window wasn’t as visible. Pixph also treats your clippings as a checklist, with buttons for marking off items when you have no further use for them. Some may appreciate that approach, but it really didn’t fit into my workflow.

Nevertheless, the ability to organize items and even add your own thoughts via a note feature makes Pixph a useful tool for people to add a little structure to their projects.

DumpPixels

If you find yourself filling up your iPhone’s Photos app with screenshots — and then forgetting to delete those screenshots later on — DumpPixels can clean up your photo library without sacrificing the information you were looking to capture in the first place.

Anytime you capture a screenshot, it appears in DumpPixels, which also copies any text that appears within that screenshot. Say you capture an article in the News app because you spot an interesting snippet of text. Within DumpPixels, you can save a note containing that text to the app’s Notes tab. You can then delete the screenshot, freeing up space in your Photos library while retaining whatever information you wanted from the screenshot.

Or at least, DumpPixels will delete the screenshot after you’ve unlocked the app. The free download only lets you save copied text from screens, while a $20 in-app purchase unlocks the deletion feature.

If there’s a limitation to DumpPixels, it’s that it only works on screenshots. If you were to take a photo of a flyer with date and address info, that wouldn’t get copied into DumpPixels — unless you were to take a screenshot of the photo itself, of course. Still, if you find yourself snapping a lot of screenshots to collect data for later use, DumpPixels could be an effective way to better manage all the info and imagery you’ve collected.

items.articleBody:
Did Denzel Washington say he "never met anyone braver, smarter or who cares more about America than Donald Trump"? No, that's not true: There is no evidence that the actor, director and producer said this. No established news outlets have reported that Washington ever said those words.

The claim appeared in a post (archived here) by the @RedEagleUpdates account on X on Oct. 10, 2026. It read:

🚨BOOM:

Denzel Washington: 'I've worked with a lot of people in my life, and I've never met anyone braver, smarter, or who cares more about America than Donald Trump. He's a great friend and an even better president. I'm proud to be a steadfast supporter, and I'll never apologize for it.'

Do you agree with Denzel?

YES or NO?

This is what the post looked like on X at the time of writing:

(Image source: post by @RedEagleUpdates on X.)

The text in the image read:

DENZEL WASHINGTON: I'VE WORKED WITH A LOT OF PEOPLE IN MY LIFE, AND I'VE NEVER MET ANYONE BRAVER, SMARTER, OR WHO CARES MORE ABOUT AMERICA THAN DONALD TRUMP.

HE'S A GREAT FRIEND AND AN EVEN BETTER PRESIDENT. I'M PROUD TO BE A STEADFAST SUPPORTER, AND I'LL NEVER APOLOGIZE FOR IT.

GOD BLESS AMERICA AND OUR PRESIDENT.

President Donald Trump shared the post (archived here) on his Truth Social account on Oct. 12, 2026.

This is what the post looked like on Truth Social at the time of writing:

(Image source: post by @realDonaldTrump on Truth Social.)

The claim also appeared in another post (archived here) on the @official.maganews account on Instagram on Oct. 12, 2026. It read:

This is according to president trumps truth social. Denzel Washington said he has worked with a lot of people and has never met anyone braver, smarter, or who cares more about America than Donald Trump. Trump is the one in the red USA hat and Denzel is the face on the left.

Denzel called him a great friend and an even better president. He said he is proud to be a steadfast supporter and will never apologize for it. That kind of public support from a man like Denzel hits different. God bless America and our president is the close.

I stand with that. Name Denzel Washington and name President Trump when they pretend Hollywood is unanimous against him. Keep the credit on the man who said he will never apologize for supporting Trump. A lot of people stay quiet. Denzel did not. He said it plain.

This is what the post looked like on Instagram at the time of writing:

(Image source: post by @official.maganews on Instagram.)

News searches

Lead Stories searched Google News (archived here) and Yahoo News (archived here) and found no matching reports about the claim from established news outlets using the search terms: "Denzel Washington," "never met anyone braver," "cares more about America," and "Trump."

The Washington Post (archived here) reported on Oct. 12, 2026, that representatives for the actor confirmed that the quote was fabricated. The story said:

'Not real,' said Alan Nierob, president of PMK Entertainment, the firm that represents the two-time Academy Award-winning actor, in an email to The Washington Post. 'No idea where it came from.'

Lead Stories also reached out to PMK Entertainment, but did not receive an immediate response.

Other fact checks

This claim was also investigated by Snopes.

items.articleBody:
So much has been said about John Berger over the past five decades that it almost feels trite to pile on. You know the familiar takeaways: that the critic and novelist taught us how to look and pay attention, believed art belongs to the people, exposed how the male gaze shapes our perception. So, it’s especially astounding that a new biography by Tom Overton has managed to both capture the scope of Berger’s influence and reframe him, first and foremost, as human.

Author Megan O’Grady, who reflects on many of the same questions as Berger in her recent book How It Feels to Be Alive: Encounters with Art and Our Selves, penned a sensitive review of the biography and its approach to addressing the complex personal life of this near-mythologized figure. It’s a poignant, refreshing read, and reminds me of the conversation around the sanctification of artists and writers like James Baldwin, whose work gets flattened in the process.

In fact, how we tell the story of an artist’s life (and afterlife) just might be our primary preoccupation this month. Lauren Moya Ford reads one scholar’s novel approach to the canonized Vermeer, searching for the influence of his signature narrative ambiguity across mediums and forms. Meanwhile, Lavinia Liang grapples with a biography of Dorothea Tanning and its treatment of her relationship with her artist husband, Max Ernst, a perennial dilemma facing any author who seeks to move an overlooked woman’s legacy out of the shadow of her male partner.

More from our critics below, plus a round-up of some of our favorite recent art books on textiles, fabric, and fiber art. One of my personal go-tos is Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers by the wonderful Sharbreon Plummer, and we also recommend books on Palestinian embroidery, Diné weaving, and the Bayeux Tapestry. Read up, and let us know what’s on your list this month!

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

 
 

 12 Must-Read Books on Textiles and Fiber Art
 

 
 

 There’s a reason the lexicon of textiles and fiber lends itself so well to storytelling — we thread the needle, weave the tale, spin the yarn. Writers have reached for these metaphors for centuries because they feel true to life, but artists know they’re also true to craft and its tangled histories. We’ve gathered a few recent books on embroidery, fiber art, weaving, and more that deserve a closer look, from Black Southern quilting and Korean bojagi to Palestinian tatreez and contemporary Diné weaving. Refreshingly, so many of these titles complicate or refuse reductive, familiar frameworks and open up new ways to understand the meditative and political dimensions of textile traditions, moving past the false dichotomy of “craft versus art” and sexist and tired notions of “women’s work.” You might even say these books piece together a new history of textile art, stitch by stitch. 
 

 
 Read More
 

 
 

 

 SPONSORED
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
Discover R. Buckminster Fuller’s Intuition

New from David Zwirner Books: R. Buckminster Fuller’s lyrical case for intuition as the force uniting the sciences and the arts. Originally written in 1968 by the creator of the geodesic dome, this concise work returns with a new introduction by Anahid Nersessian as part of the ekphrasis series.

 

 
 
 
 Learn more
 
 
 

 
 

 

From Our Critics

 
 

 John Berger in His Own Bruised Time
 

 
 

 The late novelist and art critic asked Tom Overton to wait to write his biography until after his death. The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so. | Megan O’Grady
 

 
 Read More
 

 
 

 Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places
 

 
 

 Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influence, writes historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell. | Lauren Moya Ford
 

 
 Read More
 

 
 

 The Trafficker Who Furnished the Museums of LA
 

 
 

 A team of researchers excavates the story of Earl Stendahl, a mid-century gallerist who shamelessly stole ancient Mesoamerican objects and marketed them to the institutional art world. | Armando Pulido
 

 
 Read More
 

 
 

 Dorothea Tanning Beyond Max Ernst’s Shadow
 

 
 

 A new biography attempts to make the case for Tanning’s independence and artistic strength in her own right, but remains frustratingly tethered to her husband. | Lavinia Liang
 

 
 Read More
 

 
 

 

 SPONSORED
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
Bold New Books in Art and Visual Culture from the MIT Press

From activist art and trans aesthetics to lowriders, global skateboarding culture, and Vilém Flusser’s prescient vision of the screen age.

 

 
 
 
 Learn more
 
 
 

 
 

 

In the News

Authors Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari pulled their children’s book on Palestine from Penguin after the editors reportedly asked them to temper the language they used to describe decolonial history. Happily, the title is now going to InterLink Books, the only Palestinian-owned publisher in the United States, run by author Hannah Moushabeck and her family.

In related news, bookstores in the United Kingdom are rushing to get copies of Sally Rooney’s novels from distributors after the government banned the sale of her books over her support for Palestine Action.

Required Reading

For Hyperallergic, Isabella Segalovich interviewed journalist, champion of the avant-garde, and Pop-art connoisseur Joan Kron ahead of the release of her memoir, fabulously titled The Renegade Housewives of Pop Art: A Memoir of The 1960s, coming out in December from Pointed Leaf Press.

Alissa Quart reflects on 25 years since the publication of Nickel and Dimed by the late Barbara Ehrenreich, with whom she co-founded the Economic Hardship Reporting Project, for the Nation.

Architecture writer Kate Wagner tackles a new book chronicling the inequality of American public bathrooms for an article in the Baffler with a perfect title.

Rosalyn Drexler is everywhere this fall, particularly in New York. Essayist Leslie Camhi writes in the New Yorker about the late artist and author’s resurgence in galleries, bookstores, and museums across the city.

What We're Reading

Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
I’m digging into Story Telling: A Writing Life (2026), Isabel Allende’s new memoir of nearly five decades spent on her craft (thank you to the unusually short hold queue at the Brooklyn Public Library). At 84, she speaks plainly about approaching death; not fearfully or morosely but with reverence for the life she has led and the writing that animates it. I do find it telling that the original Spanish title is La Palabra Mágica: Una Vida Escrita. “The Magic Word” certainly feels more true to Allende’s literary worlds. Maybe I should put a library hold on a Spanish copy, too …

Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor
Halloween’s coming up, so you know I had to revisit a ghost story that one could argue invented the form: Henry James’s The Turn of the Screw (1898).

From the Archive

 
 

 John Berger Lost His Eyesight to Cataracts and Learned to See
 

 
 

 After being afflicted with cataracts, the late critic and novelist reflected on the mechanics of sight. | Melissa Holbrook Pierson
 

 
 Read More

items.articleBody:
Cue the depressing rain, dark trench coats, and a dire dystopian dirge because the Blade Runner 2099 trailer is here!

Cyberpunk is charging back in confident fashion with Prime Video's latest detour into the neon-drenched dystopia of humans and rogue replicants first introduced in director Sir Ridley Scott's "Blade Runner" from 1982, then revisited in Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049."

Arriving Nov. 25, 2026, "Blade Runner 2099"'s plot turns the tables as resentful artificial beings are now the ones running the show and hunting down Earth’s humans after a successful uprising against their original makers. 

This newest atmospheric trailer was unveiled at last week’s New York Comic-Con and has us totally jacked to re-immerse ourselves in that noirish futuristic realm.

Check it out below:

It’s executive produced by showrunner Silka Louisa ("Shining Girls”) and stars Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh ("Everything Everywhere All at Once") as Olwen, playing a fading replicant Blade Runner who joins forces with Hunter Schafer’s ("Euphoria") Cora, a pure human on the run attempting to evade a squad of exterminating Blade Runners while examining their existential natures.

But aside from the dazzling visuals of the City of Angels at the gates of the 22nd century, fans will also be strapping in for some cool outer space action, as evidenced by fresh footage delivering some arresting scenes of space travel, off-world planets, and Yeoh in a bizarre helmet.

"Blade Runner 2099" hits Prime Video starting on Nov. 25, 2026 (Image credit: Prime Video)
"Blade Runner 2099"'s cast includes Dimitri Abold ("The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes") and Lewis Gribben ("Somewhere Boy”) alongside Katelyn Rose Downey ("The Nun II"), Daniel Rigby ('Renegade Nell"), Johnny Harris ("A Gentleman in Moscow"), Amy Lennox ("Only Child"), Sheila Atim ("The Woman King") and Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon”).

Launching with an 8-episode debut season and executive produced by Scott Free Productions, "Blade Runner 2099" and its new world order lands on Prime Video on Nov. 25, 2026.

items.title: Mike Rogers Spent $100K on Private Jets and Luxury Travel Last Quarter
items.subtitle: Astronomical fuel prices driven ever-higher by the U.S.–Israel war in Iran might be hitting Mike Rogers, too.

items.articleBody:
Astronomical fuel prices driven ever-higher by the U.S.–Israel war in Iran might be hitting Mike Rogers, too.

The Republican candidate for Senate in Michigan spent more than $40,000 to cover a single private jet bill last month, according to campaign finance records reviewed by The Intercept. The five-figure ticket was part of over $100,000 worth of campaign cash Rogers spent on luxury travel last quarter, most of it on private jet trips.

As economic woes shape the Michigan Senate race, Roger’s opponent, Democratic candidate and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, has attacked the Republican repeatedly for his ties to corporations and billionaire donors. Rogers, who represented Michigan’s 8th District in the House from 2001 to 2015, regularly advocated in Congress to let lawmakers receive gifts and other benefits from restricted nonprofit groups. He helped defeat a 2006 bill that would have cracked down on former congressional members’ lobbying activities and banned certain privately funded trips.

For Jeffrey Hauser, a critic of corporate political influence, Rogers’s newly revealed campaign spending on luxury services might spell a warning to Michigan voters feeling the crunch of a struggling economy.

“It seems like Mike Rogers has developed a real taste for the finer things,” said Hauser, director of the Revolving Door Project, which is not backing any candidate in the Michigan race. “That means he is likely to want to continue to court, and be courted by, the economic elite, which portends badly for working class Michiganders who prefer their Senator have some understanding of their lives and identification with their interests.”

In September, the Rogers campaign paid $93,152 to JL Jets for at least five separate private charter flights, including the $40,000 transaction. Around the same time, the campaign also dropped another $500 on the luxury chauffeur company Blacklane. From July to September, Rogers’s campaign paid an additional $4,527 to Blacklane for luxury car services, including a $2,078 chauffeur expense on August 17. The campaign spent $683 on a pair of limo rides in August and September.

Campaigning requires a lot of travel, and El-Sayed’s campaign finance records show higher total travel costs — roughly $330,000 last quarter, according to public filings. But those funds went toward commercial flights on Delta and American airlines, Hertz car rentals, gas, Uber and Lyft rides, and hotel accommodations.

El-Sayed had a busier campaign calendar with a competitive Democratic primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, while Rogers was the presumed Republican nominee since the early days of the race. El-Sayed’s campaign said he did more than 500 events ahead of the August primary, and Rogers has carried a more relaxed schedule into the general election cycle.

In a statement to The Intercept, a spokesperson for Rogers pointed to El-Sayed’s spending on meals and travel on the campaign trail as well as a series of high-dollar contributions his father-in-law made to a super PAC backing the campaign.

“Abdul El-Sayed reimbursed himself $90K, and his father-in-law, a senior advisor of CAIR, gave his SuperPAC $300K,” said Rogers campaign spokesperson Abby Ronson. “If the Intercept is looking for an FEC story, I’d take a long hard look at Abdul.” The El-Sayed campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

 

 
 
 

 Related 

 
The Questionable Case of Kristi Noem’s $50 Million Luxury Jet

 
 
 

If elected, Rogers wouldn’t be the only U.S. senator to spend big on private jets. He would appear to compete with top spenders. As public scrutiny has driven politicians away from chartered flights, only Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., spent more on private flights than Rogers did last quarter, Axios reported — and they spent it over the course of a year and a half.

The Rogers campaign did book some flights with airlines like Frontier and Southwest, spending about $29,000 on 10 flights, but luxury transportation accounted for the vast majority of the campaign’s travel expenses last quarter. 

Among Rogers’s hotel spending was a $2,000 stay at The Breakers, a luxury oceanfront hotel in Palm Beach, Florida; another $1,295 at the Grand Traverse Resort and Spa in Michigan; and $200 at the five-star Palazzo at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas. In addition to travel costs, the campaign paid $2,165 to its deputy campaign manager Tyler Henningsen in late September for car repairs at a BMW dealership in Bloomfield Hills, one of Michigan’s most affluent areas. Henningsen did not immediately respond to The Intercept’s request for comment, but the Rogers spokesperson said the car was used for campaign purposes.

Luxury transportation accounted for the vast majority of the Rogers campaign’s travel expenses last quarter.

Campaign finance rules state that spending on travel and vehicle costs is allowed, as long it’s strictly for campaign purposes. It is generally illegal to use campaign funds for personal travel; if a person uses campaign funds for mixed personal and campaign travel, they have to reimburse the campaign within 30 days. If the campaign pays for a car, that car can only be used for campaigning.

Rogers holds significant personal investments in the real estate, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity industries. His Senate campaign has received significant backing from corporate figureheads such as billionaires, Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan, the DeVos family, and Elon Musk, who through his super PAC, America PAC, has poured into the race more than $6 million since Rogers promised to “shield” the world’s richest man from congressional oversight.

On the debate stage, El-Sayed has targeted Rogers’s home in Florida and his two “yachts,” attempting to paint the former congressman as out-of-touch from everyday, working Michiganders. Public records show Rogers owned two boats measuring 32 and 39 feet in Maryland, though he reportedly sold one of them. Rogers is attempting to sell his Florida home and is living full-time in Michigan, according to news outlet Bridge Michigan.

While Rogers was in Congress, he chaired the House Intelligence Committee and was a key supporter of the Patriot Act, pushing to expand domestic spying powers. Toward the end of his time in Congress, in 2013 and 2014, he and his wife Kristi attended a pair of weekend retreats at a five-star resort, The Cloister in Sea Island, Georgia, on the dime of the right-wing think tank American Enterprise Institute. At the 2014 forum, described in 2022 by CBS News as “a private, off-the-record gathering of conservative leaders and wealthy donors,” Rogers spoke as a panelist in his capacity as House Intelligence Committee chair on “cybersecurity and national security issues,” disclosure forms said. 

Alongside Rogers, the 2014 event featured prominent conservative figures as speakers, such as then-House majority leader Rep. Eric Cantor, R-Va.; Iraq War architect Karl Rove; then-Sen. Marco Rubio, R-Fla.; New York Times columnist David Brooks; then-president of the National Economic Council Gene Sperling; and Keith Alexander, director of the National Security Agency under presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama. Also in attendance were Betsy and Dick DeVos, Donald Trump’s first-term education secretary and former Amway CEO, respectively, who have since funded Rogers’s current run and several past campaigns.

 

 
 
 

 Related 

 
Former NSA Chief Keith Alexander Accused of Pump-and-Dump Investment Scheme

 
 
 

A few weeks after the conservative retreat, Alexander stepped down as NSA director under the cloud of the Edward Snowden leaks revealing the U.S. government’s role in a global spying network. That year Alexander founded cybersecurity firm IronNet, which hired Rogers in 2015 after he decided not to run for reelection. He was later elevated to a board role at IronNet — which has since gone bankrupt — and received more than $700,000 in payments and held stock with the company worth $250,000 to $500,000, according to financial disclosure forms.

“Politicians spend enormous amounts of time with the super rich, either because they are seeking to raise money from them, consulting with them about the economy, or both,” Hauser said. “As a result, they start to develop expensive tastes.”

items.title: Symposium highlights MIT’s wide range of innovations for aging brain health

items.articleBody:
From its beginning in 2015, the premise of MIT’s Aging Brain Initiative (ABI) has been that neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s are complex, “system-wide” breakdowns that will require advances of many kinds from many sources to address. The six talks at the ABI’s symposium “Innovations for the Aging Brain” on Sept. 25 illustrated what that’s come to mean at MIT, as scientists and engineers described their latest work to improve health for the aging brain.

“The ABI is unique because it brings together researchers from a diverse array of fields,” said ABI Director Li-Huei Tsai, Picower Professor in the the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory and Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences (BCS). “Today’s symposium showcases MIT’s collective brilliance across neuroscience, engineering, chemistry, and beyond.”

One of the talks, for instance, featured a team effort including Giovanni Traverso, the Karl Van Tassel (1925) Professor of Mechanical Engineering and a physician at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, who has joined forces with Tsai and other collaborators to develop an artificial intelligence system that could improve personalized Alzheimer’s care by matching patients to the best prevention interventions for them. The system integrates data from clinical trials, patient lifestyle histories, and multi-omics data (e.g., genomics, proteomics) to predict an individual’s Alzheimer’s progression and likely response to interventions. 

Speaking alongside project leads Arvid Gollwitzer, an engineer-scientist in the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, and MIT-Novo Nordisk AI Fellow Adrián Noriega de la Colina, Traverso described how the team engineered an AI model, called FINGERS-7B, to integrate these multiple highly diverse data sources into its training, thereby amassing 8 trillion “tokens” to inform its predictions.

“Every individual is very unique in their biology, and that links to how we respond to those interventions,” said Noriega. Not only could AI predictions help tailor individual prevention measures, he added, but also it could inform clinical trial designs by better pinpointing the most appropriate populations to target with a prospective drug or other treatment.

Picower Professor Earl K. Miller focused on prevention of a different problem for the aging brain: cognitive side effects from exposure to too much general anesthesia. Noting high rates of postoperative delirium in older adults after major surgery, Miller described his research with ABI founding member and Institute Professor Emery N. Brown, a Picower Institute and BCS colleague, to develop a closed-loop system that uses brain wave-based measurements of unconsciousness to optimize anesthesia dosing. Miller and Brown’s labs have shown that regardless of their molecular means of action, multiple anesthesia drugs induce unconsciousness in the same way: by shifting brainwaves out of phase with each other, disrupting the coordination of communication across the brain’s cortex that sustains cognition and consciousness. Informed by such brain wave “signatures” of unconsciousness, the system could help anesthesiologists to safely tailor dosing during surgery.

In her talk, associate professor of mechanical engineering Ritu Raman, the Eugene Bell Career Development Chair of Tissue Engineering, described how she’s approaching the study of neuromuscular diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and muscular dytrophies, by developing advanced lab models of muscle tissue that also integrate nerves and vasculature. For instance, for ALS, her lab has been able to make the cultures from induced pluripotent stem cells derived from patients. The lab models give her team an opportunity to examine neuromuscular junctions in detail and to model how they change in response to potentially therapeutic drugs.

In many neurodegenerative diseases associated with aging, such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s, a major pathology is misfolding and aggregation of intrinsically disordered proteins, such as amyloid-beta or alpha-synuclein. In her talk, William R (1964) and Daniel L. (1995) Young Career Development Assistant Professor of Chemistry Oleta Johnson described her lab’s work to prevent aggregation before it starts. In pursuit of that strategy, she said her lab’s research is focused on developing the chemical knowledge and means to identify proteins at issue, detect that they are moving into a problematic state, and then control their conformation.

Eugene McDermott Professor in the Brain Sciences and Human Behavior Alan Jasanoff, a member of the BCS and Biological Engineering departments as well as the McGovern Institute for Brain Research, described a very different application of chemistry to aging brain research. He described how his lab develops novel chemical probes to make molecules in the brain visible in magnetic resonance imaging. These include the neuromodulatory enzyme cholinesterase, which is the target of many of the few drugs approved to treat Alzheimer’s, and also lipids, which several brain cell types mishandle in Alzheimer’s, Tsai and others have shown. His lab has also developed technology to genetically encode a novel probe in brain cells to improve MRI visualization of brain activity.

And while many researchers focus on the prominent problems that proteins or lipids present in neurodegenerative disease, Novartis Professor of Chemistry Laura Kiessling discussed a less-appreciated but still important component of cellular function: sugars called glycans that line the surface of cells. In particular, researchers have linked a glycan called heparan sulfate to Alzheimer’s disease. Kiessling’s lab, working with ABI founding member Ed Boyden, Y. Eva Tan Professor of Neurotechnology, is working to characterize and understand glycans. Her lab, for instance, has shown that glycans of different sequences organize on cell membranes so that they can bind and recruit specific proteins to distinct regions on cells.

“We are really excited about the fact that we’ve observed this now for the first time and have a toolkit to study other diseases,” she said. Understanding glycan binding could even give scientists a means to target different cells and cellular processes.

Following the six talks, more than a dozen trainees at a poster session presented even more aging brain-related projects from around the Institute, further highlighting MIT’s diversity of research in the area, something the ABI exists to encourage.

From massive AI datasets to the sugars on individual cells, the symposium highlighted how MIT scientists are pushing the frontiers of science and engineering to improve understanding of, and interventions for, the health of the aging brain.

 Our latest midterm forecast

Updated October 19, 2026

You might notice that this page looks a little different today. Because we have so many charts — and want to add even more before Election Day — we’ve created three new pages to house our Senate, House, and gubernatorial forecasts.

This page will still contain our topline forecast and the most interesting charts for each chamber. If you have any problems with navigating between these pages please let us know. -NS & EMD, 10/19/26

ELSEWHERE IN FLIPR: 

House forecast —>

Senate forecast —>

Governors forecast —>

See also: Generic congressional ballot dashboard and Donald Trump approval rating dashboard.

This is the landing page for FLIPR1, Silver Bulletin’s 2026 election forecast.2 This page is designed to be viewed on the web rather than in our email client or in the Substack app. If you’re curious about how the model works, and what’s new for 2026 (quite a lot, actually), we also have a very detailed methodology article.

The polls

The Silver Bulletin polling averages account for whether polls are conducted among registered or likely voters, and for house effects. They weight more reliable polls more heavily. They also include a “timeline adjustment”, where outdated polls are revised to reflect trends in the generic ballot. Speaking of the generic ballot, you can find a version of it with our likely-voter adjustment below; this is the version that FLIPR uses.

We draw most of the election polls used in our model from The New York Times poll database3, but collect generic ballot and congressional approval polls ourselves.

The topline

Here are today’s topline numbers for Senate and House control. They are typically based on 40,000 simulations and include a small amount of sampling error. FLIPR models House, Senate and gubernatorial elections jointly, meaning that we can calculate the probability of things like Republicans holding the Senate but losing the House.

items.articleBody:
Seldom used today, the word "expiation" refers to the act of atoning for a sin. In the case of this elegant chapel, the sin in question was regicide. 

The Chapel of Expiation is built on top of the old Madeleine Cemetery, which became an egalitarian dumping ground for rich and poor alike during the French Revolution. This included King Louis XVI and his wife Marie Antoinette, who were hastily buried with little fanfare on the days of their executions. (Ironically enough, the cemetery also held the remains of many who perished during a stampede caused by the king and queen's wedding celebrations.)

When the Bourbon dynasty was restored, the new Louis XVIII set about turning his brother and sister-in-law into martyrs. While the king and queen were quickly dug up and reburied in the royal Basilica of Saint Denis, it was soon decided that a grand monument would be erected to their memory, covering the entire square footage of the old cemetery.

It's a peaceful spot to visit today, with a courtyard garden surrounded by symbolic tombs leading up to the central chapel. Inside, marble sculptures of the king and queen kneel at the feet of an angel and an allegory of religion, piously awaiting their executions. On a lower level, an altar marks the exact spot where the king's body was exhumed.

After future revolutions ended the monarchy for good, the chapel became an ambiguous and uncomfortable symbol of the old order. Restorationists continued to attend its services as a political statement, anti-monarchists campaigned for its demolition, and the short-lived Paris Commune of 1871 even passed legislation to do so.

The chapel was eventually deconsecrated and listed as a historic monument. Nevertheless, a mass continues to be held there once a year to commemorate the king's execution, and it remains a popular destination for the small minority of French conservatives who hold out hope for a return of the monarchy.

items.articleBody:
In surreal tableaux, mythological creatures interact with flora and fauna within dream-like realms. Insects, stars, metaphysical tendrils, and all-seeing eyes accompany human bodies with the heads of raptors. Rithika Merchant’s strange yet alluring symmetry contains what may be esoteric rituals or communions with the natural world. Each speculative, fable-like narrative taps into our collective anxiety about the environment and hope for healing.

Merchant’s vibrant new body of work centers on hybrid creatures and a sense of the sacred, comprising the Mumbai-based artist’s solo exhibition The Dreaming Realm at Galerie LJ. She harnesses elemental phenomena like the earth, plants, fire, water, and the stars to emphasize both volatility and strength. Amid scenes of floods and eruptions, individuals participate in enigmatic activities or ceremonies exemplifying cooperation and determination.

Merchant incorporates “theoretical, historical, and iconographic references, drawing notably on the notion of empirical experience based on sensory perception, the Greek concept of Kairos to question the subjectivity of time, as well as research on the Beguines of the Middle Ages,” the gallery says. The Beguines were a unique lay community of financially independent Christian women who occasionally practiced mysticism. Some communities in western Europe still exist today.

In The Dreaming Realm, the artist nods to symbols of consciousness and transformation. For example, the luna moth evokes the power of intuition and transitions, while ravens represent wisdom, foresight, and a bridge to other realms. Communality forms a conceptual nucleus of Merchant’s paintings, especially in her ongoing series Interspecies Care, which focuses “on social organization, interdependence, reciprocity between species, and knowledge sharing,” the gallery says.

The Dreaming Realm continues through November 21 in Paris. See more on Merchant’s Instagram.

items.title: Going in the opposite direction
items.subtitle: All this talk about AI, and what is doing to the arts, has made me reflect on what I enjoy about art, both as an audience member, and as an artist.

items.articleBody:
All this talk about AI, and what is doing to the arts, has made me reflect on what I enjoy about art, both as an audience member, and as an artist.

My personal take (that had I studied art history and philosophy I would connect to some greater canon of thinking), is that art is human expression and craft, pursued for its own sake. A sunset or a rainbow can be beautiful, but they are not art, as they are not the result of human minds and hands.

I have always gravitated especially towards art, where the humans behind are strongly felt in the work. Art that is the result idiosyncratic taste. Art made with skills that took time and attention to acquire. Art that is shaped by the particular way the artist handle their tools, as a result of their particular body and mind. Art where the imperfections tells a story about the limitations the artist was working under. Art, where you can “see the fingerprints left on the clay”. Art that feels connected to a place and a moment in time. Art that is in conversation with the langer world of art, without pandering to it. Ect.

For the lack of a better word, I call this quality “vitality”.

The concept also connects to what I enjoy about making art.

I enjoy the act of making and playing. Of feeling my hands on the keys and knobs. Of feeling that sensory feedback loop of making a move, and sensing the result. Of being in flow. Of practicing a skill day after day, and getting better.Of going deep on a subject, and having my new found knowledge spark new ideas. Of listening and looking at stuff I made, making reflections about how to improve upon it, and trying again. Of listening to something I made years ago, and feeling the sense memory of where I was and who I was at that time. Of somebody reacting to something I’ve made, and feeling like I’ve successfully communicated something that I couldn’t with words alone.

In other words, I like living with an art practice. I like how the iterative and recursive act of making art is shaping and sharpening my mind over time. The end result - the artifact itself - is only a small part of the reward.

For me, AI is completely antithetical to all of this. My personal belief is that AI is the most unethical and antisocial technology of our time. But let’s set that aside, as that the ethics of AI is being debated in depth in another thread. Even stil, I just find AI generated/assisted art uninteresting. It’s often clear, that while there’s human intent behind it, that its “authors” have not gone through the process of developing their ideas, taste, or understanding of their medium and material very deeply. The art, in my eyes, shows very little vitality.

While I catch myself getting caught up in cynicism at times, I want to look towards the future with hope and optimism. I want to build the world I want to live in. Make the art I want to see in the world. To be more human, out of principle and out of spite.

So I want to pose this question: how can we make art that is even more human, more personal, and carries even more vitality?

For me I’m going about it in a few different ways:

I’m exploring expressive controllers (Touché at the moment), to have a more intimate and immediate connection with the sounds I’m producing.

I’m going drilling chords and scales, doing ear training, and practicing improvisation, so as to expand upon my ability to express myself spontaneously through music.

I’m chasing the sounds I want to hear. The stuff I’ve like the best by others have not fit neatly into boxes. So I’m trying to be less of a statistical average.

I’m increasingly interested as musical recording as capture of a moment in time. While sound on sound recording was revolutionary to music, I feel like DAW culture has led os to polish the humanity out of music. There’s something raw about unedited, long take performances that has a vitality to it that I can’t get enough of at the moment.

I’m exploring the use of sensors that bring the environment of the moment into the music.

I try, the best I can to collect instruments by passionate instrument makers with strong perspectives, so that I can, in a small way, collaborate, be in conversation with them, and support them.

What I want to do more of:

Play on video, and eventually learn (to dare) to play live, as to show the human behind the electronics

Learn more about electronics and DSP, as I believe the best ideas come from a deep understanding and conversation with materials

In general overcome by own introversion/hermit-tendencies and make a deeper effort to connect IRL and online.

I’m not yet a user or programmer of monome tools (but plan to - just moving at a pace that my wallet allows), but I was drawn to lines because of the sensibility that to me was about a love of craft, chasing depth, and saying no to the ideals of big business and tech. In their 20 year retrospective, Brian and Kelli described their journey as being one towards “other ways of being”. That resonated with me deeply.

So in a society that seems to be increasingly obsessed with chasing the un-human, how can we make our art more human? How can we go in the opposite direction? That’s the counter culture I want to see.

(btw - non of this should be seen as commentary about acoustic vs. synthetic sounds. I like synths haha)

items.articleBody:
15 Ancient Greek Artifacts Worth Nearly $3 Million Are Finally Returning Home

Bronze helmet with winged figures and intertwined serpents, Greek, Cretan, late 7th century BCE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

Ancient artifacts can spend decades far from where they were originally found. But for 15 Greek antiquities that were recently held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, that journey is finally coming to an end. The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office recently announced the repatriation of 15 artifacts collectively valued at nearly $3 million. The objects were seized from The Met as part of multiple investigations into antiquities trafficking and have now been formally returned to Greece.

Together, the works span thousands of years of history. Among them are five pieces of bronze armor from ancient Crete, a terracotta beak-spouted jug dating to around 1750–1700 BCE, and a Roman marble head from the first century CE.

15 ancient Greek artifacts valued at nearly $3 million have been returned to Greece after being held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Bronze helmet with horses and lions, Greek, Cretan, late 7th century BCE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

Among the returned objects are five intricately decorated pieces of bronze armor dating to the late 7th century BCE.

Some of the most striking pieces are the five examples of bronze armor. Dating to the late 7th century BCE, the group includes two helmets and three bronze armor plates designed to protect the lower abdomen. Despite their practical purpose, the pieces are incredibly ornate. One helmet is decorated with winged figures holding intertwined serpents, while another features horses and lions. The three bronze armor plates are covered with images of horses, winged horses, and sphinxes.

Bronze protective plate with sphinxes, Greek, Cretan, late 7th century BCE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

Greek authorities traced the armor back to an illegal excavation carried out in 1964 at Afrati on the island of Crete. Similar artifacts from the same excavation are already housed at the Archaeological Museum of Heraklion, meaning these newly returned pieces can finally be reunited with objects from the same archaeological site more than 60 years later.

Bronze protective plate with winged horses, Greek, Cretan, late 7th century BCE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

Other works making their way home include a nearly 4,000-year-old terracotta jug and a Roman marble head from the first century CE.

Another object making its way home is a terracotta beak-spouted jug dating to around 1750–1700 BCE. The vessel was looted from a burial site in Greece before traveling through Switzerland and the United Kingdom and eventually entering The Met’s collection. A Roman marble head from the first century CE is also among the returned works. The sculpture is believed to represent Genius, the personification of an emperor’s spirit.

Terracotta beak-spouted jug, Helladic, ca. 1750–1700 BCE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

Marble head of a veiled man, Roman, first half of the 1st century CE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

For some of the artifacts, returning to Greece also means being reunited with objects from the archaeological sites where they were originally found.

The Met says information uncovered through the Manhattan District Attorney’s investigations, along with its own provenance research, helped determine that the objects should be returned to Greece. For Greek Minister of Culture Lina Mendoni, their return is about more than recovering valuable works of art. “Every repatriation is an act of justice towards our history,” she says, “but also proof that the illicit trafficking of cultural property can be effectively confronted when we join forces with trust, consistency, and determination.”

The Manhattan DA’s Antiquities Trafficking Unit has recovered thousands of cultural objects in recent years and returned them to countries around the world. But for some of these 15 artifacts, the homecoming is especially significant. After decades away, they can once again be seen alongside objects from the archaeological sites where their stories began.

Bronze protective plate with horses, Greek, Cretan, late 7th century BCE. (Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Public domain)

Sources: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Returns Objects to the Hellenic Republic; D.A. Bragg Announces Return of 15 Antiquities to the People of Greece

items.articleBody:
John Steinbeck in 1949. Photograph courtesy of Los Angeles Daily News via Wikimedia Commons. LICENSED UNDER CC BY 4.0.

Each week, The Paris Review unlocks stories, poems, and interviews from our archive for our readers. This week, we’ve unlocked the two parts of John Steinbeck’s Art of Fiction interview from issue no. 45 (Fall 1969) and issue no. 63 (Fall 1975).  

“I have noticed so many of the reviews of my work show a fear and a hatred of ideas and speculations,” wrote John Steinbeck in an unsent letter to his editor, Pascal Covici. “It seems to be true,” he continued, “that people can only take parables fully clothed with flesh. Any attempt to correlate in terms of thought is frightening. And if that is so, East of Eden is going to take a bad beating because it is full of such things.”

For issue no. 48 of the Review, published in the fall of 1969, the magazine’s editorial staff compiled a number of comments Steinbeck had made over the years—on topics like “the art of writing,” “titles,” and “luck”—mostly sourced from the unsent letters Steinbeck wrote to Covici while drafting East of Eden. In the fall of 1975, the Review published a continuation of that interview, including passages in which Steinbeck comments on “hack writing,” “having a writer in the family,” and “fame.” This week, we’ve unlocked both interviews from the archive.

INTERVIEW

The Art of Fiction No. 45

John Steinbeck

A writer out of loneliness is trying to communicate like a distant star sending signals. He isn’t telling or teaching or ordering. Rather he seeks to establish a relationship of meaning, of feeling, of observing. We are lonesome animals. We spend all life trying to be less lonesome. One of our ancient methods is to tell a story begging the listener to say—and to feel—“Yes, that’s the way it is, or at least that’s the way I feel it. You’re not as alone as you thought.” Of course a writer rearranges life, shortens time intervals, sharpens events, and devises beginnings, middles and ends. We do have curtains—in a day, morning, noon and night, in a man, birth, growth and death.

From issue no. 48 (Fall 1969)

INTERVIEW

The Art of Fiction No. 45 (Continued)

John Steinbeck

My first gem called forth quite adverse criticism, although I considered it extremely apropos at the time. It was published on a board fence, and was in the form of free verse. It ran something like this:

Gertie loves Tom, and

Tom loves Gertie.

From issue no. 63 (Fall 1975)

 

Sign up for the Redux newsletter to receive these pieces in your inbox every Sunday morning.

Hazel Byers is the Review’s engagement editor.

items.articleBody:
Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.

Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles: 

Shaping trustworthy digital experiences for children online. An IEEE collaboration with Indonesian policymakers led to a new regulation to protect children, a first of its kind in the region. The advanced frameworks used for the design of Internet platforms and systems are based on the IEEE 2089-2021 and 2089.1-2024 standards. The IEEE 2089-2021 Standard for an Age-Appropriate Digital Services Framework Based on the 5Rights Principles for Children provides practical steps to qualify online products and services. The follow-up, the IEEE 2089.1-2024 Standard for Online Age Verification, provides a framework for designing, specifying, evaluating, and deploying age-verification systems. You can learn more about the two standards in “IEEE Makes Strides to Improve Online Safety for Kids.”

Catalyzing humanitarian outreach. Last year IEEE launched its Mobile Outreach Vehicle (MOVE) program in India. The vehicle brings educational resources to communities and can provide communication and technology support to relief workers and survivors during emergencies. In 2024, for example, MOVE helped survivors of Hurricanes Helene and Milton in the Southeastern United States. When the vehicles are not deployed, IEEE MOVE remains engaged in outreach efforts, participating in 25 STEM educational events such as one in San Diego in 2023.

Preserving Tech History. The IEEE Global Museum, developed by the IEEE History Center, presents traveling exhibits to educate the public about the history of technology and its impact on society. In “IEEE’s Global Museum Brings Engineering History to You,” you can learn about current exhibits “Unseen Signals: E. Howard Armstrong’s Radio Revolution” and “Microchips That Shook the World.”

EPICS in IEEE. This program provides nonprofit organizations with technology solutions while broadening undergraduate students’ hands-on experiences. Last year US $290,000 was awarded to a record-breaking number of service projects around the world. Among the 48 projects was one in which a student team in Macedonia created IoT-driven sensing and display devices to help measure and promote awareness of pollution and air-quality issues in the capital city of Skopje.

IEEE TryEngineering. This initiative inspires preuniversity students to pursue technology and engineering careers. It awarded US $70,379 in grants to 58 programs around the world. One is its TryEngineering Summer Institute, a nine-day summer sleepaway camp for students ages 13 to 17. More than 310 students participated last year, learning about aerospace and artificial intelligence.

IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu. IEEE-HKN has more than 260 collegiate chapters worldwide and more than 200,000 members. The honor society encourages and recognizes excellence in education, professional practice, and meritorious work within IEEE’s designated fields of interest. IEEE-HKN members last year contributed 110,442 volunteer hours to universities and communities, and they held 827 service and outreach events and 137 STEM outreach activities. Last year IEEE and HKN celebrated the 15th anniversary of their merger.

IEEE Connecting the Unconnected Challenge. This annual global competition solicits innovative solutions from startups, grassroots organizations, universities, and others working to bridge the digital divide. The Institute wrote about last year’s winners. They included a solar-powered community broadband network in Tanzania, a low-cost method for accessing the Internet that uses FM radio and a short message service, and a strategy for utilizing India’s rural broadband infrastructure to deliver medical services to people living in isolated, tribal, and other underserved regions.

Supporting Sustainable Climate Efforts. IEEE helps foster the exchange of technical knowledge and information to develop technologies for a sustainable climate. “IEEE Plays a Pivotal Role in Climate Mitigation Talks” reported how the organization enhanced its standing as a trusted, neutral authority on the role of technology in climate change mitigation and adaptation. Leaders, including 2023 IEEE President Saifur Rahman, showcased tech solutions at COP30 and the International Symposium on Achieving a Sustainable Climate. Also, “IEEE Young Professionals Talked Sustainability Tech at Climate Week NYC” reported on the group’s activities during the 2024 Climate Week NY, the largest annual climate event, featuring more than 600 activities throughout New York City.

Engineering: A force for good

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

items.articleBody:
This is the weekly visible open thread. Post about anything you want, ask random questions, whatever. ACX has an unofficial subreddit, Discord, and bulletin board, and in-person meetups around the world. Most content is free, some is subscriber only; you can subscribe here. Also:

1: Meetup changes in Rockville, Northampton, Eindhoven, Great Barrington, Cairo, Portland, and Sofia. Check the post for more information.

2: The Boston ACX meetup group has finished their Greater Boston general election voting guide. I may have more of these in the upcoming week. Still trying to figure out if we can do something for the Bay Area, but remember that SF mail-in ballot registration due date is end-of-day today (Monday), and that our main SF endorsement is Scott Wiener for Congress. We may have more later.

3: I’m continuing to work on modeling (and maybe one day automating) some parts of AI grantmaking (you can see previous efforts here). I would once again like people who are well-versed in the AI/grantmaking worlds to take a survey on how much they value various things. This one involves assigning utility weights to ~80 different AI safety accomplishments. Take it here. After you’ve taken that survey, if you still have more time/energy it would be extra helpful for my data collection if you would take this alternate version, which asks you to predict how I would answer the first survey (so I can separate out worldview differences from weight-choosing random noise).

4: Bay Area ACX meetup is scheduled for this coming Saturday, 10/24, 1 PM, at Mox in SF (1680 Mission St). I’ll probably make a post about it, but consider this an early heads-up.

5: Grantee and Manifold Markets co-founder Stephen Grugett announces his latest project: MNX is a real-money prediction market on AI. It lets people sell futures representing AI company stocks, bet on AI company revenues directly, and a few other things like Epoch Capabilities Index targets. Interestingly, despite the talk of Anthropic’s API falling from from $2T to $1.5T, both Polymarket and MNX still price it around $2T.

6: Friend of the blog Goodheart Labs is working on Common Notes, aka “Twitter Community Notes, but for everything”. They’re implementing it through a combination of AIs (who write most notes), users (who write others, and vote on which ones are helpful), and a browser extension (which makes the system show up on everything, including this blog). Check it out, and install the browser extension, here.
