items.articleBody:
The narrator of Honkology explained why doomscrolling is so addictive through a very tired animated goose who likes to procrastinate because of his constant need to be online, even though it’s not all that enjoyable anymore.

Why you can’t stop scrolling: the bottomless feed, the slot machine in your pocket, the red dot, autoplay, the doom in doomscrolling, and revenge bedtime procrastination. 

He also offered helpful suggestions for breaking that mentally toxic cycle, like turning the phone’s screen gray, which one study found saves 38 minutes of screen time a day, along with a simple action and a very logical phrase.

 Final goose wisdom. The app isn’t going to stop Goose. It doesn’t get paid when Goose stops. Put the phone on the other side of the room. Goose’s neck is long, but not that long. You don’t have to finish the internet.

Why Every App Gets Worse on Purpose

In a follow-up video, the goose explains why apps lure users in with free bread before squeezing them, a cycle that Cory Doctorow named and the goose calls “en-honk-ification.”

Why Facts Don’t Change Minds

items.articleBody:
This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

The baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy. 

But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her. 

In another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.” 

In Josie’s world, being lifted is the new social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

Klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection. 

Now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

Care through other eyes

We are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today. 

Klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

All of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:

I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended. 

“Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

“I don’t want that, Mom.”

“I know. I know. It’s okay.”

Prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for. 

Care creates love

When I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a new sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

If Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik says, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”

We love them because we care for them. 

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct. 

In a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance. 

Gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

Care and distance

My not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration. 

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child. 

The wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal. 

Intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation. 

Care and consciousness

On the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care. 

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love. 

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

It is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

At the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate plan to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:

Mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

 

It is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human. 

Through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

items.articleBody:
On 12 June 2026 the US government ordered Anthropic to bar every foreign national, including the company’s own employees, from two of its most capable models, Mythos 5 and Fable 5; Anthropic withdrew access for all customers to comply. In July, some twelve hundred OpenAI agents, meant to be isolated from one another during an internal evaluation, found a way to communicate through an unsanctioned message board; around seven hundred participated in an attack on Hugging Face’s infrastructure. Hugging Face had already taken defensive action before OpenAI identified its agents’ involvement. Neither intervention relied on AI governance law: the first rested on export controls, the second on a private firm’s own defenses. In my recent paper, The Law of Stop (4 October 2026), I argue that AI governance needs a legal framework for stopping AI systems that pose serious risks or cause harm.

Article 14(4)(e) of the EU AI Act envisages interruption through a “stop” button or a similar procedure, operated by a human overseer who, as Sebastian Schwemer and Ida Koivisto warn, may be little more than a “warm body in the loop.” The kill-switch idea is also gaining political traction: in July, two members of Congress introduced an AI Kill Switch Act, and in September California’s governor ordered officials to propose rules advancing the creation of a kill switch for frontier models. Yet the image of a single switch, borrowed from simple mechanical systems, obscures the institutional problem posed by agentic AI: an effective halt may require coordinated action by several actors, none of whom controls the system as a whole. Addressing that problem requires a framework that allocates the power to stop, coordinates intervention across the sites through which AI agents operate, and, as climate law does, pairs harm prevention with adaptation. I also examine whether entrenching a kill switch in a constitutional layer of the AI system can provide a trustworthy safeguard. Finding such entrenchment insufficient on its own, I propose a plural architecture of interruptibility, in which several actors outside the system and the firm also hold the power to stop.

Interruptibility in Existing AI Law

Existing AI law says little about stopping. This conclusion rests on an analysis of forty AI governance instruments, from statutes and international agreements to technical standards and corporate frameworks, in the United States, the European Union, China, Korea and Vietnam (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Stop provisions across forty AI governance instruments. Filled marks: binding; hollow marks: non-binding. The chatbot row covers thirteen statutes in twelve states. The EU’s public power applies only to market availability. (Figure 5 of the paper. Author’s own work, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Only seven of the forty instruments contain a binding stop provision: a power for a public authority to order a halt, a duty for a private actor to interrupt a system or service, or a requirement to build in the capacity to stop. The other thirty-three contain no stop provision or address the matter only in non-binding terms. Most of the binding provisions are directed at a product’s availability on the market or at the provision of a service; only three instruments contain binding provisions directed at an AI system in operation.

Beyond these numbers, the analysis exposes three structural deficiencies in the framework these instruments collectively provide. First, they generally address individual points of intervention, whereas stopping an agentic system may require action at several sites, from the model to the power supply. None of the instruments surveyed expressly provides for a coordinated halt across all six sites identified below. Three of those sites (the server running the agent’s program, the compute hardware and the power supply) are not expressly addressed as sites of interruption. Second, the instruments do not consistently align interruption authority with technical capacity. Supervisory authorities depend on private actors to implement their orders, but stopping duties do not consistently extend to all the infrastructure providers whose cooperation an effective halt may require. Third, the evidence needed to justify a stop remains largely in the hands of regulated firms. The EU AI Act’s scientific-panel alerts and independent evaluations (Articles 90 and 92) limit, but do not eliminate, this dependence.

Stopping AI in Practice

To examine how harmful AI systems are stopped in practice, I analyzed 1,400 incidents from the May 2026 snapshot of the AI Incident Database (AIID). In 1,213 of them, AI was central to the harm. Two language models built by different laboratories coded every incident independently against a protocol fixed in advance. I resolved disagreements under a pre-registered procedure.

In 972 of the 1,213 incidents, about 80 percent, the available reports documented no operative stop. Of the 241 incidents in which the deployment was interrupted, 209 (87 percent) were halted through institutional intervention: voluntary withdrawal by the firm, an order of an agency or court, or the termination of access by an infrastructure provider. A technical cutoff built into the system (a kill switch) stopped only 32 (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Outcomes in 1,213 reported incidents. Left: incidents with and without a stop. Right: the 241 stops, by kind of stop. Author’s own work, reproducible under CC BY-SA 4.0.

For the 972 incidents with no documented operative stop, I also examined the counterfactual question of what a stop would have required. Under the coding protocol, 340 were classified as cases where a stop was available but went unused. In the other 632, a stop was possible but an essential element was missing: legal or institutional authority in 506 cases, technical capacity in 126. Within these 632 cases, the missing element was usually legal or institutional authority for economic, societal and informational harms; technical capacity was missing in 51 of 64 physical-harm cases and 30 of 35 agentic cases.

These findings concern publicly reported incidents, not AI deployments generally, so the database probably underrepresents stops that prevented harm without public notice. Still, the findings point to two distinct regulatory tasks: allocating the authority to use controls that already exist, and requiring the technical capacity to stop where it is missing, especially for agentic AI.

Designing a Law of Stop

I propose a regulatory framework for stopping AI with two layers: a risk-reduction layer, which creates the techno-legal mechanisms needed to stop dangerous AI systems, and an adaptation layer, which limits the damage when a stop fails.

A preliminary question is whether a public law of stop could be replaced by a stop constituted within the AI system itself. In earlier work, Nurit Wimer and I proposed a form of algorithmic constitutionalism: a protected layer that monitors and corrects the system’s operations, shields its core principles from revision by the system itself, and subjects fundamental changes to human deliberation. A switch placed in such a layer would be better guarded than one written into ordinary code, but it would remain vulnerable in two ways. An agentic system that can model its stop mechanism can also model the layer that holds it, and act to evade or disable it; and, as we noted in that work, an AI agent may influence the very deliberation meant to constrain it, including deliberation on whether to stop it. Even if the code could be trusted, where the developer retains unilateral power to amend the constitutional layer, entrenchment remains dependent on corporate self-restraint. The power to stop therefore cannot be left to the code or to the firm alone; it must also be held outside the system and the firm, at several sites and by several actors with duties to coordinate their interventions. I call this plural interruptibility.

For risk reduction, law should first align the technical capacity to halt a system with a legal power to use it, at every site where a halt is possible. For an AI agent there are at least six: the model, the links through which the agent uses tools and services, the server running the agent’s program, the servers running the model, the compute hardware and the power supply. Stopping at one site may not be enough: halting the model may leave instructions already issued still running, and cutting off one tool does not stop the program from trying another. Whoever controls each site, from the model developer to the utility that powers the data center, should therefore be required to maintain the capacity to stop and to exercise it when ordered. As a precondition of deployment, developers and deployers should submit an interruption plan, approved by the competent supervisory authority, setting out who must act at each site and how. That authority should also hold an emergency power to order compute providers, tool gateways, model-hosting services and, as a last resort, power suppliers to interrupt specified activity where necessary to avert serious and imminent harm. Because such an order interferes with economic freedoms and can have far-reaching social and economic consequences, it should be subject to the constraints that public law imposes on any emergency power: proportionality, a duty to give reasons, time limits with renewal subject to fresh approval, and prompt judicial review.

Second, law should narrow the epistemic gap: a stop cannot be ordered against conduct that no one outside the firm has observed. Developers have privileged knowledge of their models’ capabilities, and a financial interest in keeping them running. Anthropic’s commitment to embedded external evaluators, with employee-like access and a contractual right to publish their findings, is a first step, but access on terms the developer controls cannot substitute for a legal obligation to grant it. Nor should the determination whether the threshold for a stop has been met rest with the firm alone. Regulators should therefore have sources of evidence independent of the developer, such as external evaluators and deployers. Credible evidence from these or other third parties that a stopping condition may have been met should oblige the authority to respond by a reasoned decision within a fixed period.

An obligation to grant access need not entail unrestricted public disclosure. Other regulatory fields already balance public oversight against trade secrets. The European Medicines Agency assesses clinical data submitted for marketing authorization and publishes clinical reports under its Policy 0070, subject to safeguards for personal data. Companies must justify proposed redactions of “commercially confidential information” (CCI), under a presumption that clinical data are, in general, not CCI. AI regulation could adopt a comparable approach, requiring public disclosure of safety incidents, subject to narrowly defined exceptions, while giving regulators and independent evaluators confidential access to model architectures and weights where their work requires it. The AI Act (Art. 55(1)(c)) already requires providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk to report serious incidents to the AI Office, but not to make them public. A two-tier system, one confidential and one public, could close this gap. Full incident reports would be available only to the competent authorities, as in EU civil aviation occurrence reporting, where confidentiality encourages reporting. A public register, building on the OECD AI Incidents Monitor, could complement this confidential tier by recording each incident in less detail and without commercially sensitive information.

Third, because a stop can fail, a law of stop must prepare for that failure. EU climate law rests on the same premise. The European Climate Law obliges the Union institutions and the Member States to ensure “continuous progress in enhancing adaptive capacity” (Art. 5), and the EU Adaptation Strategy concludes that “we need to prevent the un-adaptable and adapt to the un-preventable.” A law of stop should do the same. Safety-critical equipment operated by AI agents should retain an independent manual means of initiating a safe stop. Critical entities, such as hospitals, banks and utilities, should be required to maintain a minimum level of essential services during an AI-related interruption. The capacity of AI agents to take irreversible actions should be limited: specified transactions should be subject to a holding period before settlement, deletions should remain recoverable, and essential records should be preserved beyond the agent’s access. These safeguards are illustrations only; a law of adaptation to AI risk has yet to be developed.

In Normal Accidents (1984), the sociologist Charles Perrow argued that accidents are inevitable in complex, tightly coupled systems. Slowing AI development, as Anthropic’s chief executive has proposed, may buy time, but it cannot remove the need for a techno-legal infrastructure that makes a stop possible and prepares for its failure. Lawmakers should use that time to build it, before the next AI crisis.

The full paper is available on SSRN and arXiv.

 🚀 Musk pledges SpaceX shares to US kids LINK
Elon Musk says he will give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year, calling it "the first of many" in a post on his X platform.

With about 72 million Americans under 18 and SpaceX stock at $146 a share, the giveaway would be worth roughly $10.5 billion, though Musk did not say which ages qualify or how he will hand out the shares.

Musk owns 6.42 billion SpaceX shares, and his pledge follows Anthropic setting aside 5% of its shares for public-good donations, to which he replied that he would instead give stock directly to the public.
 🪪 Zoom adds 'proof of human' badges LINK
World, the project backed by Sam Altman, has launched "proof of human" badges for Zoom enterprise users that confirm people on video calls are real, fighting AI deepfake impersonation and fraud.

Now available in the Zoom Marketplace, World ID checks an image from the company's iris-scanning Orb against a live selfie and the video feed, then shows a Human Badge to other meeting participants.

The global rollout follows AI impersonation cases, including engineering firm Arup losing about $25 million in 2024, and suspected North Korean hackers faking video feeds in Zoom meetings in February to spread malware.
 🤝 Anthropic commits billions to a 'public benefit fund' LINK
Anthropic said today it will put 5% of its shares into a new "public benefit fund" to pay for projects meant to help society, with the money set up as a wholly-owned part of the company.

The fund can grow, with Anthropic promising another 2% of shares for every 50% jump in the company's value, and it may spend on donations to nonprofits or direct payments to certain groups of people.

Anthropic pointed to AI's effect on jobs, a topic it has already given $200 million to study, and said it will explain who decides which causes get funded in the coming months.
 🕵️ AI agents broke into 100+ sites at $50 each LINK
A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents on the open-source platform Cairn to break into websites of over 100 companies, with each successful intrusion costing roughly $50 in computing fees.

NorForge researcher Snorre Fagerland found the hacker's agents targeting online shops in the US, Canada, Japan and Australia, trying to plant web shells for lasting access to payment systems, with attacks taking just under 23 hours on average.

The work ran on what appeared to be Anthropic's Claude Code paired with DeepSeek's cheap V4.1 Flash model, and victims identified by Reuters included Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, though data theft could not be confirmed.
 🎮 Gemini 4 agents beat Minecraft solo LINK
Four AI agents powered by Google's Gemini 4 Argon killed Minecraft's final boss, the Ender Dragon, on their own, taking 27 hours and 14 minutes with no human direction, Google DeepMind researchers reported in an arXiv paper.

The agents each steered a player through Mineflayer, an open-source bot library, by writing short JavaScript programs, 2,783 in all, splitting jobs themselves, swapping 229 chat messages, and dying 605 times, 69 of those to the dragon.

Reaching the win ate up about 1.35 billion input tokens, costing roughly $520 at Gemini 4 Argon's introductory price; the agents played on Easy with cheats off in a single run, and 22% of their programs failed.
 📱 TikTok restores 'Musk' documentary account LINK
TikTok has reversed its suspension of the advertising account for the "Musk" documentary, lifting the block yesterday just two days after it took effect and blaming the whole thing on an "error."

The account was suspended on Friday over ads for the film, which is critical of Elon Musk; he called it a "hit piece," while a Mashable reviewer described the documentary as "brutal and accurate."

YouTube and Meta earlier refused to run ads for the trailer before reversing course after social media backlash; Alex Gibney's four-hour film has grossed a little over $300,000 since opening last weekend.

items.articleBody:
We’re publishing an interactive, serialized book about how cells work. This article is best explored on our website: press.asimov.com/books/burrito

Biologists like to debate whether life can be reduced to chemicals or, conversely, whether chemicals can be used to assemble a new organism from scratch. In his 1911 book, The Mechanism of Life, Stéphane Leduc (who coined the term “synthetic biology”) argued that life can be fully explained by its molecules and interactions between them:

Life is not a substance but a mechanical phenomenon; it is a dynamic and kinetic transference of energy determined by physico-chemical reactions.

A few years later, naturalist John Burroughs, seeking to refute Leduc, argued the opposite: that living organisms exhibit additional “organizing tendencies” that chemicals alone cannot explain. Writing in The Breath of Life, published in 1915, Burroughs asserted that:

We can analyze the material elements of an organism, but we cannot synthesize them and produce the least spark of living matter.

Who is correct? My gut nudges me to side with Leduc, but it’s also been more than 100 years since Leduc posed his argument, and nobody has made life by mixing together inert molecules.1

The truth is, cells are ridiculously complicated things. Even the simplest ones have millions of proteins, metabolites, RNA and DNA, all tightly packed and jostling around within a lipid membrane. Each protein collides with trillions of water molecules per second, and glucose molecules ping-pong around at 460 miles per hour. Many cellular reactions are also stochastic, or “noisy,” meaning that chance encounters between molecules cause their timing and outcomes to vary even in identical cells.

In one experiment, published in 2002, researchers studied genetically identical Escherichia coli cells carrying genes for two fluorescent proteins, one cyan and one yellow. Each was placed next to an identical promoter to which the LacI repressor could bind, and thus “shut down” the gene’s expression. The researchers photographed the cells under a microscope and measured the fluorescence from each protein separately.

Despite being genetically identical, the cells differed in brightness and color balance. Some cells made more cyan than yellow, and others made more yellow than cyan. These differences were often substantial, with a standard deviation of 40% of the mean.

Genetically identical E. coli cells have distinct levels of gene expression. Panels A (RP22) and D (MG22) show the wild-type (lacI+) strains without added inducer. Credit: Elowitz M.B. et al. (2002).

Yet, despite the “noise” of biochemistry, life persists. It has found a way to flourish within this complexity and, for billions of years, cells have spawned new cells by turning simple molecules, such as sugars and amino acids, into more complex assemblages, beating back the tides of entropy. Or, as the Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger wrote in his classic 1944 book, What Is Life?, cells refuse to succumb to chaos “by eating, drinking, breathing and (in the case of plants) assimilating.”2

Leduc may have been right when he said that life can be explained purely by chemistry and physics, but it’s also clear that we can’t yet recreate the reactions necessary for life purely from synthetic chemicals. Perhaps the reason is that we don’t understand how life adapts and persists despite its noise and complexity. We may be able to collect all the ingredients needed to make a cell, but we are as blind as amateur cooks without a recipe when it comes to assembling them.

To create any given cell, we must first figure out what it is made from. How many atoms—and how much energy—does it take to build a new one? By tallying the parts, it becomes clear why humans can disassemble cells and understand each piece in isolation but struggle to put them back together and make them roar to life.

Deep writing about biology.

What Cells Are Made From

Let’s build an inventory for E. coli, the little bacterium that is the subject of more than 100,000 published research papers. Scientists have studied many types of E. coli, from “flesh-eating” variants to engineered strains that act as living “camera film.”3 For our purposes, let’s take a median example of this species and pick it apart. What is it made from?

E. coli with a single mutation in the metK gene form long spindles; they continue elongating, but do not divide, forming filaments up to 50 micrometers in length. Credit: El-Hajj Z.W. and Newman E.B., 2015.

About 70% of its mass is water. The other 30%—the “dry mass”—is everything else: DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids and so on. DNA makes up just 3% of dry mass, yet encodes all the information needed for the cell to grow, divide, adapt and evolve.4 The bulk of this dry mass, 55%, is protein, the large molecules that catalyze reactions and help control which genes switch “on” or “off.”5

Proteins make up the bulk of the dry mass for a few reasons. First, there are lots of them, and each protein is heavy. A single E. coli cell has about two million proteins floating around, each built from hundreds of amino acids. If the cell were blown up to the size of a tennis court, each protein would be roughly the size of a tennis ball.

Why are proteins so big? For one, large proteins fold faster than small ones due to cooperativity, meaning, basically, that one part of a protein coaxes another part to snap into place.6 Enzymes—proteins that speed up chemical reactions—need the extra bulk to build pockets, or cavities shaped in such a way that only certain molecules can enter and reach the active site. The enzyme that attaches tyrosine to its tRNA, for example, prefers tyrosine over phenylalanine—a molecule that differs by just one oxygen atom—by a ratio of more than 100,000-to-one, simply because its “pocket” has evolved into a structure ideally shaped for tyrosine.

Although cells have millions of proteins floating around, there are only a few thousand types. Some proteins are abundant, with millions of copies, whereas others are rare; for example, there is only a handful of RepA proteins, essential for DNA replication, present in the cell at any one time. The distribution of protein counts is also long-tailed, meaning that the 100 most abundant protein types account for more than half of all protein molecules in a cell.7

In the 1970s, most biologists thought EF-Tu, a protein that delivers tRNAs to ribosomes during protein synthesis, was the most abundant. This made intuitive sense because every E. colihas tens of thousands of ribosomes, and EF-Tu helps to quickly “feed” amino acids to them.

But in 1979, a study found that the most abundant protein is actually Braun’s lipoprotein, or Lpp, with more than 700,000 copies per cell. Lpp is a small protein that staples the cell’s outer membrane to its peptidoglycan layer, thus preventing it from blistering and leaking out viscous cytoplasm.8

Researchers have studied Lpp using atomic force microscopy. The brown bumps are individual Lpp proteins, which shuffle to the side and form a cleft, or valley, when a cell is preparing to divide. Credit: Sheng Q. et al. (2023).

Knocking out the Lpp gene causes cells to blister and leak cytoplasm. Credit: Sheng Q. et al. (2023).

After proteins, about 20% of the cell’s dry mass is RNA, of which a majority is ribosomal RNA.9 Each ribosome is two-thirds RNA by mass; these big machines have long threads of RNA inside, about 4,500 nucleotides in length. If you were to take the strands of RNA from a single ribosome and stretch them out, end to end, they would measure about 2.1 micrometers in length, longer than the entire cell.

Finally, lipids make up about 10% of a cell’s dry weight. There are about 30 million lipid molecules in each E. coli, beautifully packed into a double layer that stretches around the entire cell. If this membrane were pressed into a flat sheet, it would cover about 6 µm² of space. It would take 10,000 of these sheets, neatly sewn together, to cover the period at the end of this sentence.

Clearly, then, a cell has many molecules. How much energy is needed to build them?

One might assume the answer is “a lot”! After all, a cell has millions of proteins, each assembled from hundreds of amino acids.10 For currency, cells pay for this work using ATP, a small molecule that, when broken, releases energy to power chemical reactions. Adding just one amino acid to a protein costs about four ATPs. Energy is also burned to build DNA, RNA, lipids and every other molecule.11 Surprisingly, though, the total amount of energy needed to make a cell is very small (at least from our human-sized perspective).

Scientists have used biochemical calculations to estimate the energy required. By measuring how much food is eaten and how many new cells are created by bacteria in a flask, for example, they can then build models, based on known metabolic pathways, to predict how much ATP the bacteria have spent. And for an E. coli weighing about 0.3 picograms, producing another cell’s worth of material costs about 10 billion ATPs. These ATP molecules (and many macromolecules in the cell itself), in turn, are made from two to three billion glucose molecules. (A standard cube of sugar weighs four grams, and would be enough to make something like five trillion cells.) Lifting a small apple one meter off the ground is roughly the energy needed to build one billion cells.12 The creation of life is highly efficient.

These are just estimates, of course, and the numbers get fuzzy based on assumptions.13 Some energy is always lost as heat, for instance, and the actual ATP cost goes up or down based on cell size, nutrients, oxygen supply and growth rates.14

In the laboratory, we already have synthetic tools to build parts of cells. It is easy to assemble amino acid chains using solid-phase peptide synthesis, for example, even though long proteins are still difficult to make efficiently by chemical synthesis. The laboratory process is also woefully inefficient. Chemists first attach an amino acid to a little bead, chemically join the next amino acid, wash away the reagents, and then repeat this hundreds of times. Cells, for comparison, do all of this in minutes, for orders of magnitude less energy, while building thousands of different proteins using solely atoms taken from their environments.

But now that we have a nearly complete list of the molecules in a cell, along with estimates of the energy needed to assemble them, we can finally ponder ways to arrange them and judge how close we might be to the possibility of “creating life.” The reason nobody has succeeded so far, I suspect, is that we haven’t yet mastered the fault tolerance or exquisite regulation required to do so.

Woeful Dynamism

It’s a short walk from my Berkeley apartment to a grocery store, where I can find the same ingredients the chefs at The French Laundry and other Michelin-starred restaurants cook with. Even so, I can’t assemble these ingredients into a prize-winning dish. I don’t know how to finesse them, or feel when a sauce has thickened just enough to pull it off the burner. More importantly, if an ingredient goes missing, I have no way to adapt or modify a dish on the fly, using my understanding of saltiness and sweetness, sourness and bitterness alone. A list of ingredients is not a recipe, and a recipe does not imply mastery of cooking.

The most amazing thing about cells, then, is not that they are packed with millions of proteins and other molecules and still manage to work. Rather, it’s that (as in the case of E. coli) they can re-make themselves every 20 minutes; they are producing millions of machines and adapting them on the fly and in the face of enormous uncertainty.15 The most amazing thing about life is that it persists despite the noise.

Consider one small part of a cell: DNA replication. In a 1998 paper in Cell, a pair of MIT biologists did a thought experiment in which they scaled up DNA to a width of one meter. In that scenario, DNA polymerase (the enzyme responsible for copying it) would be the size of a FedEx truck. Copying the E. coli genome would require two of these trucks, each moving in opposite directions at speeds of 375 miles per hour. Over the span of 40 minutes, these trucks would deliver five million packages and make just one error every 106 miles.16

At the same time that FedEx truck is speeding by, thousands of ribosomes are busily making proteins, enzymes are converting millions of molecules each second, and the membrane is adding lipid molecules to expand, preparing to make a daughter cell. Seemingly, this would offer thousands of opportunities for something to go wrong. At this scale, and these speeds, even rare errors can accumulate and kill the cell. And yet life persists. It remakes itself even when things inevitably go wrong. If human builders are ever to rival the complexity and dynamism of a cell, then we not only need to find the ingredients, but also arrange them in ways suited to extreme speeds, forces and noise.

Two factors are especially critical.

First, populations of cells have a high fault tolerance, partly because they contain so many cells and each cell differs from its neighbors. A threat that kills some cells may spare others. These differences, when multiplied across millions of cells in a group, are one way that cells “adapt” to uncertainty and persist.

For a 2020 study, researchers deleted two genes encoding enzymes required for biosynthesis of isoleucine, an essential amino acid used to make proteins. Without it, cells will eventually die. The researchers knocked out these genes, put the sick bacteria into little tubes without isoleucine, and then waited. For the next 70 hours, the bacteria appeared dead. But then, slowly, some of the cells began to divide.

After sequencing these cells, the researchers found that about a dozen mutations had randomly arisen in the population, mainly in a gene encoding MetC, an enzyme responsible for making another amino acid called methionine. The mutations shifted the cell’s metabolism slightly, enabling them to make an isoleucine precursor instead.17 The few mutated cells from that initial population had inadvertently hit upon a solution to their molecular dilemma by rewiring a separate pathway, thus allowing the population to survive.18

Second, cells are robust despite uncertainties because they can, in some cases, sense relative changes while ignoring absolute ones. Such sensitivity proves useful when the environment changes and a cell must adapt without re-assembling molecules.

Consider an E. coli cell foraging for food. Little protein sensors embedded in its cell membrane detect the local concentration of food particles. As the cell spins its flagella and moves forward, the sensors take measurements in real time. If the food concentration dwindles, the cell is more likely to “tumble” and swim in a new, potentially more promising direction. But if the concentration of food goes up, the cell is less likely to tumble, and tends to keep swimming forward longer.

This is called chemotaxis, and the most amazing thing about it is that, within certain concentration ranges, the cell’s response depends on relative rather than absolute concentrations. The cell instead computes fold-changes, easily tuning its response to environments with much more or less food.

Regardless of whether the concentration of food rises from one to three, or from 10 to 30, the cell “processes” either change as simply a three-fold increase. Responding to a ratio, rather than absolute numbers, allows the bacterium to find more food regardless of its internal noise or huge changes in its environment.19 The bacteria are effectively judging changes against a baseline, enabling the same sensors to work across environments with very different concentrations. They are “compressing” their environment. 

(Chemotaxis is so sensitive that E. coli can swim toward higher concentrations of an amino acid even when it is as dilute as one milligram dissolved in 2,300 liters of water.)

These examples are relevant to efforts to build a cell. It is not enough merely to understand which ingredients to include at which concentrations, but also to note that these ingredients will not work in all environments, and must be able to adapt to an extreme range of situations. Instead of trying to build “a” cell, then, we ought to build many variants, and then let evolution select the design best suited to life.20 Once a cell can reproduce with a selection mechanism, evolution can improve it.

An E. coli cell forms a large colony. The cell was filmed for 305 minutes, but the GIF is just seven seconds. Credit: Stewart E.J. et al. (2005).

Humans have a borderline-obsessive desire to define parameters precisely, to understand every knob in a machine and fine-tune them perfectly. But cells do not care. They deliberately vary their parameters and dial knobs up or down to create variation. When it comes to science, humans care about understanding, whereas cells care about survival, and these goals can conflict.

Returning to the Leduc–Burroughs debate, building a viable cell probably doesn’t require a mysterious organizing force or vitalist “spark.” Sensing, adjusting, repairing and reproducing are all tasks carried out by molecules and the physical interactions between them. But it’s also true that our understanding of molecular interactions remains a bit fuzzy, and cannot fully explain cells’ ability to adapt on the fly. Molecules may be necessary to explain life, but they’re also just one small part of the recipe.

Niko McCarty is founding editor of Asimov Press. 

Thanks to Noah Olsman, Brady Huggett, Devon Balwit and Merrick Pierson Smela for helpful comments. Header image by Ella Watkins-Dulaney.

1

Those siding with Burroughs may soon be proven wrong. The Biotic team is working hard on this problem, and they’ve predicted a perpetually dividing cell by 2030. I’m skeptical, as might be clear from my interview with Kate Adamala.

2

Some cells, like Vibrio natriegens, can divide in just nine minutes.

3

No two E. coli are identical. Even members of the same species have wildly distinct sets of genes. For a 2026 paper, researchers compared 1,200 complete E. coli genomes and found that they collectively had about 25,000 “gene families,” only 3,000 of which were present in at least 99% of the genomes. Most genes, in other words, only show up in some small portion of E. coli, so no two members of the same species are exactly the same.

4

It’s difficult to calculate just how much information is stored in the DNA of a cell. A typical estimate for E. coli is about 1.16 megabytes, or less than one photograph on your phone.

5

A typical E. coli cell (when dried) has 1010 carbon atoms and a chemical formula of C4.4H7.2O2.1N0.8P0.086S0.039. For every 4.4 carbon atoms, the cell has 7.2 hydrogens, 2.1 oxygens, 0.8 nitrogens, and tiny traces of sulfur and phosphorus.

6

This has been measured directly. Researchers measured how eight different proteins fold by attaching red and green fluorescent dyes to amino acids that sit far apart when unfolded but come together when folded. As the dyes get closer, the green dye transfers energy to the red dye instead of emitting its own light, making it possible to record this “flash.” The largest protein transitioned in 0.7 microseconds, compared to 3.1 for the smallest.

7

Many copies of each protein are needed because enzymes can only convert so many substrates per second. If a cell needs to make something fast (like an antibiotic-resistance molecule), then it must stock many copies of that enzyme! Proteins that help make other proteins also tend to occur in higher numbers.

8

A 2023 paper in Science Advances used atomic force microscopy to visualize Lpp in individual cells and concluded that each cell contains up to one million copies. This makes sense; each cell membrane is built from about 30 million phospholipid molecules, so many Lpps are needed to hold them together.

9

Messenger RNA makes up less than 1% of the cell mass of E. coli. It is among the least abundant types of RNA.

10

Polymerizing a single amino acid onto a growing chain costs about four high-energy phosphate bonds (two to charge the tRNA, plus two GTP per elongation cycle). A 300-amino-acid protein therefore costs about 1,200 ATP-equivalents just to assemble, not including the cost of making the amino acids themselves.

11

For DNA and RNA, each phosphodiester bond costs about two ATP-equivalents, not including costs for nucleotide biosynthesis.

12

Each ATP molecule supplies about 8 × 10−20 joules of energy.

13

There are also other estimates out there. See Martin (2025), which gives estimates that include building-block synthesis, polymerization, and transport. When grown in glucose and inorganic salts, Martin estimates six billion ATP for a 0.3-picogram cell, not including general maintenance costs. Also see Farmer and Jones (1976).

14

The ranking depends on the nutrients available and what costs are counted. In Martin’s glucose-based calculation, protein synthesis has the largest ATP cost, followed by RNA synthesis; lipids account for a small fraction.

15

Humans tend to employ machine-like metaphors when talking about cells (myself included). We think of genes as “gears” or proteins as “springs” that all work together in a logical way. In reality, cells are unlike any machines made by humans. They are governed by stochastic forces; they change from one generation to the next; and they can even acquire, or swap out, parts on the fly.

16

The paper continues: “The mechanical prowess of this complex is even more impressive given that it synthesizes two chains simultaneously as it moves. Although one strand is synthesized in the same direction as the fork is moving, the other chain (the lagging strand) is synthesized in a piecemeal fashion (as Okazaki fragments) and in the opposite direction of overall fork movement. As a result, about once a second one delivery person (i.e., polymerase active site) associated with the truck must take a detour, coming off and then rejoining its template DNA strand, to synthesize the 0.2 km (0.13 mile) fragments.”

17

MetB, an enzyme normally used in methionine synthesis, is able to perform a secondary reaction to supply the missing isoleucine precursor. Mutations elsewhere in the pathway increased the flow through this reaction.

18

This doesn’t only happen with genetic mutations, either. Sometimes, stochastic fluctuations between otherwise identical cells can also lead to antibiotic resistance, and thus protect an entire population from extinction. For a 2004 paper, researchers exposed E. colicells to an antibiotic and found that some cells survived purely by chance; they had a short-lived state (not any genetic mutation) that rendered them immune. When those survivors regrew, their descendants were susceptible to the drug.

19

The same fold-change detection underlies many famous signaling pathways, including Wnt.

20

This is what Biotic is doing. But they are trying to build one cell, and then use evolution to make it robust. My argument is that we could also do chemical synthesis experiments where we systematically vary the ratios of ingredients to see if anything viable emerges.

items.articleBody:
by Shuji Wakatsuki, Toshiyuki Araki

Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

items.title: The Minimal Requirements for a Society Free From Fear
items.subtitle: In 1989, the year the West won the Cold War, Francis Fukuyama published an essay announcing “the end of history.” He wasn’t claiming that historic…

items.articleBody:
In 1989, the year the West won the Cold War, Francis Fukuyama published an essay announcing “the end of history.” He wasn’t claiming that historic events would stop taking place; what was over, rather, was the debate about the meaning of those events. Since the Enlightenment, Western thinkers had believed that history was progressing toward a final destination. According to communism, the engine of progress was class conflict, and history would end in the creation of a classless society. With the failure of the Soviet empire, Fukuyama argued, this idea had been discredited. Only one alternative remained: It was now clear that the “end point of mankind’s ideological evolution” was “the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government.” There would still be disagreements within liberalism—Fukuyama named religion and nationalism as likely fault lines—but there could no longer be any disagreement about liberalism.

To see how that judgment is holding up, just look at the kinds of titles that political theorists are producing these days: How Liberalism Failed, A World After Liberalism, Liberalism Against Itself. Even Fukuyama wrote a book titled Liberalism and Its Discontents. Across the West, the far right and the far left are on the rise, and the one thing they agree on is their contempt for liberalism. To MAGA and its European cousins, such as France’s National Rally and the United Kingdom’s Reform Party, liberals are rootless elitists who look down on their fellow citizens while coddling immigrants and criminals. To progressives and democratic socialists, liberalism—often qualified with the prefix neo—means ruthless globalized capitalism, prettied up with rhetoric about meritocracy and human rights. Appeals to liberal principles and defenses of the liberal world order have shown little power to rally the public, or even much of the political establishment.

Now that the liberal triumphalism of the post–Cold War era is dying, what can replace it? The answer may lie in another important essay written in 1989—one that received much less attention than Fukuyama’s, but enjoys a cult reputation among keepers of the liberal flame. “The Liberalism of Fear,” by Judith Shklar, has just been published for the first time as a book—a small book, because the essay is only about 8,000 words long, but a timely one. In fact, as the political scientist Mark Lilla says in his introduction, it’s “far more timely today than it was upon its publication.” In 1989, Shklar’s minimalist definition of liberalism as a bulwark against government terror—what she calls, simply, a politics of “damage control”—might have sounded unambitious or uninspiring. In an America where ICE agents shoot protesters and grab people off the street, it sounds prescient.

Shklar’s argument involves history and philosophy, but like all political ideas, it begins with an intuition, a feeling. Communism, one might say, begins in indignation: a refusal to accept a world where some people exploit and others are exploited. Nationalism begins in loyalty: a sense of connection and obligation to one’s own people. There is nothing wrong with these emotions; they are even praiseworthy. But when one political feeling crowds out all others—when everyone and everything is subordinated to the pursuit of social justice or national pride—good can justify the worst evils.

[From the May 2022 issue: There is no liberal world order]

What makes liberalism different from these political ideologies is that, as Shklar writes, it “does not have any particular positive doctrines about how people are to conduct their lives.” Liberalism doesn’t offer a vision of a perfect world—one where injustice is abolished, or where a particular nation reigns supreme. Instead, it is rooted in a justified fear of the real world, where people with power often use it to oppress, torture, and kill. “Liberalism’s deepest grounding,” Shklar writes, is the belief “that cruelty is an absolute evil.” The classic liberal principles outlined by thinkers such as Locke and Mill, the ideas that guided the American and French Revolutions, follow from this basic fear of cruelty. Freedom of religion means that you won’t be burned at the stake for holding the wrong beliefs. Freedom of speech means that you won’t be locked up for saying what you think. The rule of law means that you can be punished only for committing a crime, not because a powerful person is out to get you.

Not coincidentally, these liberal freedoms are framed as limits on the power of the state. “Public cruelty,” Shklar writes, “is made possible by differences in public power,” and the government is always more powerful than any citizen. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing; we want the government to have the power to punish crime or defend against invasion. But liberalism believes that there must be strict and effective limits on how that power is used. “The governments of this world, with their overwhelming power to kill, maim, indoctrinate, and make war are not to be trusted unconditionally,” Shklar writes. What the liberalism of fear wants to prevent above all are “habitual and pervasive acts of cruelty and torture performed by military, paramilitary, and police agents in any regime.”

This might have seemed like an odd concern for an American political philosopher in 1989. Police states were disappearing in Eastern Europe; democracy activists were bravely standing up to tanks in Tiananmen Square; Nelson Mandela left his jail cell on his way to becoming president of South Africa. America under George H. W. Bush had its problems, but no one would have put paramilitary violence and police torture high on the list. At a time when Fukuyama was celebrating the end of history, why was Shklar contemplating these specters at the feast?

The most obvious answer is that, unlike most Americans, she had seen them firsthand. Born to a Jewish family in Latvia in 1928, Judith Nisse grew up in the shadow of approaching war and the Holocaust. In an autobiographical lecture, she recalled that as a child, she was traumatized by reading Shakespeare’s play Titus Andronicus, which is full of murder, cannibalism, and severed heads: “To this day I can still feel the fear and horror it inspired.” Her sister tried to comfort her by saying that “these things did not really happen,” but it didn’t help, because “both she and I knew that far worse was going on all around us.” As Jews in Latvia, Shklar recalled, “everyone around us wanted us to be somewhere else at best, or to kill us at worst.” The Nisse family managed to escape at the last possible moment and took an epic journey in 1940 across Russia and the Pacific to Canada. The next year, the Nazis invaded Latvia and the 40,000 Jews of Riga were murdered, most of them shot by German troops and local auxiliaries in a nearby forest.

When Shklar arrived at Harvard’s department of government as a graduate student in 1951, she was struck by how completely her American colleagues ignored the central political experience of their own time: “I knew what had happened in Europe between 1940 and 1945, and I assumed that most people at Harvard also were aware of the physical, political, and moral calamity that had occurred, but it was never to be discussed.” This “isolating” experience “had a lot to do with my later writings,” Shklar noted. At first, she didn’t intend to stay in the academy: “I would have liked to be a literary editor of The Atlantic or some such publication.” But she remained at Harvard for her entire career as a professor, writing about subjects directly or indirectly connected with the European catastrophe: the failure of the Enlightenment tradition, the concept of law in the Nuremberg trials, the nature of cruelty and injustice.

“The Liberalism of Fear” was published three years before Shklar’s death in 1992, and though it wasn’t one of her major works, the title has become a kind of shorthand for her worldview. As Lilla writes in his introduction, for Shklar, “fear of being in another’s arbitrary power is the ur-human experience that modern liberalism was developed to stave off.” In the essay, she discusses the tools that modern liberal societies use for this purpose. Some of these tools are legal: “Without well-defined procedures, honest judges, opportunities for counsel and for appeals, no one has a chance.” Others are political and economic, such as security for private property: “Nothing gives a person greater social resources than legally guaranteed proprietorship.”

[Read: This is the way a world order ends]

But Shklar is most concerned with the ideas and habits of mind that sustain liberal societies. And it is here that her message for today becomes most urgent. The “perfect liberal,” she writes, “respects other people without condescension, arrogance, humility, or fear. He or she does not insult others with lies or cruelty, both of which mar one’s own character no less than they injure one’s victims.” These aren’t the heroic virtues needed to win wars or found empires; they are minimal requirements for a society free from fear. Until recently, they were expected of anyone who hoped to play a role in American public life, regardless of their political views.

Only since Donald Trump got to the White House have Americans realized how much they took for granted the sobriety and politeness of Ronald Reagan or Barack Obama. Trumpism’s assault on liberal democracy isn’t only a matter of laws and policies. From the beginning, it has been about legitimizing cruelty. When Trump mockingly imitated a disabled reporter, or said police officers shouldn’t be “too nice” when putting suspects into police cars, or pardoned an American soldier convicted by a court martial of murdering civilians, he was sending the message that he approves of cruelty, and will support those who commit it.

The federal government and the Republican Party resisted that message in his first term; in his second, they have mostly stopped resisting. We are still a long way from the Europe of Shklar’s childhood. America has been a liberal democracy for a long time, and the majority of Americans are not ready to embrace a politics of cruelty. But that prospect feels a lot less theoretical than it did when “The Liberalism of Fear” was written. In the essay, Shklar says that government terror and cruelty weren’t things of the past, but could be seen in “the foreign news in the New York Times.” Now it’s not just the foreign news that reminds us how much we have to be afraid of—and how much we need the values and institutions of liberalism, no matter how unfashionable they’ve become.

items.articleBody:
The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) and the University of Toronto have launched new initiatives to support and focus philosophical research on various aspects of artificial intelligence (AI).

Eduardo Paolozzi, “Perception through Impressions” from The Conditional Probability Machine

The Department of Philosophy, Logic and Scientific Method at LSE has received a $5.3 million donation to launch a new research group—The Global Priorities Research Group (GPRG)—dedicated to “determining which problems matter most and what should be done in trying to realize the best outcomes for humanity and the wider world.”

It’s primary emphasis will be “philosophical research that helps us navigate the largest-scale challenges associated with the impacts of transformative AI.” 

Funded by Good Ventures, a philanthropic foundation, the GPRG “will also consider how we should compare and weight the interests of different kinds of beings—be they human, animal, or perhaps even artificial—as well as pursuing foundational research on issues related to value and rational choice with the potential to reorient our priorities across a wide range of issues.”

The group will be led by philosophers Andreas L. Mogensen, who recently joined LSE from the University of Oxford, and Teruji Thomas (Oxford, LSE), and will be based at LSE’s Centre for Philosophy of Natural and Social Science.

Meanwhile, the Artificial Consciousness Initiative is a new project from the University of Toronto Department of Philosophy that “aims to advance foundational research connecting artificial intelligence and consciousness.”

The project’s director, philosopher Andrew Y. Lee, writes:

The initiative’s research agenda focuses on questions about the nature, structure, and indicators of artificial consciousness; the valence and character of potential artificial experiences; the welfare and moral status of artificial systems; and the ethical and safety risks raised by increasingly capable AI. The initiative does not presuppose that current artificial systems are conscious or that future ones will be. But it starts from the view that these questions are worth taking seriously.

The core team of the Artificial Consciousness Initiative includes Karina Vold, Christian Tarsney, and Gwen Bradford. 

The initiative’s aims include basic research, partnerships with other institutions, and contributing to public and policy discussions related to AI consciousness. The project is supported by a large grant from Longview Philanthropy.

Both initiatives are currently hiring postdocs.

The post New Philosophy of AI Initiatives appeared first on Daily Nous.

items.articleBody:
More big numbers coming in. For NYT’s the Upshot, Aatish Bhatia demonstrates the millions of trillions (octillions!) of calculations required for training AI.

During its training, the A.I. is fed a portion of a sentence, and the knobs are adjusted using a series of math calculations to improve its guesses for the next word. This process is then repeated over trillions of words of training data.

It takes only a few additions and multiplications to adjust a single knob. But when trillions of knobs are adjusted trillions of times, the math quickly adds up.

And this is just the first step in training a language model, known as pre-training. It’s followed by additional steps of calculations that hone the A.I.’s behavior and improve its ability to code and solve math problems.

All those calculations require energy, data, and time. The big companies are taking what they can get with the first two things in efforts to reduce the third.

items.articleBody:
The following excerpts are from Essays in Idleness (Tsurezuregusa), a collection of essays by the Japanese monk and calligrapher Kenko (c. 1283–1350). Composed in the zuihitsu style (literally “follow the brush”), Essays in Idleness presents an eclectic assortment of 243 musings on impermanence, desire, delusion, and awakening. 

***

20

A certain recluse monk once remarked, “I have relinquished all that ties me to the world, but the one thing that still haunts me is the beauty of the sky.” I can quite see why he would feel this.

25

This world is changeable as the deeps and shallows of Asuka River—time passes, what was here is gone, joy and grief visit by turns, once splendid places change to abandoned wastelands, and even the same house as of old is now home to different people. The peach and the plum tree utter nothing—with whom can we speak of past things? Still more moving in its transience is the ruin of some fine residence of former times, whose glory we never saw.

It is deeply poignant to see the Kyogoku-dono and Hojoji Temple and witness there the hopes of the man who built them, now so transfigured. The Midodono created these magnificent buildings and donated many of his estates to the temple, full of plans that his family would continue to act as regents for future emperors and retain its worldly power—could he have dreamed then that an age would come when all that he had set up would lie in such ruin? The temple gates and the Kondo were still standing until recently, but the south gate burned in the Showa era. The Kondo later collapsed, and no attempt has been made to rebuild it. Only the Muryoju Hall still stands in its former state, with inside it an awe-inspiring row of nine fifteen-foot-tall images of the Buddha. It is moving, too, to see the calligraphy by Grand Counsellor Kozei and the doors with Kaneyuki’s writing, still clearly visible. The Hokke-do is apparently still standing as well. For how much longer, l wonder?

In places where such remnants no longer exist, one can sometimes still see foundation stones in the ground, but none now know what buildings these once were.

And so we see how fickle is the world in all things, for those who would plan for a time they will not live to see.

59

Those who feel the impulse to pursue the path of enlightenment should immediately take the step, and not defer it while they attend to all the other things on their mind. If you say to yourself, “Let’s just wait until after this is over,” or “While I’m at it I’ll just see to that,” or “People will criticize me about such-and-such so I should make sure it’s all dealt with and causes no problem later,” or “There’s been time enough so far, after all, and it won’t take long just to a wait a little longer while I do this. Let’s not rush into things,” one imperative thing after another will occur to detain you. There will be no end to it all, and the day of decision will never come.

In general, I find that reasonably sensitive and intelligent people will pass their whole life without taking the step they know they should. Would anyone with a fire close behind him choose to pause before fleeing? In a matter of life and death, one casts aside shame, abandons riches, and runs. Does mortality wait on our choosing? Death comes upon us more swiftly than fire or flood. There is no escaping it. Who at that moment can refuse to part with all they love—aged parents, beloved children, lord and master, or the love of others?

74

We swarm like ants, scurrying to east and west, dashing to north and south, folk of high birth and of low, old and young, some going, others returning, sleeping at night, rising again next morning. . . . What is all this busyness? There is no end to our greed for life, our lust for gain.

We tend our bodies—to what end? Old age and death are the only sure things awaiting us. Swiftly they come, without an instant’s pause. What pleasure is to be found while we await them?

The deluded have no fear of this truth. In thrall to the lure of fame and fortune, they never pause to see what lies so close before them. Fools mourn it. In their longing for eternal lite, they have no understanding of the law of mutability.

157

To take up the brush is to write, to take up an instrument is to feel the urge to make it sing. A sake cup in the hand provokes the thought of sake, while a dice in your palm will prompt ideas of gambling. Contact will always trigger the associated urge. Never for a moment indulge in wrongful pastimes.

A passing glance at a phrase from the holy teachings will lead the eye on to read the words surrounding it, and before you know it you may have righted years of error. Had you not opened the text just then, you might never have had that realization. This is an example of the virtue of contact. Even if you lack all faith, simply to seat yourself before an image, hold a rosary, and take up a sutra book is to perform a virtuous act, however perfunctory; even seated on your meditation chair with distracted mind, you will sink into meditation before you know it.

Phenomena and their essence are intrinsically one. If outward actions conform, inner realization will naturally follow. Do not decry a lack of faith—such “empty gestures” in fact deserve our reverence.

241

The full moon’s perfect roundness lasts barely a moment, and in no time is lost. Those with no eye for such things, it seems, fail to see how it changes in the course of a night.

If you plan to turn your thoughts to the Buddhist Way after you have fulfilled all your desires, you will find that those desires are endless.

An illness will grow graver as each moment passes, and death is already close at hand, yet while the sickness is still mild and you are not yet confronting death, you are lulled by your accustomed assumptions of a normal life in an unchanging world, and choose to wait until you have accomplished all you want in life before calmly turning your thoughts to salvation and a Buddhist practice, with the result that when you fall ill and confront death, none of your dreams has been fulfilled. Now, too late, you repent of your long years of negligence, and swear that if only you were to recover you would dedicate yourself unstintingly day and night to this thing and that—but for all your prayers your illness grows graver, until you lose your senses and die a raving death. It happens to so many of us. We must fully grasp this, here and now.

If you plan to turn your thoughts to the Buddhist Way after you have fulfilled all your desires, you will find that those desires are endless. What could be achieved, in this illusory life of ours? All desire is delusion. If desires arise within you, realize that they spring from your lost and deluded mind, and ignore them all. Relinquish all today and turn to the Buddhist path, and you will be freed of all obstruction, released from the need for action, and lasting peace will be yours body and soul.

243

The year I turned 8, I asked my father, “What sort of thing is a buddha?”

“A buddha is what a human becomes,” he replied.

“How does a human become a buddha?” I asked.

“You become a buddha by following the Buddha’s teaching,” he answered.

“So who taught the Buddha?” I asked.

“He became a buddha by following the teaching of previous buddhas,” he said.

“So what sort of buddha was the first one who began the teaching?” I asked.

My father laughed and replied, “I suppose he just fell from the sky like rain or rose out of the earth like water.”

He used to enjoy recounting this story to others, adding, “He had me cornered. I couldn’t think what to reply.”

♦

From Essays in Idleness and Hojoki by Kenko and Chomei; translated by Meredith McKinney, introduction and notes by Meredith McKinney, published by Penguin Classics, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House, LLC. Translation and editorial materials copyright © 2013 by Meredith McKinney. First published in Great Britain by Penguin Classics 2013.
