items.articleBody: Mutations in Syntaxin11 (STX11), a Q-SNARE, result in a fatal immune disorder known as familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis 4 (FHLH4) in human patients. A key diagnostic feature of FHLH4 is defective T and natural killer cell cytotoxicity. Here, we show that STX11 directly binds and regulates Orai1, the pore-forming subunit of calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels. CRAC channels enable store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) from the extracellular space and are crucial for granule exocytosis and nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT)-dependent gene expression in activated lymphocytes. STX11 depletion strongly inhibited SOCE, CRAC currents, NFAT activation, interleukin-2 gene expression, and degranulation in FHLH4 patient T lymphocytes and cell lines without affecting membrane trafficking. Remarkably, defects of cytolytic granule exocytosis, as well as interleukin-2 expression, could be reversed by ionomycin in patient T lymphocytes, and a constitutively active, H134S, mutant of Orai1 rescued calcium entry in STX11-depleted cells. Further analyses showed that STX11 ‘primes’ Orai1 for optimal on-site multimeric assembly, which was Stim independent but required for gating. Priming of ion channel pore subunits is, therefore, a primary function of specific SNAREs which may have preceded their role in membrane trafficking and vesicle fusion.

items.articleBody:

Human beings are not impressive animals at first glance. We are not especially strong. We are not particularly fast. We do not have claws, thick hides or sharp teeth. Our great advantage is that we can learn from one another.

One person finds a better way to hunt, cook, build, speak, trade or travel. Others copy it. Then someone improves it. Others copy that too. Over time, these small acts of copying become culture.

Copying is not always wise, though. Sometimes a new method of doing something is better. Sometimes it’s worse. The challenge is knowing when to switch to a new approach and when not to.

A new paper in Personality and Individual Differences asks who is better at making that choice. The authors study how intelligence and personality shape social learning, or the practice of learning from others.

The researchers focus on two mental habits:

The first is “content bias.” This is the tendency to adopt a novel solution when it is better than the old one.

The second is “maintenance bias.” This is the tendency to stick with a solution because it is familiar.

Both habits are useful. Without content bias, people would fail to implement real improvements. Without maintenance bias, they would chase every fad.

Human progress requires both. You need enough openness to notice a better idea. You also need enough caution not to discard what already works.

The researchers created two simple tasks. In one, participants learned a code to open a padlock. In the other, they learned a route through a maze.

After practicing the initial solution, study participants were shown a new one. Sometimes the new solution was better. Sometimes it was about the same. Sometimes it was worse.

Then came the key choice: stay or switch.

The basic result is reassuring. People were generally more likely to switch when the new solution was better. They were less likely to switch when it was worse. In other words, people showed content bias. They could typically tell when the new way was actually an improvement and then implemented it.

But there were also signs of maintenance bias. When the old and new solutions were equal in quality, most people stuck with the one they already knew. This is probably because all else equal, a familiar solution is less risky. A new method may look equal on paper. But you still have to pay the cost of learning it. And the new method might have unpredictable outcomes or side effects.

Importantly, the researchers also measured intelligence and personality.

Intelligence was measured with several tests, including vocabulary, pattern reasoning, working memory and processing speed. 

Higher intelligence predicted a greater willingness to switch to new solutions, especially when those solutions were better. Smarter participants were more likely to adopt real improvements.

This makes sense. Intelligence helps people solve novel problems. Smart people are better at noticing when a new approach is superior.

More interestingly, though, smarter people were also more likely to switch even when the new solution was similar or inferior to the original approach.

The authors suggest that the reason for this is that more intelligent people face lower costs when they experiment with new ideas. Trying out a hard or awkward new solution carries fewer penalties for intelligent people. They also enjoy the challenge.

Intelligence helps people not only by making them choose better, but also by making potentially bad choices less costly.

A smart person can try a novel solution. If things go wrong, they are better equipped to recover. For a less intelligent individual, the same mistake is more costly.

Personality played a role too. The researchers looked at the Big Five personality trait openness to experience. Open people tend to be curious, imaginative and more willing to try new things. 

So you might expect people high in openness to be better at finding better solutions.

That isn’t what the study found, though.

Openness did not predict switching to superior solutions. Instead, open people were more likely to switch to solutions that were similar or worse. Open people were not especially better at identifying improvement. Rather, they were drawn to novelty itself.

This finding captures both the upside and the risk of high trait openness.

Open people challenge routines and resist conventions. A healthy society needs these creative types. Still, novelty isn’t the same as progress. Sometimes the new thing is worse.

Sometimes the old solution has been around a long time because it works.

Intelligence and openness, two traits linked with higher levels of education, are also associated with interest in novelty. Even if the novel approach is not better. And even if it’s worse. But if you’re a smart person with all of the accompanying benefits your intelligence can supply, you can more quickly recover from your mistakes. Most others can’t.

You might see a connection between this finding and luxury beliefs. 

If you are a bright individual, you will have some difficulty imagining what mental life and everyday existence can be like for someone whose IQ is more than 10 or 15 points away from your own.

This is especially true if you have only ever spent time around similar individuals to yourself. Ironically, highly intelligent people are one of the groups most susceptible to this blind spot in their thinking. I grew up around many people with average or below average intelligence. Sure, they had some difficulty with getting through Algebra II or explaining the motifs of the assigned reading. Overall, though, they were just as capable of everyday problem solving, responsibility, and good moral character as anyone else. Still, people who are not in the top half of intelligence often find it helpful to have some guardrails and healthy heuristics, or rules of thumb, for wise decision-making. And frequent and regular reminders of what good decisions look like and how to avoid bad ones.

Human beings have been shaped to imitate. But not all imitation is equally valuable. 

A healthy culture needs smart people who can spot new and improved solutions. It needs curious people willing to test new paths. And it needs enough respect for the familiar to remember that not every novelty will necessarily lead to progress.

items.articleBody:
A technique for training and life

EBEHs are a technique I use when pool swimming.

EBEH stands for Easy, Build, Easy, Hard
(I say it as ee-bees).

An EBEH means:

Swim a length at an Easy pace

In the next length, Build with increased effort

Then drop back to the Easy pace

Then give it a Hard, near all-out effort for the fourth length

Then repeat, straight back into an easy recovery.

Whenever I remember to swim EBEHs I think, “These are good for so many reasons.”  If you’re training for something physical, they might help, and I find the principles that make EBEHs effective apply so well as an approach to many things in life.

Here are some of the principles that I think make EBEHs so good:

Break a large indeterminate goal into manageable chunks

Rather than thinking, I’ll swim for 40 minutes, or for 2km, I can just focus on completing my next EBEH.

The Hard lengths are hard, but the Build lengths get me ready for it. I know what’s coming next and can anticipate it.

Even when I'm just contemplating hard work, like going for a swim training workout, I find this helps me get going and keep going.

Track progress and know where you’re at

Rather than counting to, say, 10 lengths and losing count, with EBEHs I can always tell which part I’m on. Did I just sprint? If I’m swimming back, then I should be going easy.

Clear goals and immediate feedback are two of the conditions that help create flow. An endless, indeterminate path is hard to stay motivated for. With EBEHs, I always know what I'm doing now and what's coming next.

Intersperse effort with breaks

As in life, you can’t sprint all the time. If you’re always pushing hard, you burn out. You stop looking forward to the activity and start dreading and resenting it. But sometimes sprinting is a good thing.

With EBEHs, you build up to it. You sprint, but you know you’ll have a break on the other side. And then you do it again.

Many things in life are more like a marathon than a sprint. Planning periods of intense effort with breaks, I find, works really well.

Recover while still moving

One subtle effect of EBEHs I've noticed is that I rest without stopping completely—I recover while still swimming on the easy lengths.

If I were to just swim, then my rest would be stopping at the ends. But EBEHs encourage me to work hard and then catch my breath and recover on the nice easy lengths, ready to go again.

I’m not tempted to stop. I keep going and cover more as a result.

It’s similar to having run up a hill. You don’t want to run up so hard that you have to stop at the top. Can you run up so that at the top you slip back into your standard pace and recover while still running?

I’m not against stopping to rest—I love it!—but I find EBEHs raise my baseline and change what feels like rest. Easy swimming becomes recovery rather than something I need to recover from. For endurance, I like how it normalises keeping going.

Working in chunks makes progress add up quickly

An EBEH is a shorthand for four lengths. I don’t have to count individual lengths. I aim for 3 EBEHs and I know I’ll cover 12 lengths. Just a few more EBEHs and I’m at 20.

Progress feels faster when every one I count means I've actually done four.

If you’re training for something, maybe give EBEHs a try. And even outside training, I find the same pattern surprisingly useful. Is there anywhere you could apply the principles of EBEHs?

My training partner and I discussed this, and other things swimrun, on the Low Tide Boyz podcast

I learned EBEHs from a good friend who I do swimrun with, who came across it on an old training plan. I did a lot of EBEHs recently, so they’ve been on my mind.

items.articleBody:
I did a web search on the above phrase, in prep for a podcast, and in ten pages of results didn’t find anything I thought reasonable. Which promotes me to write this, hoping it can show up for others when they so search. This content isn’t new, just restated, maybe better. 

When considering purported evidence for meteors or ball lightning, we are much more forgiving than when considering purported evidence of telepathy or ghosts, as reasonable priors for the former are much higher than for the latter. That is, we more easily believe that former cases happened. The assumptions we’d have to make to let us think that we’d seen examples of the latter seem far more extreme.

When considering purported evidence for aliens-on-Earth, we should similarly ask how extreme are the assumptions we’d need to make to make sense of it. Many have dismissed and ridiculed such sightings, even when many independent sober folks all say they saw roughly the same amazing things, largely on the basis of claiming that aliens-on-Earth requires extreme assumptions, and so has a very low prior. I disagree.

To evaluate a prior re aliens-on-Earth, we should collect the key facts in need of explanation, seek the most plausible assumptions required to predict those, estimate an a priori chance for each assumption, and combine those into a total prior chance. Here are the key facts, as I see them, for a minimal aliens-on-Earth concept.

The universe looks dead, untouched by life or civilization, both far and near.

We are still alive on Earth, and have not been killed off by aliens. 

Any aliens on/near Earth haven’t changed, built, or done much noticeable.

While advanced aliens could be either totally invisible or very obvious, most seen on Earth are instead near the edge of visibility.

Most aliens seen are impressive, but not doing much useful, or helpful, or hostile.

I’d respect others who tried similarly to list the key data to be explained, and then offered their highest prior explanation of this data, even if they disagreed with mine.

Here are my best guess highest-prior assumptions (with priors) to predict these minimal aliens-on-Earth concept facts, in addition to our usual consensus cosmology:

(0.3-1) Grabby aliens model, which estimates that such aliens appear ~ once per million galaxies, at median date of now, then expand at near light speed.

(0.01-0.1) Life started at Eden, then panspermia seeded Sun’s ~10K # stellar nursery, then a ~Klyr distant Sun sibling made advanced aliens many Myr ago.

(0.01-0.1) Aliens made no-colonize rule. As siblings might break it, sent team to Earth w/ goal: persuade us to follow rule; kill us as last resort. 

(0.3-1) Team given low discretion, simple plan: domesticate Earth via be near, impressive, not too hostile, don’t show more that might give us the ick.

The total prior here is 10-5 to 10-2, mid estimate of ~3x10-4. This is higher than the typical ~10-6 prior in a murder trial, so it is high enough to take seriously.

Here are some added facts that would also need to be explained under less minimal concepts of aliens-on-Earth:

Aliens often grab humans, do stuff to them, that they notice and remember.

Alien ships often break and crash.

Alien ships often contain bio-squishy residents.

To explain these added facts, I’d add more assumptions, like:

(0.03-0.3) Alien team at Earth has somewhat escaped home control. 

(0.03-0.3) Alien tech/ability has rotted, they are now often incompetent.

(0.03-0.3) Alien made rule requiring bio-squishy forms, at least at Earth.

So I’m more skeptical of reports with these features.

items.title: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
items.subtitle: This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier.

items.articleBody:
This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open, which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4, with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too!

In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant.

This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively?

That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs.

Share

Why Muse Spark Open should take off — and why it may not

One thing we see again and again at Interconnects through our open model analysis is that Western open-weight models get astonishingly more adoption than Chinese models with the same performance-to-size footprint (even though the Chinese models usually come out first)! Muse Spark Open is landing into this environment, at the same time as when open-ended LLM agents are finally real (~GLM 5.2 capabilities and on). 

Riding off a rapid increase in performance of Chinese models, the open ecosystem has been living through an acceleration in demand. The inference providers are rapidly scaling, the open post-training economy is forming, and countless enterprises are looking to own their intelligence. Muse Spark Open’s performance falls somewhere above GLM 5.2, near DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and behind GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3. It should be squarely “good enough” to slot right into this.

For some background, from the Muse Spark Open model card on Hugging Face:

Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter open weights model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal. This open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. We recommend deploying Muse Spark Open as part of a broader AI system, with additional guardrails suited to the specific use case.

Here’s the distribution of the various Muse models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

This is included to loop back to the original model card snippet. It was shared that this open-weight model underwent additional safety training to prepare for this open release. Many observers saw this release as potentially a model that was “broken” during the safety training, as it came out after Muse Spark 1.3. 

In reality, this was much more likely a safety tune of Muse Spark 1.2, which would only be a 1 point drop on Artificial Analysis to shore up safety behaviors. When Meta released Muse Glimmer, the 30B agentic model, Alex Wang said that they were preparing to release the Muse Spark 1.2 model as open weights, which fits with the above.

If anything will hold Muse Spark Open back, it’ll be the specific license they designed for it. In summary, this custom license has pretty much all of the restrictive license behaviors we’ve seen (and criticized here) in the last few years of building with open models. They are as follows:

Users of the models in products must display “Built with Muse” on their products. Meta did this with Llama, and Kimi has tried it, but almost no one complies.

There is a revenue-gating factor, where companies that make more than $20M per month across their entire business deploying the model need a separate license with Meta. Other prominent open model providers are doing this too, in order to set up revenue share agreements for re-selling inference.

Muse Spark Open makes you agree to an acceptable use policy, which in the true “open source software” corner of the world makes this model extremely not open-source.

All of the above applies to outputs from the model as well, and derivatives, so there is legal ambiguity if you can safely use the model for synthetic data.

The license does permit using Muse Spark Open for internal research and applications.

We’re at a weird equilibrium where this license is complex and unproven in court, but many players will likely ignore it. Many, many people will build on this model from various inference providers, and Meta will only likely go after egregious violations. 

For now, licenses haven’t been the determining factor of AI adoption, but this could change in the future. This is why we think it’s an unnecessary strategic risk for labs trying to compete and regain adoption to have complex, non-standard open licenses for their models.

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber.

Is Meta a tier 1 (OpenAI/Anthropic) or tier 2 (Gemini/xAI) frontier lab?

Just a few days before Muse Spark Open, Meta unveiled their closed frontier models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full.1 On traditional benchmarks, these are very strong models only behind Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 and similar to OpenAI’s GPT-6-Astra or Google’s Gemini-4-Argon.

These major releases are coming just over a year out from Meta’s massive AI redirection, characterized by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s Personal Superintelligence post, which got a lot of criticism at the time. Meta is the only American company with frontier open and closed models. Alibaba’s Qwen has followed a similar strategy, but with a far more open-leaning approach.

The vibe checks across all of these models have been solid, but the expectations were for them to not immediately challenge the level of refinement of the most recent Anthropic and OpenAI models in real-world usage. I’m excited to try them more — time to sign up for another AI subscription.

I like this recent run of form from Meta, driving their own products and directions in the popular Muse agent, taking wins like the leading US open-weight crown when useful. Whether or not it’s financially successful, it’s a unique perspective that fits their history as a business.

It often feels like there’s a revolving door of which lab is nipping at the heels of the Anthropic-OpenAI leading duo. It’s not clear that in the long run Gemini and xAI are out of it, but those two are much more muddled in their offerings than Meta today. If you listen to Zuck and Alexandr Wang on The Cheeky Pint, they clearly had a very specific vision of a high-ownership, high-compute per researcher lab that I would expect to pay off. Many labs die due to layers of bureaucracy and misaligned incentives. Meanwhile Alex Wang has over 200 direct reports — i.e. it’s a very flat org with minimal management — and they’re releasing very consistent model and product improvements.

Leave a comment

Much of my worldview of building models is that you need the resources, the compute, the data, and the talent (all downstream of large sums of money), but organizing them is very hard. Gemini is sometimes described as a place where it’s impossible to get any work done or grow — which is embellishing the issue, as many people love it there, but there are kernels of truth to it. Layers of management easily get in the way of making a great model.

While I’m praising Meta today, the Llama failure has often been described as that sort of management going too far, with model decisions being made out of politics rather than performance. xAI is in its own lane, where it may be closer to having too much talent turnover or not enough organization to sustain great models for a long period of time.

When we look back at the last few years, all of Meta, Gemini, and xAI have produced models pretty much at the frontier of performance, but what has distinguished OpenAI and Anthropic is their consistency in maintaining frontier status. Anthropic seems the most poised and organized, with a plan and vision for how these organizations should work, and they’ve gained a lead from it. OpenAI has been more hot and cold, but manages to keep up at the frontier of deployed models while being the leader in public scientific breakthroughs (from Navier-Stokes to o1’s inference time scaling).

Here’s the state of play among the companies that this post focused on, plus Xiaomi V2.6 Pro representing the leading open-weight model overall. The ranking would be Anthropic > OpenAI > Meta ~ Gemini > xAI ~ Chinese Open Weights > U.S. Open Weights.

Share

Open questions for the AI industry

After a long time of predicting the frontier model game getting too expensive for many to keep up, we may be seeing this play out among Western models. We seem very far from “one person wins” with RSI given how close all the models are to each other, but we’re narrowing down the number of labs who can compete in the US from a much wider net with surprises, to the 5 of Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Gemini, and xAI. If Microsoft starts releasing models, as they’re posting strong scaling science results, they could join this list — given their financial backing with a hyper-scale business and direct access to OpenAI’s intellectual property for training models.

The best models we’ve seen from the “tier 3” players like Mistral, Nemotron, Reflection, Arcee, etc. have had an increasingly hard time impacting either the open or closed frontiers. These models still can get substantial adoption, enough to start growing a business, but the costs of building true frontier models are now measured in billions per major model and only huge companies can sustain that.

Despite this massive scaling in resources, the technical core of the industry still doesn’t have a high hit rate on predicting how successful a model will be in real-world usage. Yes, evaluations are a good proxy, but why do the leading labs like Anthropic go from hit models like Claude Fable 5 to total duds in Claude Opus 5 and then back to hits with Opus 5.5? There are billions of dollars to be made in predicting this accurately, and the labs are surely trying, but the models fundamentally still are largely unknowable in the long-tail.

Of all of the players left in the race, betting on Meta, Gemini, and Microsoft financially seems much easier from a long-term perspective due to their rich balance sheets. This is the “AI will take a while and OpenAI/Anthropic do not have secret sauce” perspective. After all, it’s the fastest revenue growth industry ever — competition will naturally be immense.

Currently, Meta is valued under $2T and Anthropic is approaching their barnstorming IPO at the same price. Meta seems half a step behind on the same technology, but in the long-term view these seem to be starting from almost the same point and Meta has an extremely profitable core business. One of the two valuations needs to correct massively. A fun thought experiment I’ve been pondering with friends is: What do you expect Anthropic’s public valuation to be in November of 2027? How about 2028?

Leave a comment

The longer Meta and the “competitors” to OpenAI and Anthropic stick around, the more negative valuation pressure will exist around the AI IPOs (and that’s not to say anything about pricing in safety risks). Being at the absolute frontier could be financial tumultuous, while valuable. Time will tell — we know markets can stay irrational a very long time.

1

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are presumably different pretraining runs, with Full being a larger model, but it’s not clear and this is up there with the AI industry’s traditions of horrible names. There’s a chance that “full” is just a more looped version, given all the recent news on looped architectures, but I’m not confident enough to put that hypothesis in the main text.

items.articleBody:
La Conquete, by Jose Clemente Orozco, via WikiArt.

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at Icon’s fundraising, employment in China’s solar industry, grid-scale battery reliability, Tesla’s flying roadster, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

Housekeeping items this week:

I was on MTS Live talking about robots, prefabricated construction, and other things.

I’m quoted in this Dispatch article about data center construction.

Housing and Cities

From the annals of “suspicious discontinuities,” New York City has a tax break for new projects that set aside some proportion of the units as affordable housing called “485-x.” If a project has more than 99 units, the required share of units that are “affordable” goes up, and so do the wages that need to be paid for construction workers, resulting in a very large number of projects that are exactly 99 units. [X] [Housing Wire]

DR Horton, the largest homebuilder in the US, signed an agreement to access the services of Canadian construction automation startup Promise Robotics for more than 1250 homes. Promise seems to offer some sort of AI-driven, robotic factory-based construction service. “Promise Robotics applies AI across the homebuilding production process by interpreting existing home designs, generating production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrating manufacturing, and connecting that production with site installation.” [Promise Robotics] One possible future I see for construction automation is “AI + robotics changes the logic of prefab construction and makes it more attractive,” so it’ll be interesting to see if things like this play out.

Also in construction automation news, construction 3D printing startup Icon raises a $200 million series D, at a $1.4 billion valuation. [Dealroom] This is surprising to me: I had sort of assumed things weren’t going well for the company. Though this does seem to be a “down round” — in 2022 its valuation was supposedly “approaching $ 2 billion” — I’m nevertheless adjusting my probabilities of success for Icon upward somewhat.

Some interesting data from Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies on immigrants in the US construction industry. One stat I found notable: between 2013 and 2024, the number of foreign-born workers who were construction laborers or carpenters increased massively, even as the number of native-born workers in those occupations declined. But for electricians and plumbers (licensed professions), most of the increase came from native-born workers. [Harvard JCHS]

Manufacturing

GlobalFoundries, the semiconductor manufacturer that was spun off from AMD in 2009, will operate two new fabs planned for New York, funded by $21 billion from Japan. The US government is also taking a 4% equity stake in the company. [GlobalFoundries]

ASML says it can’t currently meet customer demand for lithography machines for 2027 and 2028, and is looking for ways to increase capacity. [ASML]

Ruthless competition in China’s solar industry: employment at China’s five biggest solar manufacturers fell 21% last year, and 31% the year before. [Reuters]

The US isn’t the only country with a small number of companies that make the grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) needed for power transformers. Only two EU companies, Thyssenkrupp and Stalprodukt, make it, and as in the US they can’t make the highest quality steel. “The global leaders—the companies that make the world’s best GOES—by and large are in [South] Korea and Japan,” Alimento says. “In the U.S. and in the EU, domestic manufacturers are not capable of making that quality of GOES, because it is a heavily protected trade secret.” [IEEE Spectrum]

Thanks to ongoing memory shortages as a result of AI data center construction, smartphone shipments are down 20% year over year. [Counterpoint]

 

 
 Read more

items.title: Democratic Ads Exaggerate GOP Law’s Impact on Medicare

items.articleBody:
Democratic ads in multiple congressional races are accusing Republican candidates of “gutting Medicare,” voting for “huge cuts to Medicare” and “cheering on Trump’s attack on Medicare.” Several ads cite President Donald Trump’s major domestic policy law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But the law’s changes to Medicare are narrow in scope and affect relatively few beneficiaries.

The law could have triggered much larger cuts to Medicare, under a 2010 law that requires automatic spending reductions whenever Congress passes legislation that results in higher deficits. But Congress subsequently waived those cuts — as lawmakers of both parties have done regularly in the past. 

Recent Democratic attack ads, however, misleadingly frame the OBBBA or Republican policies as a major assault on Medicare.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a Wisconsin Republican, was “the deciding vote to gut Medicare,” claims an ad from House Majority PAC, a group working to elect Democrats to Congress. An ad aired by his Democratic challenger, Rebecca Cooke, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee similarly says he “voted to make huge cuts to Medicare and Medicaid.”

Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a Democrat running for reelection in northwestern Ohio, is airing an ad that claims her Republican challenger, Derek Merrin, will “cut your Medicare.”

The Wisconsin and Ohio ads both cite the OBBBA. 

In New York’s 3rd Congressional District, which covers part of Long Island, an ad from Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi’s campaign describes his Republican challenger, Mike LiPetri, as “ready to do Trump’s bidding, gutting Medicare.” In the same race, an ad from a Democratic-aligned outside group called Article One PAC criticizes LiPetri for “cheering on Trump’s attack on Medicare.”

The New York ads don’t include any citations for those claims. But it’s unclear what else, other than the OBBBA, they could be referencing.

The Cook Political Report rates the House races in Wisconsin and Ohio as toss ups. The New York district is rated as likely Democratic, though some news outlets continue to describe it as competitive or a race to watch, and both parties are putting millions of dollars into ads there in the closing stretch, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Medicare, which covers older adults and people with disabilities, is popular with large majorities of the public — and common fodder for often-misleading campaign ads that accuse one candidate or another of wanting to slash seniors’ benefits.

The OBBBA did include large cuts to federal healthcare spending. But the bulk of those cuts involved Medicaid, the public insurance program for people with low incomes. The law’s changes to Medicare are much narrower, and will not affect benefits or eligibility for the vast majority of enrollees. 

“These are important policies,” said Jack Hoadley, a research professor emeritus at the McCourt School of Public Policy at Georgetown. “But next to something like the Medicaid changes, they’re pretty marginal.” 

We reached out to the Cooke, Kaptur and Suozzi campaigns, as well as House Majority PAC and Article One PAC, about the basis for their claims and haven’t received a response. 

As we said, some of the ads cite the OBBBA. It’s possible these claims are also referring to the automatic cuts the law could have triggered indirectly under pay-as-you-go rules. Democratic groups airing other midterm ads in Maine and Colorado, which don’t explicitly cast the cuts to Medicare as “huge,” have cited the PAYGO rules, in part, as backup. But as we’ll explain, Congress routinely votes to ignore those rules, and similar attacks could be made against Democrats for legislation they’ve enacted in the past.

“Derek Merrin will fight to protect Medicare and Social Security benefits for the seniors who depend on them — including his own mother,” Michael Stwarka, a campaign spokesman, told us in a statement, accusing Kaptur of “fearmongering.” “Suggesting Derek would cut Medicare simply because he supports lower taxes is a desperate stretch designed to scare voters.”

The Van Orden and LiPetri campaigns did not respond to our requests for comment.

Democrats aren’t the only ones invoking the OBBBA to attack their opponents over Medicare. 

In the New Hampshire Senate race, an ad from a Trump-aligned super PAC makes the contorted claim that the Democratic candidate, Rep. Chris Pappas, voted for “devastating cuts to Medicare” — because he opposed the legislation that waived the automatic cuts that Republicans’ own law could have triggered. But Pappas opposed that legislation for other reasons, and he voted against the OBBBA in the first place. 

We’ll explain what the OBBBA actually did when it comes to Medicare, and the context surrounding the pay-as-you-go cuts it could have triggered.

OBBBA’s Changes to Medicare Are Small in Scope

Medicare covers around 70 million people, at an annual cost of about $1 trillion. The OBBBA includes a few provisions that could impact costs or eligibility for certain beneficiaries, though they make up a small subset of total enrollment. 

One provision ends Medicare eligibility for certain lawfully present immigrants who previously qualified for coverage, including refugees, asylees and people with Temporary Protected Status, though they would still be required to pay into the program through payroll taxes. (Immigrants without legal status are already barred from Medicare and other federally funded health programs.) Lawful permanent residents, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and citizens of certain Pacific Island nations are still eligible for Medicare under the law.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office projects that will result in 100,000 fewer people having health insurance, and reduce Medicare spending by $5.1 billion over 10 years.

Another provision blocks the implementation of a Biden-era rule that aimed to make it easier for low-income Medicare beneficiaries to access financial assistance through Medicaid, by streamlining enrollment in so-called Medicare Savings Programs. Those programs allow Medicare beneficiaries with low enough incomes to have their premiums and, often, out-of-pocket costs covered by Medicaid.

CBO estimates that OBBBA’s suspension of the rule will lead to 800,000 fewer Medicare beneficiaries receiving those extra subsidies, saving the government $66 billion over 10 years. Most of those savings will accrue to Medicaid, but the change is expected to reduce Medicare spending as well, because higher out-of-pocket costs will likely lead those beneficiaries to seek less care. The Biden administration, in announcing the now-suspended rule in 2023, estimated it could increase Medicare spending by $7.6 billion over five years.

The OBBBA also broadens the category of drugs that are exempt from price negotiations under Medicare. While not technically a cut — it’s expected to increase Medicare spending by $4.9 billion over a decade — beneficiaries who need certain high-cost drugs could pay higher prices than they would otherwise have as a result.

Restricting immigrant eligibility “certainly is a cut, because people are now not getting coverage from a program where they were otherwise going to,” said Jeannie Fuglesten Biniek, deputy director for the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, a health policy research organization. 

She noted this is “the first time that there has been a change to Medicare eligibility that actually took Medicare benefits away from somebody.” 

Suspending the Medicare Savings Program rule is “a little trickier,” she said. “It is likely to reduce use of Medicare services, so it does reduce Medicare spending. I think people may have different views on whether that is a cut.”

Fuglesten Biniek said those changes could have a significant impact on the people they affect. Immigrants who lose Medicare will have few other options for coverage unless they’re still working, and low-income beneficiaries may delay or forego care without financial assistance.

But she said the changes are relatively small in scope, especially compared with the bill’s changes to Medicaid. Those provisions, which include work requirements and more frequent eligibility checks, are expected to cut more than $900 billion in federal Medicaid spending over 10 years and lead to 7.5 million more people becoming uninsured, according to CBO.

“The changes to Medicaid are unprecedented. They’re enormous. I think there’s no way to deny that,” she said. “The changes to Medicare are more on the margins — but they are, I think, concentrated among particularly vulnerable beneficiaries.”

Indirect Effects of PAYGO Rules

After the OBBBA’s passage last year, some Democrats pointed to its potential indirect effects on Medicare.

Under a 2010 law called the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go (or PAYGO) Act, legislation passed by Congress is supposed to be budget-neutral. If Congress ends a year having passed legislation that, on net, will increase the deficit over five or 10 years, it’s supposed to trigger across-the-board cuts in federal spending. Some programs, including Social Security, are exempt, though Medicare is not. 

Because the OBBBA is projected to add $3.4 trillion to the deficit over 10 years, CBO estimated last year that it would trigger automatic cuts to Medicare totaling $45 billion in 2026 and more than $500 billion over a decade. Those cuts would take the form of a 4% reduction in payments to healthcare providers serving Medicare patients.

However, Congress has never allowed Statutory PAYGO cuts to actually go into effect, despite passing numerous laws that have added to the deficit since 2010, as the Congressional Research Service said in a September report. In every case, Congress either included a PAYGO exemption in the law itself, or passed subsequent legislation preventing the cuts from taking effect.

That’s what Republicans in Congress did with the OBBBA. The November 2025 law that reopened the government after a six-week shutdown also wiped out any PAYGO effects from the OBBBA. (Van Orden, the Wisconsin representative, voted for it; Merrin and LiPetri were not in Congress.)

Democratic ads may be referring to this when they tag Republicans with supporting “huge” Medicare cuts or “gutting” Medicare. But it’s something both parties have done. 

In 2021, for example, a Democratic Congress passed a COVID-19 relief package, the American Rescue Plan Act, that would have triggered $36 billion in automatic Medicare cuts in 2022 and billions more in future years.  

“Everybody seems to not worry about it,” Rep. John Yarmuth, a Kentucky Democrat then serving as House Budget Chair, told Politico at the time, referring to the strategy of passing such a bill and then counting on future legislation to avert the steep cuts it would trigger. “I don’t know, I’ve been told it’s pretty much perfunctory that we’ll get it done.”

Congress subsequently passed legislation deferring those cuts, and they never went into effect. 

GOP Ad Twists the Facts in Attacking Pappas

Democrats aren’t the only ones claiming their opponents support large Medicare cuts. 

An ad from No Going Back PAC Inc. — a group linked to Trump’s main super PAC, MAGA Inc. — uses the PAYGO cuts that could have been triggered by the OBBBA as the basis for an attack on Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democrat running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire against Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu.

“Pappas went after seniors’ healthcare too, voting to cut Medicare by $500 billion,” the ad’s narrator says. No Going Back PAC has spent more than $1.8 million on the ad since it began airing on TV and streaming platforms Oct. 7.

The claim here is convoluted, and misleading. The ad cites Pappas’ vote against the November 2025 bill that ended the government shutdown, which Democrats had brought about in an unsuccessful effort to force Republicans to extend expiring health insurance subsidies. 

As we explained above, that bill also included a provision that negated any PAYGO cuts that would have been triggered by the OBBBA’s impact on the deficit. 

But Pappas voted against the November bill for unrelated reasons, as New Hampshire Public Radio reported at the time — namely, that it did not guarantee the extension of more generous subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans. 

“Chris Pappas voted against this bill because it didn’t extend the ACA enhanced premium tax credits,” a campaign spokesperson told us. 

And, of course, Pappas voted against the OBBBA, which is what created the risk of those cuts to Medicare in the first place. In effect, Republicans are attacking Pappas for the potential consequences of their own bill. 

We reached out to the person listed in Federal Election Commission paperwork as No Going Back PAC’s treasurer, as well as to MAGA Inc., and have not received a response.

Credit card donations may be made through our “Donate” page. If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102.

items.articleBody:
Reformen, Einsparungen, finanzieller Druck: Was bedeutet das für die Rolle der Wissenschaft in den Redaktionen? Holger Wormer von der TU Dortmund kommentiert aktuelle Entwicklungen der deutschen Medienlandschaft. Er appelliert an Politik und Wissenschaft, für einen starken, unabhängigen Wissenschaftsjournalismus einzutreten.  

Während der Coronapandemie wurde viel darüber diskutiert, wie der Wissenschaftsjournalismus gestärkt werden kann. Was ist aus den Ideen geworden? 

Holger Wormer ist Professor für Wissenschaftsjournalismus an der TU Dortmund. Seine Forschungsschwerpunkte sind Qualität und Ethik in Wissenschaft und Journalismus. Er war Mitglied von drei Arbeitsgruppen der Deutschen Akademien der Wissenschaften zur Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation sowie einer der Gründer des Rhine Ruhr Centers for Science Communication Research und des mehrfach ausgezeichneten Projekts medien-doktor.de. Derzeit entwickelt er einen neuen Studiengang „Wissenschaftskommunikation & Medienkompetenz“. Foto: TU Dortmund

Während besonderer Ereignisse rückt der Wissenschaftsjournalismus immer wieder in den Fokus. Das war auch schon bei den biopolitischen Debatten Ende der 1990er so, als alle über das Klonen und Stammzellen gesprochen haben. Sogar manche Regionalzeitungen haben damals gesagt: Das ist alles so wichtig, wie stellen neue Wissenschaftsredakteur*innen ein oder gründen eigene Ressorts. Nach den Terroranschlägen vom 11. September waren politische Themen plötzlich wieder absolut dominant. Bei Fukushima stellte man dann wieder fest, dass die wissenschaftliche Expertise nicht in allen Redaktionen so ausgeprägt ist, wie sie sein sollte.

In der Pandemie keimte erneut ein bisschen Hoffnung, dass langfristige Strukturen entstehen, wie sie die Wissenschaftspressekonferenz (WPK) schon seit Jahren fordert: eine engere Zusammenarbeit innerhalb der Medienhäuser zwischen Wissenschaftsredaktionen und Ressorts wie Politik und Wirtschaft. Im Zuge aktueller Sparmaßnahmen aber hat man den Eindruck, dass sich wieder jedes Ressort selbst das Nächste ist. Noch dazu haben Chefredaktionen normalerweise wenig, manchmal gar keine Ahnung von Wissenschaft. Sie unterschätzen dessen Bedeutung für politische Entscheidungen und das Interesse von Nutzer*innen.

Im Juni hat die Chefredaktion von „ARD-aktuell“ angekündigt, das Ressort Wissen der „tagesschau“ zu kürzen. Welche Folgen wird das haben?

Bei ARD-aktuell hieß es nach der Pandemie: Wir haben dazugelernt und stellen deshalb in der Redaktion zentrale Ansprechpartner*innen für Wissenschaft zur Verfügung. Das ist bei einer Anstalt wie der ARD besonders wichtig. Denn man kann noch so gute Wissenschaftsredaktionen über verschiedene Sendeanstalten im Land verstreut haben: Wenn diese Themen nicht in den zentralen Redaktionskonferenzen bei ARD-aktuell vor Ort vertreten sind und kompetent diskutiert werden, setzen sich diese Themen oft nicht durch. Dann setzen sich vor allem die Themen aus Politik, Ausland, Wirtschaft oder vielleicht Kultur durch. Es ist daher gravierend, erst zu sagen: „Wir haben aus der Pandemie gelernt“, – und genau diese Neuerungen dann handstreichartig wieder abzuschaffen. Aber daran sieht man: Der öffentlich-rechtliche Rundfunk ist finanziell unter Druck. Bestimmte Ressorts und Themen stehen in der internen Hierarchie traditionell quasi unter Naturschutz, also schafft man die kleinsten und in diesem Fall jüngsten ab, die sich am wenigsten wehren können.

Thesen zur Zukunft des Wissenschaftsjournalismus

Anlässlich ihres 40. Geburtstags hat die Wissenschaftspressekonferenz (WPK), der größte deutsche Berufsverband für Wissenschaftsjournalist*innen, 20 Thesen für die Zukunft des Feldes veröffentlicht. Schon seit der Gründung im Jahr sei deutlich gewesen, dass Wissenschaftsjournalismus eine politische Bedeutung habe – sei es 1986 mit der AIDS-Krise, Tschernobyl, den globalen Treibhausgasbilanzen oder dem Ozonloch. In der Erklärung heißt es, der Wissenschaftsjournalismus sei „so viel mehr als „Erklärbar“ und Evidenzvermittler: Er hat eine wichtige Kontrollfunktion für das Wissenschaftssystem, für Machtdynamiken und Finanzierungslogiken, er ist Impulsgeber und Dialogpartner in ganz verschiedene Richtungen.“
 
In einem Dialogprozess mit verschiedenen Akteur*innen aus dem Bereich des Wissenschaftsjournalismus wurden die Thesen entwickelt und bei der Konferenz Wissenswerte vorgestellt und diskutiert. Es geht darin unter anderem um die Wächterfunktion in der Demokratie, um den Stellenwert von Wissenschaftsfreiheit und Pressefreiheit, den Platz der Wissenschaft in den Redaktionen, die Stärkung sozial- und geisteswissenschaftlicher Themen sowie einer Schutzpflicht gegenüber Forschenden. https://wpk.org/blog/thesen-zur-zukunft-des-wissenschaftsjournalismus/

Neben der Wissenschaftsredaktion von ARD-aktuell gibt es viele andere Wissenschaftsangebote von ARD und ZDF, zum Beispiel Funk-Formate wie MrWissen2go. Wie signifikant sind die Veränderungen bei ARD-aktuell für die gesamte ARD?

Diese Formate sind wichtig und richtig, viele spezielle Wissenschaftsmagazine sind aber bereits jetzt im linearen Fernsehen verstärkt auf Randzeiten verschoben oder ganz eingestellt worden. Daher ist es wichtig, dass Themen aus den Wissenschaften auf einer Nachrichtenseite mit großer Reichweite wie der tagesschau schnell und einfach zu finden sind. Damit gelangen die Wissenschaften in den Alltag der User*innen, ohne dass sie lange auf Social Media-Plattformen gesucht werden müssen. Auch bedeutet weniger Wissenschafts-Content bei ARD-aktuell z.B. weniger Verlinkungsmöglichkeiten auf weiterführende Angebote wie Dokus, Podcasts oder Social Media-Angebote.

Wie beurteilen Sie die Veränderungen im Rahmen der Programmreform beim Deutschlandfunk1?

Man könnte argumentieren, dass dort an vielen Stellen Reformen sinnvoll wären, etwa eine stärkere Adressierung auch jüngerer oder bildungsfernerer Zielgruppen. Man darf aber auf der anderen Seite nicht unterschätzen, dass solche Leuchttürme des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks als Leitmedien dazu da sind, Basis-Informationen und Anregungen zum Beispiel für Lokal- und Regionalmedien zu liefern. Es ist wichtig, dass die Wissenschaft in der aktuellen Berichterstattung auch auf eigenen, festen Sendeplätzen vorkommt und nicht nur einmal im Jahr in der Hauptnachrichtensendung, wenn mal ein Nobelpreis nach Deutschland geht. Die Journalist*innen, die darüber kompetent berichten, machen das zudem nicht aus dem Stegreif, sondern beschäftigen sich kontinuierlich damit und sind dabei auf regelmäßige Sendeplätze angewiesen.

„Es ist geradezu rätselhaft, wie in einer Welt, die so stark von wissenschaftlichen Fragen geprägt ist – wie bei KI, Umwelt, Klima, Energie oder Gesundheit – nach wie vor die politische Berichterstattung einen so viel höheren Stellenwert hat.“

Holger Wormer

Es ist geradezu rätselhaft, wie in einer Welt, die so stark von wissenschaftlichen Fragen geprägt ist – wie bei KI, Umwelt, Klima, Energie oder Gesundheit – nach wie vor die politische Berichterstattung einen so viel höheren Stellenwert hat. Die Aussagen von Politiker*innen werden über Social Media sowieso in die digitale Welt gespült. Es gehört zu den Thesen der WPK, dass Wissenschaftsjournalist*innen dann aber mit Hilfe von wissenschaftlicher Expertise prüfen sollen, was an solchen Aussagen eigentlich dran ist.

Wissenschaft steckt in vielen Themen. Ist es trotzdem die richtige Strategie, Kompetenzen in spezifischen Wissenschaftsressorts zu bündeln, statt sie zu streuen?

Beides ist notwendig. Es braucht Wissenschaftsjournalist*innen in den zentralen Redaktionen, aber auch kompetente Personen, die von einer festen Basis aus ausschwärmen können. Der Wissenschaftsjournalismus muss sich bewegen und schauen: Was sind große Themen und politische Debatten, in denen Wissenschaft eine Rolle spielt? Wir brauchen Leute, die rausgehen und über Aktuelles berichten, aber es braucht auch die kontinuierliche Berichterstattung über Wissenschaft mit festen Sendeplätzen und Personen, die langfristig Themen verfolgen können.

Wie sehen die Entwicklungen in der Zeitungslandschaft aus? 

Fairerweise muss man sagen, dass wir in Deutschland von einem sehr hohen Niveau gekommen sind. Wir hatten eine breite, starke Regionalzeitungslandschaft, die sich inzwischen immer stärker konzentriert hat. Inzwischen stehen die Zeitungen in vielen Fällen mit dem Rücken zur Wand, weil wir zugelassen haben, dass die großen Tech-Plattformen den Werbemarkt zu größten Teilen abgreifen. Vor 25 Jahren haben Zeitungen ungefähr zwei Drittel ihrer Einkünfte über Anzeigen generiert, das ist längt vorbei. Die Abo-Preise wurden erhöht, aber die Menschen sind immer weniger bereit, Geld dafür zu zahlen, auch weil es so viele vermeintlich kostenlose Angebote gibt, für die man im Zweifelsfall „nur“ mit seinen Daten bezahlt. Die Verlage können sich qualitativ hochwertigen Journalismus immer weniger leisten. Wissenschaftsjournalismus ist nicht das Billigste, weil die Recherche aufwändig ist, Journalist*innen auch mal auf eine Konferenz fahren und für viele Fachartikel bezahlen müssen.

„Die privat finanzierten Online- und Printmedien können das Problem nicht allein lösen. Es braucht es eine massive Regulierung der Monopole der Tech-Plattformen durch die Politik.“ 

Holger Wormer 

Gibt es Möglichkeiten, aus dieser finanziellen Krise herauszukommen?

Die privat finanzierten Online- und Printmedien können das Problem nicht allein lösen. Es braucht es eine massive Regulierung der Monopole der Tech-Plattformen durch die Politik. Und es ist finanzielle Unterstützung notwendig, die natürlich staatsfern sein muss. Es sollten keine Steuern vom Staat eingetrieben werden, sondern zum Beispiel Beiträge, ähnlich wie beim öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunk. Wir haben am Institut für Journalistik zusammen mit einem Kollegen aus der Medienökonomie vor wenigen Jahren einen weiteren Vorschlag für ein Finanzierungsmodell gemacht, das ähnlich funktioniert wie im Wissenschaftsbereich. Wir haben uns angeschaut, wie sich die Strukturen der Deutschen Forschungsgemeinschaft, auf eine „Deutsche Journalismusgemeinschaft“ übertragen ließen. Die DFG bekommt Milliarden direkt aus der Politik zugewiesen und trotzdem haben die meisten den Eindruck, dass das keine gigantischen Abhängigkeiten schafft, sondern dass man in der Lage ist, Geld gut nach wissenschaftlichen Kriterien zu verteilen. Ähnlich könnte die Finanzierung aus dem Journalismus heraus organisiert werden, vielleicht mit Intermediären wie Stiftungen. Anders wird es nicht gehen, wenn wir in zehn Jahren noch die Qualität im Journalismus haben wollen, die es an vielen Stellen noch gibt.

Die aktuellen Rundfunkbeiträge werden aus verschiedenen Richtungen massiv kritisiert und in Frage gestellt. Wie kann es in einem solchen Klima gelingen, zusätzlich Gebühren für Print- und Online-Journalismus einzuführen?

Das sind Debatten, die gezielt geschürt werden. Der Einfluss von den Tech-Plattformen ist – im Schulterschluss mit Populist*innen – so groß, dass solche Narrative weit verbreitet werden. Zudem haben wir bisher zu wenig erklärt, warum Journalismus notwendig ist, während das beim Straßenbau jede*r irgendwie einsieht.

Natürlich ist es vor diesem Hintergrund schwierig, solche Ideen durchzusetzen, aber je länger wir warten, desto schwieriger wird es. Dann kommen wir gegen die Meinungsmacht von Medienmonopolisten und einer populistischen, ultranationalistischen Bewegung nicht mehr an. Der Journalismus wird das erste Opfer sein, aber die Wissenschaft wird das genauso spüren. Und ohne mutige Vorschläge aus der Medienpolitik wird es nicht gehen. Jenseits dessen muss auch die Politik erkennen, dass unabhängige Medien und Informationskanäle genauso Teil der berühmten kritischen Infrastruktur sind wie intakte Straßen, Brücken, Krankenhäuser und Stromleitungen.

„Ohne mutige Vorschläge aus der Medienpolitik wird es nicht gehen. Jenseits dessen muss auch die Politik erkennen, dass unabhängige Medien und Informationskanäle genauso Teil der berühmten kritischen Infrastruktur sind wie intakte Straßen, Brücken, Krankenhäuser und Stromleitungen.“

Holger Wormer

Wie beurteilen Sie die Rolle der Wissenschaft in den aktuellen Entwicklungen?

Ich bin entsetzt darüber, dass viel zu wenig zur Situation des Journalismus aus der Wissenschaft kommt. Es gibt aus der Journalismusforschung und nun auch ein paar Stimmen im Kontext der WPK-Thesen, die deutlich gemacht haben, dass die Wissenschaft sich für ein intaktes Mediensystem einsetzen muss. Aber vor dem Hintergrund von Wettbewerb und knapper werdender eigener Mittel ist die Wissenschaft als Ganzes aus meiner Sicht erstaunlich still. Es ist abzusehen, dass hier einer von zwei „unverzichtbaren Eckpfeilern einer demokratischen Gesellschaft“, wie wir das in einem Papier der Akademie der Wissenschaften mal genannt haben, massiv beschädigt wird. Da müssten die Wissenschaftsorganisationen lauter werden. Stattdessen guckt man meist vor allem, dass die eigene Einrichtung besonders gut dasteht.

Auch mit Verweis auf abnehmende Ressourcen des Wissenschaftsjournalismus bauen wissenschaftliche Einrichtungen ihre eigene Öffentlichkeitsarbeit aus und versuchen, Zielgruppen direkt zu erreichen – sei es über Social Media oder eigene Magazine. Ist das die richtige Strategie? 

Das ist sicher nicht der effizienteste Weg – zumindest nicht, wenn jedes Institut für sich selbst um Aufmerksamkeit buhlt. Die Idee, selbst Aufmerksamkeit mit großer Reichweite aufbauen zu wollen, halte ich aus ökonomischer Perspektive für Unsinn2 . In den Gesamtmarkt muss man für hohe mediale Aufmerksamkeit so viel investieren, dass man das als kleinere Institution kaum schaffen kann. Es gibt erfolgreiche Ausnahmen, aber es ist illusorisch zu glauben, dass das Wissenschaftssystem das professionelle Mediensystem mal eben so mit bedienen und ersetzen kann. Es wäre mein Appell an die Wissenschaft, zu sagen: Wir brauchen Ansprechpartner*innen in den Redaktionen. Wir brauchen Journalismus, der nicht die Partikularinteressen einer Institution vertritt, sondern für die Vielschichtigkeit der Wissenschaft steht und als kritischer Beobachter von außen auftritt.

„Im Wissenschaftsjournalismus arbeiten Menschen, die im Regelfall Wissenschaft gut finden. Die sind nicht deshalb böse, weil sie mal jemanden vors Schienbein treten.“

Holger Wormer

Wenn Wissenschaftseinrichtungen wirklich – zumindest in Teilen – ersetzen wollten, was im Journalismus wegbricht, reicht es zudem nicht aus, das eigene Forschungsergebnis zu anzuteasern, sondern man müsste sagen: Was bedeutet dieses Ergebnis, was haben konkurrierende Einrichtungen dazu herausgefunden? Ich muss dann auch widersprüchliche Ergebnisse anderer erwähnen. Wenn man Journalismus ersetzen will, muss man auch journalistische – und im Übrigen wissenschaftliche – Standards einhalten. Sonst ist das keine redliche Wissenschaftskommunikation, sondern blanke PR.

Ist es aus Sicht der Presse- und Öffentlichkeitsarbeit nicht auch von Vorteil, die eigene Message direkt kommunizieren zu können – ohne den „Umweg“ über den Journalismus?

Ich denke, dass man sich von der Vorstellung trennen muss, unbegrenzten Einfluss auf das zu haben, was veröffentlicht wird. Das ist der Preis der Unabhängigkeit. Wenn es Fremdbeobachter*innen gibt, die kompetent und gut ausgebildet sind, dann muss ich Einfluss abgeben. Wie in anderen Bereichen blickt auch die Wissenschaft in Teilen abfällig auf den Journalismus, weil man vielleicht mal schlechte Erfahrungen gemacht hat. 

In unserer Qualitätsforschung3 sehen wir tatsächlich immer wieder: Dieser oder jene Beitrag war jetzt nicht so gut. Aber wenn daraus resultiert, dass sich Akteure aus der Wissenschaft am Bashing eines ganzen Feldes beteiligen, schießt man sich ins eigene Knie. Im Wissenschaftsjournalismus arbeiten Menschen, die im Regelfall Wissenschaft gut finden. Die sind nicht deshalb böse, weil sie mal jemanden vors Schienbein treten. Auf dieser Basis kann man ein bisschen vertrauensvoller miteinander umgehen. An vielen Stellen gibt es bereits Kooperationen zwischen Wissenschafts-PR, Forschenden und Journalismus. Es wäre toll, wenn wir das ausbauen können, ohne die gegenseitige Unabhängigkeit zu gefährden.

items.articleBody:
Cover image by Gerd Altmann from Pixabay

By Megan Sumeracki

As a learning expert, I (Megan) still get asked about learning styles all the time. Recently I was chatting with a colleague and was excited to tell her that I’m getting through so many more books now that I’ve fully embraced audio books. She smiled at me and said, I think somewhat nervously, remind me again why learning styles isn’t a thing?

I get it! Learning styles is so tricky because it feels like it is real. In some ways it is—we have learning preferences. There IS more than one way to learn. It’s just that matching those preferences is not needed to maximize learning, and combining the various ways to learn helps everyone.

In this digest, a round-up of Learning Scientists resources and resources by others all about the myth of learning styles and the harm it can do to embrace this myth.

Learning Styles: A Misguided Attempt to Highlight Individual Differences in Learners by Carolina Kuepper-Tetzel

One of our early and most popular posts on learning styles, individual differences, and the individual differences that we should probably pay more attention to.

Dual Coding and Learning Styles by Megan Sumeracki

A post highlighting the similarities, and importantly the differences, between dual coding (evidence-based) and the learning styles matching hypothesis (myth)

Learning Styles vs Dual Coding: A Battle of Two Theories, a video by Doug Neill (Verbal to Visual)

This video is fantastic, I think. They cover a paper by Cuevas and Dawson (2018) that pits learning styles and dual coding against one another. 

If you want other resources covering the Cuevas and Dawson (2018) paper, you can check out this Learning Scientists Blog post written by Megan Sumeracki, and this episode on the Learning Scientists Podcast.

Catering to Learning Styles Isn't Just Ineffective: It Can Harm Learning by Cindy Nebel

Another post of ours covering learning styles and the harm that perpetuating this myth can do. You can also check out this Learning Scientists Blog post written by Carolina Kuepper-Tetzel on the potential harm of the learning styles myth.

How do Learning Styles Affect Learning Predictions? by Megan Sumeracki

Spoiler alert: learning styles can cause problems!

We’ve talked about learning styles again and again and again. I’m sure at least some of you are getting sick of talking about it. I can’t wait until every learner and educator is so sick of hearing about it that learning styles is no more. I mean, surely we’re done debunking this myth, right? I wish that were the case. But I get asked about this regularly in my classes and still see things pushing the myth online.

If you’re NOT sick of this topic, and you’ve read this far and still want more, below are some older digests related to this topic:

Weekly Digest #9: How to Talk About Learning Styles (this one is from 2016, when The Learning Scientists Blog was only a few months old!)

Weekly Digest #124: Pesky Learning Myths

Click here to search all Learning Scientists Blog posts tagged “Learning Syles”

items.articleBody:
Vibe-coded plugins are everywhere but does that mean that they’re actually taking over the market? We look at the trend and speak with two developers working with AI as part of their process.

The age of vibe-coded plugins is undeniably upon us. They’re everywhere: blocky, dark and uniform instruments and effects that all tend to look the same, with large knobs and small print. Made with the help of artificial intelligence, these plugins are clogging up the marketplace, filling email inboxes with marketing hyperbole and vying for your hard-earned dollar, pound or Euro. But is anyone actually buying them?

Plugin Slop

Thanks to the availability of AI agents, it’s easier than ever to churn out software, even if you don’t know how to code. While this seems cool on paper – “I can make any plugin I can imagine!” – the reality is less exciting, with cookie-cutter compressors, clippers and bog-standard VA synths piling up in the forums. 

A recent article in Futurism called “The Economy Has Spoken: Stuff That’s AI-Generated Has Almost Zero Value” points out that products made by AI are extremely unpopular. It mentions CGTrader, an online marketplace for 3D assets used by video game developers, film editors and 3D-printing fans. One in six models on the site now are AI-generated, but they account for only $1 out of every $90 in revenue, according to the story.

“The upload numbers alone would suggest a takeover,” the article continues. “The revenue numbers say otherwise, and buyers refusing to pay for AI-generated models is saying something bigger than no thanks: it is a signal of how far they trust AI generation itself.”

This is about 3D models, but AI-generated music - which is closer to home for Attack readers - tells a similar story. Although it accounts for about half of daily uploads to streaming sites like Deezer, listenership remains around 1% to 3%. And, although we don’t have numbers for paid downloads of vibe-coded plugins, general online reaction to AI-built plugins would indicate a similar reaction.

[quote align=right text="The Economy Has Spoken: Stuff That’s AI-Generated Has Almost Zero Value"]

Support and Reliability Are Real Concerns

Beyond the bland GUIs and uninspiring sound of slop plugins, however, lie real causes for concern. Bedroom Producer’s Blog, a site that regularly covers freeware, is on the frontline of the slopification of music production. In a recent article, site editor Tomislav Zlatic points out the danger in the distance in coding know-how between the AI agent and the prompter: “Vibe coding hands you a wall of code that whoever ‘made’ the plugin probably can’t read, much less debug. A badly coded plugin can destroy your work on a project, or, even worse, it can cause loud bursts of noise that damage your hearing.”

Being able to trust the plugin was the biggest concern expressed when we asked for people’s opinions about vibe-coded plugins on social media. “I see it like modding a video game,” said musician Mike Jones. “Could give novel functionality, but I would not trust it to always work.” 

Andrew Booth, who creates software for internal use as part of his job, says similarly, “I’d feel nervous about fully vibe coded stuff since there might be aspects of how it works, how it interacts with other stuff, how it performs that you haven’t really specced and tested completely enough.” 

Bob Rogue of Black Corporation sums it up when he writes, “Try, for sure. Buy, I’d be reluctant without knowing what the support system is like.”

Våld Labs and AI Assistance

Not every plugin made with AI came out of this vibe-coding black box. Some are built by a human coding alongside AI. Jaime Paiva makes plugins and hardware under the name Våld Labs. His recent soft synth, Tresse, combines the open-source code from Mutable Instruments’ Plaits with original synth engines. And he made it with the help of an AI agent.

“Våld Labs is a one-person operation,” says Jaime, who balances his development projects while also working a full-time job. “Without AI agents it would not be realistic to build instruments of this scope, across hardware, DSP, desktop and iOS, while also doing the design, testing, documentation and release myself. AI gives me some of the leverage of a small team without turning the project into design by committee.”

Unlike with obviously vibe-coded plugins, reaction to Tresse has been largely positive (“People are far more interested in what the instrument does and how it sounds than in what was in the toolchain”). Jaime employed AI to do some software engineering like debugging and other repetitive work. However, he does still code. “Sometimes writing the thing directly is faster than explaining it, waiting and then checking what came back,” he explains. “To do that at all you need to be able to read the code, understand what it is doing and know what you are changing. AI is a tool in the workflow, not the workflow itself.”

When asked if he considers Tresse to have been vibe coded, he answers in the negative. “Vibe coding, as I understand it, is describing a result to an AI without engaging with how it is implemented, and then iterating through subjective instructions: ‘make it fatter,’ ‘I don't like this.’ The code is a black box you talk at.”

Tresse was AI-assisted from end to end, but, he asserts, it was “the opposite of a black box. I had to design around everything that did not exist in Plaits. Then I developed the custom engines. I defined how the parameters behaved, tested the DSP and made the musical decisions about what stayed and what didn't. AI got me through parts of that enormously faster. It didn't decide what Tresse should be.”

The Promise of Vibe Coding: Something No One Else Has

When the idea of vibe coding first started getting talked about a few years ago, being able to build something no one else had felt very exciting. Mass-market instruments and effects require not only a lot of time and effort but also a large enough market to buy them and recoup that effort. With vibe coding, the promise went, you could make whatever suited your individual needs without having to consider a wider customer base.

Enter Artists in DSP’s Amorph, a plugin that lets you vibe code instruments and audio effects inside a DAW. “You describe an instrument or an effect, Amorph writes it and compiles it in your DAW, on the track you have open, and you play it,” explains Leonardo Biasca-Caroni, the co-founder and CEO of Artists in DSP. “If it’s wrong, you say what to change and it compiles again. After that a new idea is a patch inside that, not another plugin.” If you like what you’ve made, you can also share it for other users to try.

“The example I keep coming back to is Modular Town by Bungle Society,” says Leonardo, by way of explaining what’s possible with Amorph. “He spent roughly four months developing a hand-drawn town containing a semi-modular synth, delay, reverb, sequenced bass and drum machine. The buildings have musical roles and modulation is patched by connecting different parts of the town. The concept grew from his desire to make an instrument that felt like a place rather than a conventional control panel.”

Not everyone, of course, is on board with Amorph. “Some musicians are against anything with AI in it, and they won’t try it whatever we say,” says Leonardo. “A lot of that comes from AI being sold as something that makes the music for you. I understand that. Amorph doesn’t generate music. It generates the instrument. What comes out is your playing.”

Ultimately, Leonardo sees Amoprh as existing alongside plugins from established developers, not as a replacement. “I don’t see prompt-built tools competing with a well-made plugin from a specialist,” he says. “If a finished plugin does the job, buy it. Amorph is for the thing nobody sells, or the thing you want to keep changing.”

Do We Need to Redefine Vibe Coding?

Although it’s easy in theory to dismiss any software made with the help of AI, in reality it may not be that simple, if just because AI is more prevalent in plugins than we may have realized. “It’ll start to be unlikely that you’ll find people making software that has zero AI assistance,” says commenter Andrew in our online poll. “It’s just too useful at finding bugs, filling out some boilerplate or other assistance, even for a coder who’s fully capable of doing everything by hand.”

It may be helpful, then, to redefine what exactly vibe coding means. Does it apply to any AI assistance at all, or rather for software that came out of an AI black box? “Vibe coding for me is more towards the end where AI does most or all of the coding for you – and the result is something that you definitely couldn’t have done yourself and potentially don’t even understand,” writes Andrew.

Jaime of Våld Labs agrees that not all AI usage is the same. “AI is imperfect, and there are legitimate concerns about how it is used,” he says. “But treating every use of AI in creative or technical work as the same thing misses something: a lot of people can now execute ideas that would previously have needed far more money, time or people. Some of those ideas might be genuinely good.”

No matter how we parse it, however, if we keep getting inundated with bad products, the entire industry will suffer. “The problem remains,” sums up Leonardo of Artists In DSP. “If the (developer) doesn’t take the time to get it right, or doesn’t have the skills and the taste to make something that is useful and works well, the plugin will be bad. It was the same when the DAW made recording cheap: a lot more music, most of it not great, and also records that would never have been made otherwise. If the artist has the skills and the taste and stays with it, the plugin can be as good as they are.”

[quote align=right text="AI is imperfect, and there are legitimate concerns about how it is used"]

Some Things to Keep in Mind

We're not saying all plugins created with the help of AI are automatically bad. As we've explored here, there are developers working with AI who are doing good work. But there are some things to keep in mind when purchasing or downloading AI-assisted or AI-made plugins – and going forward, it seems like they will be ever more common.

Do your due diligence. Just like you wouldn't download a dodgy-looking piece of software to your computer for fear of malware, keep security in your mind when choosing plugins. Security issues could be as innocuous (but no less annoying) as instability that leads to crashes, or as frightening as exploitable code that bad actors can take advantage of to deliver malware into your system.

Additionally, are these plugin developers really in it for the long haul? Operating systems are updated nearly constantly. Are they going to keep up with Apple's relentless pace of a new OS every year? When the iPhone first dropped, there was a wealth of music-making apps available. Within a few years, though, most of these were unusable because the people on the other side of the code stopped updating them. Today's vibe-coded plugins could very well be tomorrow's abandonware.

Lastly, CPU optimization is an important thing for DAW-based musicians. The plugin may promise the moon but unless it can deliver that space rock without also taking down your computer in the process, it's basically useless. Only buy vibe-coded plugins with a demo that you can try first.

It's a brave new world out there, and not necessarily one that most of us want. Things will probably shake out to some semblance of normalcy within a few years. Until then, use your best judgment, don't fall for marketing hype, and if it seems shady, it's best to stay away.

items.articleBody:
The European Union has removed Panama from its tax haven “blacklist” in a move acknowledging corporate and tax transparency reforms made by a country infamously synonymous with offshore financial secrecy.

The update to the EU’s list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes was made by EU Finance Ministers last week, and comes a decade after Panama dealt with the fallout from the Panama Papers, an investigation led by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung into 11.5 million financial and legal records. The investigation exposed how a single Panama-based law firm registered 214,000 shell companies in over 200 countries, enabling companies and people to hide wealth and transactions.

“The Panama Papers revelations exposed weaknesses in the global financial system, with a particular focus on Panama and the lax regulations regarding transparency that were in place there at the time,” said Luis Moreno, an economist with the Global Alliance for Tax Justice and International Taxation Director at Latindadd.

“After the Panama Papers, Panama addressed various recommendations — including those from the OECD regarding tax transparency — which is precisely why it has now been removed from the ‘blacklist,'” Moreno added.

items.articleBody:
Der Einsatz von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) im Migrationskontext ist nicht neu: Seit zehn Jahren setzt das Bundesamt für Migration und Flüchtlinge (BAMF) bereits KI-Technologien ein. Doch nun will die Bundesregierung mit einem neuen Gesetzentwurf die Automatisierung im Migrationsbereich pauschal erweitern. Auf der Suche nach effizienteren Verwaltungsprozessen ignoriert das Gesetz zum Einsatz Künstlicher Intelligenz in der Migrationsverwaltung (KIMVG) die nötigen Voraussetzungen für eine faire Anwendung von KI‑Systemen. Statt klare Grenzen für den Einsatzkontext und konkrete Angaben für die technischen Voraussetzungen zu formulieren, setzt der Entwurf auf einen weiten Spielraum. Eklatante Risiken, insbesondere die drohenden Einschränkungen bei fairen Verfahren für Menschen, die Asyl oder Visa beantragen, werden in Kauf genommen oder nicht ausreichend adressiert.

AlgorithmWatch empfiehlt deshalb:

Änderungen an § 7 AsylG und § 86 AufenthG streichen: Keine KI-Entwicklung anhand von personenbezogenen Daten von Menschen aus dem Migrationsbereich

Die Weitergabe von personenbezogenen Daten an Dritte ausschließen

Effektive Maßnahmen gegen diskriminierende Algorithmen definieren

Transparenz und Nachvollziehbarkeit für Betroffene und Öffentlichkeit herstellen
